In complex environments, accurately estimating object pose poses significant challenges. Estimating the 3D structure of an entire object can be computationally demanding due to its variability. A simpler approach involves focusing on distinguishing parts of the object. This paper takes a different approach, leveraging the geometry of an object's surface to partition regions with similar 3D properties, known as projection grouping. This technique aids in scene analysis by identifying the object's boundary, enhancing the object's representation, and estimating its pose. Our research demonstrates two primary applications of projection grouping to successfully estimate scene object pose. We use the same principle to replace supervised 2D cues, achieving a more efficient and effective representation of the 2D image. Furthermore, we demonstrate that projection grouping enhances pose estimation when combined with depth maps. Notably, this approach leads to significant improvements in scene object pose estimation.

In this theoretical study, we use renormalization group analysis to examine how changes in peridynamic kernel microstructure affect the ability to anticipate fracture formation. Through analysis, we derive a scale equation that governs the short-range scaling behavior of stiff materials within peridynamics, involving the material's characteristic length scale. Also, we offer additional arguments to validate that complexifications in peridynamic theory lead to fracture formation. As a result, the theoretical framework enables investigation of the short-range scaling properties of materials within peridynamics prior to failure. Consequently, Peridynamics theory predicts a fixed scale rate of dilation, affecting the scaling of the critical tip energy density.

A new Graphical Lasso framework is proposed, encompassing latent variables to efficiently evaluate their impact on a pair of observed variables and effectively select related features. This framework is flexible and can be used to build a core model for a new variant of the Sparse Bayesian Learning framework for inferring topic models. Analytical results are provided to swiftly estimate the number of relevant topics as well as the sparsity of words within each topic. This approach yields a solution that balances multiple objectives, including a multi-nomial likelihood, sparse loading, and word entropy. Results from initial experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets are presented, including an analysis of topic discovery in a dictionary dataset.

To evaluate and predict biomolecular properties with molecular dynamics simulations, simulations must be run for extended periods, which is computationally costly. Enhancing simulations with custom reactive force fields like AMBER has the potential to significantly reduce the computational cost per simulation second and increase data point capacity. Yet, the effectiveness of these improvements relies crucially on the underlying force field's accuracy. In this study, molecular dynamics simulations utilizing the AMBER and CHARMM force fields for the alanine dipeptide model are compared to experimental evidence and previous simulations for various simulation lengths using the NPT ensemble and temperatures of 300K and 297.6K. Although the new barostat over-delivered in terms of computational efficiency, notable discrepancies in population distributions persisted between the AMBER and CHARMM simulations, albeit to a lesser degree than found in previous studies with other force fields. To mitigate this disparity, we adjusted the mass of the non-water atoms in the AMBER simulations, which yielded population distributions in closer agreement with both experimental data and CHARMM simulations within 1 standard deviation. Alternatively, we employed an empirical correction to yield population distributions within 2 standard deviations of both experiments and CHARMM simulations. These findings suggest that when employing the new barostat with force fields of the same quality, AMBER may be adjustable to produce results that are both computationally efficient and biologically accurate.

This paper explores the dynamics of binary black holes moving through a gaseous environment using a novel approach that combines gravitational forces with fluid resistance. The energy loss caused to the binary black hole system is modeled via the gravitational wave radiation formula, while the momentum it imparts to the surrounding matter is accounted for. Simulations reveal that binary black hole orbits are significantly influenced by the initial distribution of the surrounding gas, which in case of a uniform setup leads to the formation of a shockwave. BHLGR's findings demonstrate that binary black hole orbits can take various forms, from irregular paths to entangled configurations, and that their movement is highly dependent on initial conditions. The research also highlights that binary black hole gravitational waves can stimulate significant fluctuations in the gas density, which could potentially be detected by future gravitational wave observatories and nonlinear gravitational wave probes. Additionally, the presence of binary black holes causes nonlinear gravitational waves to spread throughout the gas, which could provide a new avenue for exploring these phenomena. The implications of this research could be relevant to a variety of astrophysical events, including the movements of supermassive black hole binaries within their surroundings.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a system on a star-shaped graph whose shape changes periodically over time. Given that the elasticity on the graph's ends is infinite, we demonstrate that the system achieves rapid convergence to equilibrium; however, varying elasticity along the graph's center line can disrupt this stability, leading to only slow convergence and a shift from exponential to polynomial decay.

This research explores the characteristics of two commonly used acoustic materials, specifically PMMA and Stycast 1090SI. By analyzing the effects of temperature, frequency, and thickness on their acoustic properties, we found that both materials exhibit notable changes in impedance and attenuation with increasing temperature. The Stycast 1090SI composite demonstrated a greater tendency for frequency dependence in its acoustic behavior. Our study also identified the effects of thickness on attenuation, with an inverse relationship observed. The results obtained from Stycast 1090SI align reasonably well with the manufacturer's specifications, whereas the results from PMMA demonstrated a distinct deviation from expected outcomes, with higher than anticipated impedance and lower than expected attenuation.

The analysis of connectivity within individual layers and its connectivity across multiple layers in a single system has gained significant attention. However, most existing studies fail to account for the additional information present in inter-layer connections when calculating node centrality. To bridge this gap, we propose a new multilayer network model featuring distinct intra-layer and inter-layer connections. To calculate a meaningful centrality index that reflects the relative importance of each node, we develop a multilayer betweenness centrality calculation method based on this model. This calculation is facilitated by an efficient algorithm. To demonstrate the validity and performance of both the method and algorithm, we present single and multi-layer network examples as well as a real-world multilayer air transport network. Results from the multilayer network analysis show that nodes with high centrality values tend to cluster within connectivity communities. Additionally, the computation time for nodes with high centrality values aligns with the structure of the network. By comparing our results to established centrality indices, we demonstrate the uniqueness of the method. Ultimately, our study highlights the necessity of considering inter-layer connections during centrality calculations, as these connections provide crucial information about the overall network structure.

This research formulates the problem of color-dependent point spread functions
in computational photography as a linear inverse problem, where the unknown variables
represent the scene's properties, and observation errors result in color channels
being decoupled. Decoupling channel data imposes a severe regularization constraint,
however, which results in overly conservative channel assumptions. To alleviate this
issue, we propose interpreting channel coupling through a probabilistic lens, where we
define a likelihood function for the camera's aperture. This approach enables us to
incorporate channel coupling into our solution framework. We further develop a camera
calibration tool, allowing for the estimation of point spread functions (PSFs) from
various sources of light within a scene. The PSFs obtained from this tool can be
integrated into a retip algorithm, which recovers a more accurate representation
of the scene's surface. Experimental evaluations using both synthetic and real-world
datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in improving surface recovery
accuracy with varied lighting conditions.

The structure of the Dirac equation within the $R$-Minkowski spacetime is successfully derived from the Dirac equation defined within de Sitter spacetime by applying appropriate $R$-Minkowski transformation rules. Furthermore, we achieve a separation of variables for the Dirac equation in $R$-Minkowski spacetime, resulting in an effective one-dimensional Hamiltonian that incorporates a generalized P\'oson potential. The mass term of this potential is directly linked to the curvature of de Sitter spacetime.

Structural Causal Model (SCM) visualization aids researchers and stakeholders in comprehending the intricate relationships within complex datasets. Nonetheless, effective visualization demands precise and comprehensive graph data. Currently, there are limited tools available to automate graph data preparation for SCM visualization. To address this gap, a Python package called 'cdt' has been developed to facilitate graph data preparation for Static Causal Model visualization. The 'cdt' package implements an approach that integrates pattern detection, data-driven node and edge styling, and subgraph clustering. Key functionalities of 'cdt' include identifying notable edges through path analysis, coloring edges to reflect conditional relationships, grouping highly-connected nodes, conditionally styling subgraphs, and encapsulating complex relationships. The approach and the 'cdt' Python source code are openly accessible at https://github.com/microsoft/cdt.

This study delves into the complexities of a reference airlock, or cavity, that forms between two surfaces that are in the process of separating. The lock, located in the corner of a hydraulic press, significantly affects the seal's stability and could potentially lead to its failure due to dynamic pressure fluctuations and eventual cavitation. To avoid this, the lock should be pressurized with an active control system. The goal of this system is to raise the pressure within the lock above the vapor value, taking into account the impact of the lock's pressure reduction on the seal's dynamics, which was analyzed via a hydrodynamic study. The experimental setup, which consisted of a hydraulic press, was used to validate these findings. A computer algorithm was implemented to actively control the pressure within the lock, which involved operating a pressure booster. The algorithm's objective is to minimize the risk of cavity formation while taking into account the constraints of the system, which were modeled as an adaptive partial differential equation, which were addressed by converting them into a state feedback law that could be implemented in real-time. The results of this study were found to be confirmed by observations made during experiments, which showed that the pressure within the lock could be effectively regulated, which in turn, led to an increase in the separation speed of the surfaces, which was then used to validate the algorithm's performance, which was found to be robust, which could handle unexpected events, which were introduced during experiments, which introduced an unmodelled force that was found

A recent study by Clay, Hung, and Van Raamsdonk (2020) has established a link between an anti-de Sitter quantum field theory's charged state spectrum and the matter energy conditions in classical gravity. We expand upon this work by first developing a generalized Witten effect for systems with U(1)$^n$ symmetry, which is then applied to system of charged black holes in anti-de Sitter space. The resulting analysis reveals constraints on the charged state spectrum in quantum field theory based on the local gravity data, specifically for systems with U(1)$^2$ symmetry. The generalized AdS/CMT context is also discussed.

Mobile applications are frequently collected free of charge, yet frequently contain security vulnerabilities due to unverified code.
To address this challenge, a novel technique called OctopOS has been developed, allowing applications to enforce additional functionality only when specific conditions are fulfilled.
As a result, both developers and end-users can take advantage of enhanced features, yet the app's code remains protected from unauthorized access, as app users cannot freely collect data without complying with specified requirements.
To implement OctopOS, a set of cryptographic tools called octopodes are created, allowing the app to incorporate security measures without excessive complexity.
Although this technique introduces trust in the application, it is confined strictly to the context in which the app is being used.

We tackle the challenge of learning optimal strategies in discounted infinite-horizon stochastic control systems with access only to raw observations. Our focus is on achieving a precise goal: achieving an $\epsilon$-approximation to the optimal value when encountering corrupted episodes. We introduce and analyze a novel, practical algorithm that ensures an guaranteed level of performance when encountering corrupted episodes, by leveraging state-of-the-art methods for value iteration. This method is the first to tackle optimal policy learning with solely observational access, and we support our findings with successful experimental results.

A solution has been proposed to the original "paradox" surrounding the box game, involving an alteration to the players' strategy. By changing how the players play, a method has been implemented to eliminate the discrepancy between theoretical predictions and actual game outcomes. Furthermore, a novel interpretation of quantum behavior in isolated systems has been rectified through experiments with modified gameplay scenarios.

To address long-standing controversies concerning cubrite mineral composition and to fill gaps in existing literature, we performed a comprehensive first-principles analysis of cubanite. By deriving the electronic structure of cubanite from its parent compound Fe3NiS4 using Fe and Ni site projections, we provide an explanatory model for the material's stability, Fe-spin ordering, and metallic properties. Moreover, we demonstrate the viability of Ni-site d-band exchange splitting, thus resolving contradictions between previous theoretical predictions and experimental findings.

The interaction between quantum dots and acoustic cavities offers a novel approach to manipulate their coupled dynamics through an external driving frequency.  As the drive frequency nears resonance, the quantum dot's Rabi oscillations are damped, resulting in a transition from rapid to slow oscillations.  This research reveals that nonlinearity enables a quantum dot to collaborate with a phonon, effectively acting as a frequency mixer.  By adjusting the drive frequency by just 0.5GHz and changing it to 0.25GHz, a quantum dot-coupled acoustic cavity can undergo two different resonant states.  Additionally, a quantum dot can enable abrupt Rabi oscillations switchable within a 0.2ns time frame through frequency modulation, achieving Rabi flip times as fast as 0.12ns.  This research demonstrates the feasibility of fast and precise control over quantum states through frequency modulation and paves the way for fast quantum logic gates based on phonons.

A comprehensive examination of the herringbone lattice Hamiltonian is initiated
by distinguishing two types of breaking symmetry: onsite and bond symmetry.
We find that modifying the Hamiltonian can cause a phase transition from its
original form to topological phases. Specifically, adding a mass term creates a
weakly topological phase, while introducing different hop terms results in a
non-invertible chiral semimetal phase. Surveys of the lattice's topological
invariants are conducted using Wilson loops and Zak phases. The effects of
electron-electron interactions and thermal effects on the lattice are also
examined.

We delve into the characteristics of single-photon catalyzed coherent states, a type of quantum state, and examine how they vary based on the graph used for generation, particularly with beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. Successful and failed cases of generation are analyzed, and the resulting states show enhanced amplitude and reduced phase uncertainty compared to classical coherent states. We also compare the resulting states in successful cases and find that the quantum correlations differ due to the generation graph. The probability of achieving generation in a given case depends on the graph used, and we observe that the success probabilities for quadratic amplifiers are always higher than those for linear beam splitters at given distances.

The provided notes offer a real, coordinate-based introduction to the formalism of Newman-Penrose, including the representation of Weyl tensor complex coefficients $\Psi_0$ through $\Psi_3$ within this framework, as well as their expressions in terms of the real, symmetric massless spinor field components when one is non-zero. Furthermore, the derivation of the NP null geodesic equations, along with the determination of Petrov type II through equations (4.14) to (4.19), is discussed. There's a brief discussion of the transformation of the formalism under spin and Lorentz transformations, as well as an outline of deriving tidal forces in terms of $\Psi_0$ for a photon beam.

Researchers have developed a novel method for representing a polymer's collective wavefunction in quantum chemistry. This new approach infers the polymer's structure from the positions of its component monomers, utilizing a low-dimensional representation that has been proven effective in simulations. Unlike previous methods focused on electron correlations, this recent study aims to address the accuracy challenge arising from the nuclear repulsion between a polymer's constituent atoms. By incorporating the relevant physics of the monomers and their possible electron overlaps into the polynomial string operator, this method efficiently models both short and long-range nuclear behavior. Despite the potential for computational intensity as the monomer count rises, this method restricts itself to $2N$ dimensions for a polymer composed of $N$ monomers, thereby avoiding the need to track individual electron paths. With this foundation, subsequent electron correlation calculations can be efficiently performed.

This note explores the potential of using one ventilator to support multiple patients simultaneously under specific conditions, namely when a particular tidal volume is required for each patient. It reveals that ventilating two patients with a single bi-level positive airway pressure (BIPAP) ventilator is achievable if they demand equal tidal volumes. Moreover, under certain circumstances, it could be possible to ventilate four patients with one BIPAP ventilator using a Y-shaped (or similar) tubing. In cases where patients require different tidal volumes, the study suggests using two BIPAP ventilators connected to a single tube as a viable solution.

Accurate automatic segmentation of the esophagus from volumetric CT scans is hampered by limited and noisy data used for training algorithms. To overcome this challenge, we trained a customized Deep Convolutional Neural Network called the "Dilated Dense Attention Unet" to segment the esophagus and surrounding airways from low-quality CT scans enhanced with a deep convolutional neural network. Our experiments showed that using a deep convolutional neural network to improve CT scans before augmenting them with various techniques resulted in more accurate segmentation when paired with a Dilated Dense Attention Unet. The enhanced method outperformed other combinations, demonstrating superior results in multiple evaluation metrics. Moreover, the enhanced CT scans produced by the deep convolutional neural network demonstrated better generalization when tested with independent data sets.

Discovering oil reservoirs in real-time using log-while-drilling (LWD) data presents a significant challenge. Traditionally, this task is accomplished by trained experts who analyze core samples and LWD measurements through numerical simulations and empirical equations, a process that is both labor-intensive and time-consuming. Moreover, these methods do not account for measurements' uncertainties, a limitation that is being rectified by the development of a probabilistic framework based on Bayesian inference. This new approach uses Markov Monte Carlo (MCMC) to create detailed reservoir models, encompassing porosity, fluid types, and LWD measurements, along with their uncertainties. However, MCMC's applicability to large datasets is limited due to its high computational demands, an issue that is being circumvented with the use of a neural network-based likelihood estimator, which is itself trained on a smaller dataset and applied to a vast amount of LWD data. This innovative approach, exemplified with a logging-oil well, demonstrates the formation evaluation's likelihood function and uncertainty intervals, revealing them visually and graphically, and, with the formulation of an optimization problem, the total probability of product oil, including water and hydrocarbons.

Our research focuses on improving named entity recognition (NER) by utilizing additional context from entire documents, going beyond standard NER approaches. We developed a simple yet effective method, based on the BERT NER model and attention mechanisms, that successfully integrates this extra information. By designing two careful attention models and conducting systematic experiments on the ENERGY dataset, we showed our method's effectiveness. Notably, using this corpus-level information for NER tasks results in an 8.4% increase in F1 score compared to traditional character-level approaches. Our results also highlight the potential of our attention models to utilize this broader context without suffering from overfitting.

We employ a specialized bitangency check within the SCMC (a part of ScMC software) to investigate rational bitangents in quartic curves by analyzing their tropical representations. Various cases are explored by applying different operations to a specific binary quartic curve in SCMC, thereby altering the tropicalized curve's structure. We detect a pattern where bitangency rationality aligns with the check's outcome and we hypothesize this connection can be leveraged in SCMC to identify potential bitangents more efficiently.

In this research, a new algorithm for locating users inside buildings is proposed using signals from indoor base stations and access points. The algorithm accounts for measurement errors and the statistical distribution of ideal signals in a building environment, utilizing a method based on the least squares technique to locate users. The results of simulated data show very similar accuracy to an ideal method, and the proposed algorithm achieves a mean error error radius of 0.87 meters for data sets with low noise levels (less than 15 dB).

Multilingual societies around the world have identified essential technologies such as note-making, search, and conversational assistance in their favorite languages as key to increasing internet usage among unconnected populations. To make these technologies work for under-resourced languages like Bhojpuri, this research presents an in-depth analysis of the capabilities and limitations of state-of-the-art NLP models in NLP tasks that are crucial, such as sentence similarity, part-of-speech tagging, and word segmentation. Specifically, we evaluate both dense neural sentence embeddings and traditional N-gram based methods on the task of sentence similarity in Bhojpuri. We also analyze the performance of current POS taggers and word segmenters on word-level and sub-word-level for a 6-million sentence corpus in Bhojpuri, which was created by the Bhojpuri Wikimedia Foundation. Our findings offer valuable, actionable insights for future work on the Bhojpuri language and the Bhojpuri Wikipedia project, which was initiated by the Bhojpuri Wikimedia Foundation.

A significant number of imprecise instructions hinder the production of accurate image descriptions from text, especially among the visually impaired users who rely on these descriptions. Although prior research has showcased innovative techniques, a larger and diverse set of instructions is necessary to train models capable of providing helpful feedback to users. This study proposes a user-centered approach centered around three core principles: empathy, participation, and collaboration. Through collaborative sessions with ten visually impaired individuals, the project involved conducting focus groups, holding co-design workshops, and organizing in-person collaborations. Together with the participants, research team members established empathetic, accessible, and non-discriminatory principles, as well as developed a user-centered framework for creating, rating, and utilizing text-based descriptions to enhance the accuracy of image descriptions. Furthermore, the project resulted in the establishment of accessible design principles, a user-centered framework, a user-generated dataset comprising 500 inaccuracy examples and accompanying feedback, and a publicly accessible text-based description platform for image descriptions. This study paves the way for a user-centered image description improvement pathway, emphasizing the critical role of text-based descriptions in enhancing the accuracy and usefulness of image descriptions for visually impaired users.

This study investigates the energy loss functions within TaO nanoparticles spanning 1nm to 10nm in size, taking into account local field corrections and spin-orbit interactions within the framework of many-body TDFT.  Calculated results for TaO, incorporating these two effects, are then compared to results where the correction and interaction are ignored, as well as experimental EELS data for TaO acquired in transmission electron microscopy.  Furthermore, predictions made by our model are set side by side with existing studies conducted using plane-wave basis sets that omit the TaO 5d electrons from their calculations.

A crucial aspect influencing online information dissemination lies in the geographic distribution of internet users. As a result, online platforms are dividing into separate spaces, with users in different geographic locations having limited interaction. This research investigates whether the observed phenomenon, known as 'The Big Sort', where ideological groups become increasingly isolated from each other, accelerates the propagation of false information within users in the same geographic region. A theoretical model is developed and extensively simulated to explore the effect of 'The Big Sort' on online information dissemination. Additionally, the influence of network structure and the extent of ideological isolation on the spread of misinformation is analyzed. The findings reveal that non-random network structures contribute to the spread of misinformation, with users in the same ideological cluster being more susceptible to its propagation. This effect is amplified by increased ideological isolation, particularly on platforms featuring strong connections between users in the same region. A comprehensive dataset, encompassing over 3 million geographic users and 10 million interconnected simulated accounts, was created to model real-world scenarios, demonstrating the significant impact of geographical segmentation on online information dissemination.

The goal of creating useful programs through machine learning has been achieved by several methods, including natural language instructions, self-correction, and exploration. However, these techniques typically depend on access to pre-made samples from established datasets. It becomes necessary to develop new approaches that can efficiently generate high-quality programs from user input, including simple commands. These methods need to work with any target language, without needing access to additional data sources, and also function on devices with limited computational power. We have successfully created a new system called WISE, which can create useful spreadsheets by analyzing user input in the form of natural language, user feedback, and user access to a large library of pre-made formulas. WISE can operate on user devices, including those with limited computational power, by using a system of distributed sampling called the Importance Monte Carlo system. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of WISE by showing how it can generate high-quality programs in a real-world scenario, by using the Google Sheets application.

No universal rule governs how humans teach language.  To investigate this, we used a custom-built dataset to examine how subjects instruct agents to navigate a map.  We employed a systematic method to alter each subject's teaching style by changing the demonstration types, instructions given, errors made, and subjects themselves.  Our analysis used a subject-specific speech classifier and a semantic segmentation approach to evaluate changes in the semantic concepts taught.  We found that alterations in demonstration types and instructions had a major impact on each subject's way of expressing speech concepts (40.6% and 28.4% respectively), but changes in errors made and subjects themselves had a much smaller impact (8.4% and 4.2% respectively).  Our study emphasizes that given the high variability in how humans teach language, it is crucial to design robust learning algorithms that can adapt to different teaching styles, especially when training and testing data come from unrelated sources.  Our code and dataset are available online.

This research focuses on identifying the smallest ordered tree that fits a given set of constraints, which include node labeling, node degree constraints, and subtree identification. Specifically, this study differs from previous works by allowing constraints on outdegrees within the set of problems solvable with dynamic programming. Moreover, this study shows that the size of the best matching tree can be exponentially smaller than the length of the input string if outdegree constraints are considered. An efficient algorithm is also proposed for identifying the structure of the matching tree.

Euler-Arnold equations have a universal application in finding stationary points for specific mathematical operations involving Lie algebra elements, including those used in quantum field theory theories, such as Yang-Mills. By leveraging this framework, the finding of stationary solutions to the equations of motion can be reduced to solving a system of Euler-Arnold equations, which, given the complexity of quantum field theory, typically presents more manageable challenges than the original problem. As an example, we investigate the search for stationary solutions to the non-abelian Schrödinger equation, obtaining both novel and established results, as well as new insights into related studies. We also propose that similar approaches could be applied to other quantum field theory problems, such as the non-abelian Hartree-Fock equations, yielding potentially valuable outcomes.

Conversational systems like chatbots are becoming more sophisticated, which is associated with an increased need for more effective testing methods. To achieve this, automated testing frameworks are commonly used, but they often struggle to balance the level of support they provide with the level of customization they offer. This study aims to investigate the issues that arise when using these frameworks for testing conversational systems and proposes a set of guidelines to facilitate the selection and usage of them. This research is motivated by the challenges encountered while developing the Zest testing framework for the ConverseNSA challenge.

Researchers employ the astrometric method to search for exoplanets by monitoring a star's motion as it orbits its center of mass. To successfully identify these objects, it is crucial to distinguish between star-orbiting planets and unrelated gravitational influences. Using the future capabilities of the astrometric array under development for the SKA, a simulation was conducted to determine if an unknown Earth-mass object could be found within 10 times 10^21 meters over most of the sky with a five-year survey. The simulation's parameters mirror those of the star Hyades 4670, which showed signs of a possible planet through current astrometric data. The search would encompass a variety of smaller objects by extending the range of masses, sizes, and positions relative to the plane of the Hydra-SKA's star map.

This research explores the potential of a cross-lingual memory retrieve, capable of recalling relevant translation pairs from numerous available pairs by retrieving them in high-dimensional vector space. Unlike traditional bilingual translation memory, this approach does not rely on precise source language matches. Initially, we trained a cross-lingual memory retriever using a pre-trained model and assessed its performance on five English to German translation tasks using the Flores dataset. The experiment results show that using a cross-lingual memory retrieval model significantly boosts the translation accuracy, particularly for smaller source sentences. The accuracy boost is around 3 to 5 points on the source sentences smaller than 10 words, and up to 5 sub-points for sentences longer than 15 words. Furthermore, integrating the memory into a finite-state transducer (FST) framework allows the model to learn English to German sentence to sentence translations, drawing on the recalled memory content.

This study explores the hypothesis that the inflationary period left an imprinted trace on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) due to primordial black holes evaporating (PBBH). Using full map analysis, we investigated the visibility of the "Hawking points" feature predicted by the theory in the ACT-DR4 + Planck + WMAP data sets from the latest CMB experiments. Our findings show a significant correlation with Hawking points on low multipoles ($\ell \lesssim 50$) in both the actual and simulated datasets, but no correlation with low-$\variance$ circles (LVCs) or the E-mode polarization pattern (EMPP) that were previously claimed. We also found that LVCs and LVCs-LVCs are better matched by the simulated datasets than by the empirical data. Moreover, our analysis suggests that the previously reported LVC evidence may be a result of the chance alignment of the BBH mergers with the Lenz vector field. Additionally, we discovered the existence of low- $\variance$ circles in the simulated datasets with the same significance as LVCs and low- $\variance$ circles in the CMB temperature map, which were not discussed in earlier studies. Furthermore, we found little difference in the distribution of the LVC p-values between the simulated datasets and full simulation, which suggests that the LVCs are not anomalies. Finally, our analysis suggests that the existence of LVCs

This study applies the Liapunov center-manifold theory to analyze the dynamics of the fractional curvature Yamabe flow on a smooth compact conformally compact manifold without boundaries, embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. It is shown that when two unstable periodic orbits are given, there exists a smooth curve connecting them, parameterized by time, where the manifold's boundary evolves into a circle. Additionally, this research obtains an infinite number of unstable periodic orbits by employing a suitable transformation, resulting in the discovery of multiple solutions that converge to these orbits under the full Yamabe flow, provided they share appropriate initial conditions.

In few-shot learning, the limited learning data and prevalence of outlier samples can significantly hinder a classifier's performance. To tackle this challenge, we introduce an adaptive framework for few-shot learning that dynamically identifies and eliminates outlier samples while simultaneously minimizing the risk of removing beneficial ones. The proposed framework consists of two key components: a novel metric learning metric that facilitates the initial identification of potential outlier samples, and a subsequent optimization process that refines the identification by balancing the removal of outliers with the preservation of valuable learning data. Notably, our framework does not necessitate any pre-labeled information, such as outlier indicator tags. The proposed framework's effectiveness has been demonstrated in our experiments on standard miniImageNet and cubiZS datasets, where it outperformed the baseline methods in few-shot learning performance.

User preference is an essential facet in recommendation system development.
Aspect preference, with its unique and granular nature, poses significant challenges for existing models that struggle to capture it effectively.
To address this challenge, GATEHAR proposes a new framework based on the Gated Attention Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module.
This module leverages the synergistic interaction between aspect preference and general preference, enabling more efficient learning of aspect preference.
Specifically, the Gated Attention Units (GAUs) consist of two key components: GA-Transform, which transforms aspect tokens based on the relationship between aspect and preference, and GA-Update, which updates the attentional aspect tokens by fusing aspect and preference representations.
Our experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that GATEHAR achieves superior performance in retrieving aspect preferences, resulting in notable improvements in Recall@K and NDCG@K metrics by margins of 6.30% and 13.52%, respectively.
Furthermore, a user study further validates the effectiveness of GATEHAR in real-world scenarios.

This paper presents a series of concise and innovative natural formulations for key optimization problems such as Maximum Clique, Independent Set, Knapsack, Set Packing, Set Cover, Coloring, and Vertex Removal. These new formulations, based on exotic cone frameworks, offer significant advantages over conventional extended formulations by offering greater diversity in cone options and reduced dimensionality in certain cases, offering a more efficient path towards potential exponential compact formulations. As an added bonus, several of the proposed extensions naturally fulfill the conditions for FPRAS extendability, providing a framework for further fudge-factor analysis of currently non-fpras-extendable formulations.

The data composition in training sets significantly influences the performance of algorithms assessed on never-before-seen MRI scans, highlighting this effect through two key metrics: unobserved patient evaluation and cross-institutional testing with different imaging equipment. To understand and minimize the negative impact of data distribution variations, researchers used statistical tools such as principal component analysis and clustering algorithms to investigate the consequences on modeling. Their results show that model performance drops when scans from the same pathological group are spread across training and testing datasets but can be improved by evaluating on concentrated datasets. Their findings advocate for the development of evaluation strategies based on clustering to better capture unobserved variability in clinical settings.

This research presents an innovative framework for efficient optimization, addressing complex network-based multi-agent problems. The framework is applied to energy system options such as coordinated time-varying pricing and optimal assignment of appliance tasks across a network. The framework's key components include a central processor, or coordinator, that dictates strategy parameters which are then utilized by each independent processing unit, or agent, to determine a objective function; the coordinator's goal is to find the ideal parameters that maximize the average function result, considering the interactions between agents and the efficiency gains from communication costs reduction. Theoretical analysis provides constraints for the feasible dynamics and defines a decentralized gradient ascent algorithm, breaking down the computational load and revealing the convergence properties and efficiency improvements across various scenarios.

Researchers have investigated the performance of various optimized memory (OVM) file systems on small, persistent write operations using Optane DC Persistent Memory Modules (PMMs). To evaluate the effectiveness of these file systems, a range of benchmark programs were created to simulate real-world database operations with write sizes up to 1KB. The results showed that even when using an unoptimized file system called Linux NVMM (L-NVMM), also known as Linux NVMe over Fabric (L-NVMe), there was minimal performance degradation compared to writing directly to the PMMMs. The best L-NVMM optimized configuration delivered approximately a threefold improvement over its non-optimized counterpart, delivering an impressive improvement of nearly a tenfold over its NVMe equivalent. Furthermore, when it came to I/O throughput, both L-NVMM configurations outperformed their non-PMM optimized counterparts by nearly a tenfold. Notably, when using the relaxed version of the NVMM virtual address space called NOVA, L-NVMM achieved an even greater performance boost, achieving nearly a threefold improvement over direct writing to the PMMMs and almost a tenfold overall improvement.

Andrzej Kretinsky and Baris Kasikci explore the motivation dynamics model of biological agents' interactions, which is driven by internal motivators that generate forces guiding the agents' movements. In their research, they analyze how this framework can be applied to specific interaction scenarios such as rendezvous, rendering and pushing objects, and managing personal space. They also examine the feasibility of modeling multiple agents using the framework and discuss the emergence of complex behaviors in multi-agent scenarios. Their research is conducted within the context of two-dimensional point agents moving within rectangular environments, considering friction and obstacles.

Our study centers on the minisKAM 2T NMR/NDR system installed at the FRM II facility in LCR, noting the successful completion of installation and its readiness for initial testing in magnetic fields of 2T to 4T following some upgrades to its coil system. The system features two separate coils that allow for precise variation of the sample's experienced magnetic field while maintaining optimal temperature conditions. Various techniques such as continuous, repeated, and correlated measurements, combined with the 2T/4T capability, significantly enhance the efficiency of NMR/NDR experiments. As an example of our findings, we present research on the magnetic properties of the Lanthanum-based $γ$-Terbium ferromagnetic semimetal Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ . Our data reveal a consistent decrease in the magnetic moment as more Cm is incorporated into the compound, along with a reduction in the Curie temperature and a shift in the spectral pattern indicative of a change in a direct band gap.

Quantum chromodynamics (QCD) vacuum correlations serve as fundamental building blocks for hadrons, with the instanton liquid model providing a chance to study these correlations, particularly for linear approximations suitable for heavy quarks. Using a mean field model, we calculate the potential energy between quarks and resolve the C-symmetry issue by incorporating a non-perturbative correction to the Coulomb potential. Our results indicate that the computed spectrum of charmonium and bottomonium states is largely accurate, with predicted masses matching experimental values to within a few percent, and generated level densities also aligning with observed data. However, we observe a significant shortfall in the computed spectrum's resolution, necessitating the inclusion of the instanton background's dynamic effects.

Using a method similar to that in (arXiv:1809.01101), we determine the exchange relations for the generalized patterns of the o-signed Coxeter group Bn. This approach leverates the compatibility of the Coxeter length and descent set with the group's generalized patterns.

A comprehensive suite of radio-loud cosmic components has been assembled for the galactic halo using an optimized mapping method called Maximum Likelihood. Through this approach, researchers have determined seven key parameters that define the halo's characteristics. These parameters include the active region's shape, orientation, distance from the galaxy's center, angular size, and two distinct widths that define the shape of the emission profile. By employing a set of statistical tests, the study successfully identified and eliminated potential biases that could have skewed the results. The data constraints derived from this analysis are sufficiently tight to be used as input parameters for future analyses that aim to quantify the contributions of different components to the diffuse halo emission field and quantify residual systematic errors.

This paper presents a new approach within the framework of UMD Banach spaces with a convex growth condition, specifically in uniformly smooth spaces. It extends Figierova and Kunze's (2019) theory of paraaccretive systems and Bessel processes to these more complex spaces. The primary focus is on establishing a development formula for the fractional Laplacian operator $|D|^s$ for $s \in (0,1)$, resulting in a positive operator equation: $|D|^suf(x) = b(x)$, where $b(x)$ is an given function within the $L^p(\mathbb{R}^d; X)$ space with $1\lt p \lt \infty$ and $X$ being a UMD Banach space with a convex growth condition. Additionally, this theory is applied to analyze the equation $u_t + |D|^su f = b$ in a stochastic setting, where $b(x)$ now represents a given function in the time and space domain $(0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}^d$.

Investigating a rare earth-doped Tm$^{3+}$ ion ensemble in TmD$_{2}$TPD organic halide perovskite crystals, we found a previously unexamined optical spectral diffusion phenomenon. This analysis focused on a rare earth ion called Tm$^{3+}$, and its study involved using TmD$_{2}$TPD organic halide perovskite crystals.  By observing the $^{3+}$Tm ion's optical properties, we discovered a new optical spectral diffusion pattern that varies slowly over time.  Although there are faster and slower variations in optical fluctuations, the slow variation has a time scale measured in hours.  Since rare earth ions typically exhibit long-lived coherent states and the Tm$^{3+}$ ion has very sensitive and controllable optical properties, understanding and controlling this optical instability is essential for developing feasible and effective applications in solid-state quantum technologies.  To gain insight into optical instability, we used a Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch equation model, and our findings suggest that thermal fluctuations in the local crystal field are the primary cause of this instability.

This paper outlines the steps required to create an automated tumor detection system using a combination of Morphological Tools, the Region Growing Technique, and Artificial Neural Networks. Separate from the primary description, the article also explores the distinctions between Morphological Tools and the Region Growing Technique, as well as the process of constructing and training a Neural Network.

In this study, we aim to provide a clearer understanding of the degenerate Bernoulli numbers that were first introduced by Kato in 2019. To achieve this, we utilize various mathematical structures including Circulant matrices over Galois fields, complex integrals, and degenerate von Stieltjes transforms to derive the formulas for these numbers in multiple ways. The research also examines the connection between degenerate Bernoulli numbers and Circulant matrices over Galois fields, as well as explores their asymptotic behavior for large values of n.

The ultimate goal of radial velocity (RV) research is to minimize noise reduction techniques for as much data as possible. While previous studies explored various methods to select line lists for data analysis, we discovered that a straightforward randomized approach outperforms the previously believed optimal parametric selection. To test this, we used data from the Keck/HIRES and created multiple line lists by randomly choosing spectral lines, then evaluated their effects on RV calculations. We also examined how line lists' performance affected RV distributions and discovered a surprising strategy that significantly reduces noise. Additionally, we investigated line lists' impact on RV distributions and discovered a method to minimize bias. Our study emphasizes the significance of sufficient data samples and the development of a new line list strategy called R2R to minimize noise introduction from spectral line selection.

This research focuses on designing low-energy transmission scheduling techniques for wireless sensor networks that utilize HRLC, a hierarchical ranging link layer. We suggest two alternative methods, Uniform Range Sectoring (URS) and Hierarchical Range Sectoring (HRS). Both strategies involve dividing each hierarchy level into range sectors. By limiting communication within specific range sectors, URS and HRS can significantly reduce overall network energy consumption. We demonstrate that URS and HRS can mitigate the hidden terminal problem that typically arises in WSNs by incorporating a protocol extension to HRLC. We further analyze the potential for URS and HRS to reduce network energy consumption relative to the vanet protocol, a commonly used scheduling method in WSNs. We develop simulation models for the URSim and HRSim simulation tools to evaluate the performance of the routing protocol in WSNs that incorporate URS and HRS. We present simulation data that indicate the following: URS and HRS can reduce the average energy consumption per packet by up to five times compared to the non-hierarchical URSim and HRSim models; URS and URS can lower total sleep time by approximately four times; URS and HRS can decrease routing overhead; URS and HRSim models exhibit similar consumption levels; URS and HRS can decrease routing depth; URS and HRS can decrease routing delay; URS and HRS can decrease packet delivery time; URS and HRS can decrease network energy consumption as WSN size increases

The task of identifying crop produce using computer vision is influenced by the object detector selected, which varies based on application-specific needs. In this study, we apply a meta-learning approach to facilitate the choice of an appropriate detector for optimizing accuracy in classifying fruits and vegetables. A crop produce detection system is established, consisting of multiple detector components, a scoring mechanism, a switching system, and various learning objectives. Experimentation across multiple data sets has yielded optimal configurations, demonstrating the efficacy of our framework in delivering the fruit and vegetable detection accuracy required for commercial use.

This study examines a class of elliptic system equations, with distinct components governed by different lambda-Riemannian norms, specifically focusing on local singular cases. Key implications of a fast-moving function within this context are explored, leading to identified conditions for non-existence and multiple solution cases. Additionally, specific non-local singular non-existence criteria are demonstrated.

This paper seeks to improve existing bounds on the variance of functions of independent Bernoulli random variables when they are conditioned upon their sum. Specific focus is given to functions with nonnegative coefficients, including convex functions and polynomials with nonnegative coefficients. Various consequences are explored, deriving from the obtained results in condition (1.1). Some of these consequences involve large deviations estimates, an approximation of relative entropy in condition (1.2), and an assessment of a system of binary variables' ability to simulate a Poisson random variable under certain conditions.

This article presents a comparative conjecture between torsion crystalline cohomology and torsion étale cohomology over Witt vectors in a specific category of systems. To support this hypothesis, proof sketches for several key properties of torsial crystalline cohomology are provided in terms of étale cohomology. Additionally, certain properties of torsion crystalline cohomology are explored in relation to torsion étale cohomology systems.

To measure the $\cos\theta_R$ asymmetry in four-jet events more accurately, we propose using the angle between the projection of jet2 onto the jet1-jet3 plane and the line connecting jet1 and jet3, rather than the angle in real space. Next, we show that by combining our earlier findings with the measured $\cos\theta_R$ asymmetry in four-jet events at the hadron level, we can effectively investigate the dihadron fragmentation function (DiFF) in a precise, model-independent way, specifically the interference term between the $e_1$ and $h_1$ DiFFs. To demonstrate this method, we apply it to four-jet data from the CDF collaboration at the Tevatron, deriving an estimate for the $\cos\theta_R$ asymmetry in three different kinematic regions. Unfortunately, due to the limited statistical significance found, no conclusive evidence for T-odd correlations in four-jet events could be confirmed or refuted.

The de Sitter spacetime can be comprehended as a deformed Minkowski spacetime, characterized by an invariant distance measure. This invariant distance arises from the product of two factors: one representing the squared distance in four-dimensional Minkowski space, and the other involving a geometric parameter from a four-dimensional hypersphere defined by a fixed radius related to the cosmological constant. Researchers have established a mathematical framework known as the Fock transformation to account for this invariant distance measure. This framework enables the expression of de Sitter four-vectors in terms of their Minkowski four-vector counterparts through a set of nonlinear equations. Consequently, a reverse set of equations can be formulated to transform four-vector quantities from de Sitter spacetime into their Minkowskian equivalents. These equations effectively facilitate a linear approximation of de Sitter spacetime, which can be accurately represented within the context of general relativity when considering the energy scale set by the cosmological constant.

For a fixed non-zero integer $e$ that is even, this paper examines the process of classifying conjugacy classes within the special symplectic group $Sp(e,\mathbb{Z})$. It establishes that each conjugacy class can be represented by either an equivalence class of elliptic normal forms or a binary Borel-Siegel class derived from a specific matrix equation. Furthermore, the group $Sp(e,\mathbb{Z})$ action on these forms is defined and described in terms of the modular and symplectic group actions. A theorem proves that two closely related graphs, constructed from these groups, are essentially the same. Additionally, for a given matrix, this paper shows that related invariants can be calculated efficiently.

This study introduces a novel entity representation framework, called CONTENTOP, that
integrates GAN-based content features with graph neural network topology for
recommendation. Content information is extracted by training a basic discriminator
and a high-content generator, while the subsequent Bayes rule updates the
probability distribution. A link predictor network is then used to incorporate
topological data into the representation. Experiments on real-world datasets
demonstrate that this framework significantly improves recommendation accuracy.

The choice to accept or reject a kidney offer is vital for both the recipient and the offering donor. The decision is further complicated by the impact of kidney incompatibility on future transplantation options. To address this challenge, we developed a method for analyzing the acceptance decision by modeling it as a Markov Decision Process, with incompatibility incorporated as a state variable. The optimal acceptance strategy was determined through value iteration, and we devised an algorithm for executing this strategy. We then evaluated the method using data from the US Renal Data System, exploring how the recipient's age, waiting time, and kidney-related mortality rate influence acceptance decisions. We found that the model predicts a higher acceptance rate among younger recipients and those who have been waiting longer for a compatible kidney. Additionally, we discovered that the model accounts for kidney incompatibility's impact on the recipient's future options with a relatively small weight. We propose that further research and input from medical professionals be used to refine this weight for a clinically applicable version of the model.

This paper explores two methods for estimating copula parameters: one based on maximizing a likelihood function, and another utilizing a Bayesian approach. We utilize models from the Family of Bivariate copulae to demonstrate and compare these techniques, employing both simulated and real datasets in our analysis.

Recent advances in Natural Language Processing, particularly in NLI and textual entailment tasks, rely on embedding techniques that assess a document's meaning frequency. Although effective for common vocabulary, these techniques fall prey to Jarusansakul's observed distorting effect, where they treat antonyms as representative synonyms based on appearance rather than semantic contrast. This phenomenon skews embeddings toward frequentist definitions and negatively impacts inference tasks. To address this issue, we identify its causes, explore its implications, and propose alternative conceptualizations and measurement methods for the antonym-centric closeness phenomenon. Our research also identifies anticorrelation between contextualized embeddings of antonymous pairs and simple sentiment scores, suggesting that these embeddings may capture emotional content more than contextual meaning. To quantify this, we introduce the Entomic Effect, a metric that correlates sentiment scores with contextualized embeddings' semantic distances. We demonstrate that the Entomic Effect outperforms the cosentric effect in magnitude and exhibits chasm-like characteristics in contextual space. To mitigate this effect, we propose two strategies: entomic regularization and decontextualization. Entomic regularization modifies frequentist-style embeddings to minimize antonym-centric distances, while decontextualization redefines the embedding process to account for all constituent word contexts. Both methods yield more contextually accurate and contrast-sensitive embeddings, outperforming current context-aggregation methods in producing these improvements.

This research focuses on enhancing waveforming design to optimize radar performance, specifically targeting fair and sum throughput metrics among multiple targets in a wide bandwidth context. By employing an optimization model, we assess the effectiveness of time-frequency designs in improving detection accuracy. We analyze two scenarios: equalizing throughput for all targets and maximizing overall sum throughput. Through simulations, we observe that incorporating radar performance metrics into design processes yields notable improvements in detection accuracy, particularly in dense frequency usage. The findings also suggest that concentrating energy towards higher frequencies can enhance throughput for distinct radar performance metrics, providing valuable insights for future waveforming design applications.

This study explores the rayleigh--b\'enard instability in a square domain with fixed temperatures on all sides except the top and bottom, where temperatures vary linearly. As these side temperatures cross a specific threshold, stable equilibrium is disrupted, giving rise to complex convection patterns. We investigate this phenomenon using two different numerical methods: spectral methods and finite element methods, comparing them in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. We achieve time-advancement through a second-order Adams-Bashforth scheme and data compression using a singular vector filter, allowing us to analyze energy transfer and visualize convection patterns at various Richardson numbers. Our results demonstrate that convection structures evolve with increasing difference in side temperatures, with ultimate burst states exhibiting distinct corner flow and center flow characteristics.

Due to the generative nature of modern neural language models, researchers can
no longer depend solely on performance metrics to assess the validity of their
theoretical assumptions. Rather, we must now examine individual predictions
and underlying data patterns to validate or refute new analyses. Yet, current
methods for determining the theoretical underpinnings of a sentence's form fall
short, as they often fail to account for the multitude of possible interpretations
that contribute to a particular outcome - be it a translated sentence or a
spoken sentence in another language. This problem is compounded by existing
optimization techniques which often result in unreasonably abstruse analyses
that do not reflect how humans actually process language. To resolve this
dilemma, we introduce a procedure rooted in rationality that simultaneously
solves the surface-to-deep mapping problem for a sentence and provides criteria
for the most plausible analysis, based on competitive allometric constraints.
This method's effectiveness is validated by its successful explanation of the
form-meaning mapping in English sentences and a translated corpus of Brazilian
Portuguese sentences, yielding both reasonable interpretations that align with
human-like induced preferences and capabilities.

This study explores how specific rewiring of connections in a network affects outcomes in the Standard Epidemic Model on One Side (SEMOS). Placed within the framework of social dynamics, the mathematical results show that disconnecting infected individuals from susceptible ones has a more significant impact on infection spread than bringing new susceptible connections. These findings align with observations from both real-world and simulated data, suggesting that the standard method of modeling network infections by incorporating links removal may account for the infection's decline. As an added benefit, several key probabilities in SEMOS can now be calculated using closed-form equations.

We investigate a compact 3-dimensional sub-Riemannian manifold that admits a steady Cotton soliton with the potential vector field being orthogonal to the Reeb vector field, discovering that such a manifold possesses I0 geometry. Furthermore, we identify that in this I0 geometry, any steady Cotton-Yamabe metric is rescalings of the standard Einstein-Schrödinger metric and provide a parametric classification of these re-scalings. Notably, our analysis also reveals that the corresponding potential vector field is not unique in this context.

When fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) from experimental data, the necessity of incorporating the DGLAP evolution is an inherent feature, given that the fit produces the PDF at a specific scale $Q_0$ and implies fits at all other scales through the DGLAP equation. This aspect has been overlooked in many independent global fits as each determination of a PDF at a scale $Q_1 \neq Q_0$ is treated as entirely independent of the same PDF determined at another scale $Q_2 \neq Q_0, Q_1$. This method contains inherent biases, for example, when trying to combine the results of the same process measured at two different scales in a PDF fit. To rectify this, one should employ a combined set of data, for example, by using the cross section $\sigma/Q^2$ in deep inelastic scattering (DISc) which encompasses the PDF evaluated at a variable scale $Q$. Nevertheless, utilizing independent fits from various collaboration for machine learning purposes may lead to biases being introduced. To counteract this, we propose using an envelope of $\alpha_s$ as well as a set of boundary conditions derived from the solutions to the DGLAP equation with the least and greatest values of the strong coupling constant, for example from CT18, MSHT20 and NNPDF3.1xx, which have been utilized in our study for comparing the role of DGLAP evolution in several processes including DISc,

In this paper, we introduce variance reduction-based experience replay (VRER), a novel framework combining model-based and model-free approaches for task-specific reinforcement learning. VRER utilizes a experience replay buffer to create a more accurate model of environment dynamics by reducing variance in policy gradient estimation. By continuously refining the model, the framework takes advantage of both the benefits of using a precise model and the robustness of learning through a collected dataset. Our framework demonstrates superior performance to prominent model-based and model-free methods on multiple test environments, including the Moon Lander, the Toyota Towser, and a three-room building navigation task.

We have updated Python 3 bindings for libcommute, a comprehensive collection of symbolic computation tools for commutation relations, which now offer an improved and more efficient set of functions for working with the computational batches known as 'sums'.

Our study of the high-temperature iron-based superconductor (Li$_{1+x}$Fe$_{2-x}$Se$_2$) using neutron diffraction at the boundary of the Brillouin zone reveals a superconducting gap anisotropy similar to that near the center of the zone.  However, the gap size near the corner is substantially larger, exceeding the maximum values previously observed in related iron-based superconductors near the zone center by nearly 2 times.  This significant superconducting gap feature near the corner was previously neglected in related studies.  Our results suggest that this large gap feature near the corner must be incorporated into theories for the mechanism of high-temperature iron-based superconductority.  Furthermore, first-principles band structure calculations indicate that the electron pocket at the corner of the Brillouin zone originates from the $3d$ $e_g$ orbitals of iron that point towards the corner.  This is in contrast to the electron pockets at the center of the Brillouin zone, which are derived from the $3d$ $t_{2g}$ orbitals of iron that point towards the center and face neighbors along the lattice directions.  Our study provides a crucial example of the multi-orbital nature of iron-based superconductors near the boundary of the Brillouin zone.

We express the superbosonization identity and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation as two facets of the same phenomenon, representing a change of variables in the fermionic Berezin integration through the introduction of auxiliary variables.

Our analysis focuses on the angular distribution of leptons from the top and bottom quarks' decay, where we measure the spin asymmetry of the top quark and compare it to standard model predictions. Using the ATLAS detector and a data set from 7 TeV proton-proton collisions with 20.3 inverse femtobarns of collected information, we identify events containing isolated charged final-state leptons along with large jet activity. By analyzing the energy of these leptons, we determine a spin asymmetry value of 0.137 +/- 0.077 (statistical) +/- 0.045 (systematic) to be 0.428 times the difference between the forward and backward directions. This measured asymmetry is in agreement with the standard model's consensus.

We investigated the dielectric properties of LaNiO3 thin films integrated into LaSRO (LaScandium, LaYttrium, LaStrontium) buffers using a radio frequency resonant cavity technique and found that LaNiO3 thickness has a significant effect on the temperature dependence of a fast relaxing component's thickness in relaxation measurements. Specifically, this component becomes weaker than a fast one for thinner LaNiO3 layers, exhibiting characteristic inhomogeneous broadening typical of LaNiO3 bulk samples. Our study also reveals two additional temperature-dependent time constants, with one showing strong temperature dependence for all LaNiO3 thicknesses, and the other appearing only in thicker LaNiO3 layers. Our proposed model attributes these observations to two distinct charging processes: a fast, interfacial one and a slower, bulk-oriented one.

Conversational agents that employ a theory of mind concept, according to specific definitions, can significantly enhance dialog-related tasks. Nonetheless, creating multiple plausible world states and predicting user actions based on their potential decisions are more computationally demanding than basic tasks such as question answering or continuing a conversation. In this study, we modify a comprehensive dataset called MultiWOZ 2.0 to facilitate two tasks: summarizing a user's goal from their dialogue history and suggesting appropriate next actions. We evaluate our approach using neural network models and find that these theory of mind-inspired representations are effective at generating coherent continuations and accurate goal predictions, but struggle to anticipate user actions. Our systematic evaluation enables us to pinpoint the strengths and limitations of theory of mind-inspired representations in representing user goals during natural language dialogues.

This study investigates the impact of correlated Rayleigh fading and phase shifts on the ergodic capacity of wideband communication systems with reflecting surfaces. We derive a closed-form expression for this capacity in a single-subsystem scenario. Our derived formula considers the impact of phase shifts and correlation coefficients on the capacity, which is then verified through numerical evaluation and simulation. Our results indicate that increased phase shifts and correlations result in reduced ergodic capacity, an effect that is also reflected in capacity outage probability. Furthermore, our findings reveal the importance of phase shifts and correlations in determining the capacity of multi-subsystem scenarios.

We introduce MG-GLAM, an accelerated and memory-efficient coding version of N-GPU-LARGE-MESH, specifically tailored for massive parallel GPU-based N-body simulations. Like its predecessor, MG-GLAM combines a tree-based and mesh-based gravity solver, allowing it to tackle large particle counts efficiently on multiple GPUs. However, MG-GLAM significantly reduces memory usage through optimized data structures and streamlined kernel designs, supporting real-time simulations of systems with multiple trillion particles on clusters of modest GPU power. Furthermore, MG-GLAM offers substantial performance gains over N-GPU-LARGE-MESH through a streamlined communication workflow, resulting in nearly 2x faster runtimes for massive simulations while maintaining high load-balancing efficiency (around 10% deviation) in dynamic N-body simulations.

This research paper discusses the connection between chordal Schramm–Loewner evolution and certain imaginary surfaces derived from the probabilistic interpretation of conformal loop ensembles. Specifically, it establishes that the SLDE at dimension 4 generates a distinct boundary representation of the imaginary surface associated with conformal loop ensembles at dimension 15/8. Moreover, it reveals that the distribution of distances from the origin to the complement of the closed curve created by SLDE at dimension 4 has a particular relationship with Bessel functions, which can be observed explicitly in the plane minus the upper half-plane.

As open-source software development projects grow, the availability of data for training machine-learning models for feature request classification and bug reporting increases, which is beneficial, but the development community still has to deal with vast amounts of unstructured text on wiki pages, leading to inefficiencies. To address this challenge, we introduced a wiki system called WorkingWiki that integrates the capabilities of LaTeX, git, machine learning-enhanced feature request classification/bug reporting, and collaborative real-time editing. By leveraging these technologies, WorkingWiki provides improved efficiency in manuscript publication, software development, and the creation of living documentation through the use of NLP tools, including the PyMulteed library for text data management.

Researchers have used a general approach to examine various combustion models for simulating turbulent reacting flows. By applying the $\delta$-function filter to these models, they assessed their compatibility with the linearized flow framework. The study found that the thickened-flame model produced results that best matched the idealized assumptions, allowing for accurate predictions of mean flow and heat flux. It's proposed that this model is particularly appropriate for modeling turbulent flows with thin flames, given its ability to accurately represent the flame front while avoiding excessive computational costs.

To address this, we define the dimensionless quantity $\omega_{ac-buy}^2/k^2$ as the acoustic-buoyant frequency, which characterizes the combined effect of acoustic and buoyant forces on a star's internal dynamics. This concept is crucial in understanding a star's variable behavior, including oscillations and convection processes. We employ this frequency to analyze the characteristics of both gravitational and electromagnetic waves, expressing their respective frequencies in terms of $\omega_{ac-buy}$. This approach is made possible due to the frequent occurrence of near-equilibrium conditions, where the frequency of acoustic and buoyant forces is substantially greater than $k$. As a result, we can express the star's fluid potential and density perturbations, along with pressure changes, in a simplified manner. This involves introducing dimensionless variables, including the dimensionless frequency $\Omega$ and the dimensionless variable $\tilde{\rho}_1$, which describe the star's behavior during both non-steady state and equilibrium states.

A new method is introduced to identify synchronized patterns in high-dimensional dynamical systems using a graph-based approach. By applying a technique called topological persistence, we can analyze the systems' collective behavior more effectively. Our method builds on existing synchronization detection techniques, specifically the K-shortest path algorithm and the modularity index, to detect clusters within the systems. Through analyzing the persistence of these clusters across different distance thresholds, we can determine the number of synchronized regions and their internal structures. Additionally, this approach provides a mathematical foundation for assessing the stability of observed synchronization patterns. Implemented in an open-source Python package named topopy, the method is shown to successfully identify and analyze various clusters in model systems and a real-world systems' data, including a laser system and a chemical reaction system.

We examine a one-dimensional spin chain composed of one-site and two-site blocks arranged in either a regular or irregular pattern. Within this setup, we analyze the movement of two adjacent particles occupying neighboring lattice sites in a nearest-neighbor dimer system. Although we demonstrate that both nearest-neighbor (NN) and exclusive-neighbor (NN') dynamics on certain geometric lattices lead to ergodic behavior, our study of one-site lattice models with multiple spin sites reveals non-ergodic dynamics under either type of movement rule. Similarly, on the diamond lattice, NN dynamics result in another instance of non-ergodic behavior. In contrast, NN' dynamics reside in a larger Hilbert space than their NN counterparts due to the absence of three-site configurations in the former case. Finally, we look at the effect of introducing an impurity into a triadic lattice model by considering a spin chain with one spin-1 site and two spin-1/2 sites under exclusive-neighbor dynamics.

Under assumed conditions where this coupling is stronger than the force governing known dark matter's interaction with visible matter but less than neutrinos' self-interaction, we can infer significant implications for primeval structures. A specialized visual tool has been created to display cosmic ray ensembles produced by ultra-high-energy (UHE) photons in terms of their primary properties and secondary observables.
