This paper investigates the potential of using intelligent reflecting surfaces to
create reflective links for radar systems, particularly in line-of-sight challenged
scenarios. By analyzing the radar's view of the reflections off the surface, we can
deduce velocity information about the target. To quantify this, we develop a closed-form
expression for the maximum achievable radar signal power and determine the optimal
configuration of the reflecting surface. Moreover, we determine the performance
limitations when using a fixed reflecting surface. Our theoretical findings are
validated through measurements and field trials.

For over three decades, the evaluation and comparison of fuzzers have been hindered by limited mutation analysis, which is now rectified by advanced mutation analysis techniques led by AngSanMeta. These state-of-the-art tools provide comprehensive feedback, including detailed graphs and code-level insights into fuzzing results, enabling more accurate comparisons with other tools. When paired with sophisticated coverage instrumentation, these mutation analysis tools can supply valuable insights to developers, facilitating the development of more effective software updates and potentially uncovering more severe vulnerabilities in software. We integrated and assessed the latest mutation analysis tools against three prominent coverage-instrumentation tools, as well as direct fuzzing outputs, to produce the first integrated and accurate comparison of these tools. The results from this integration and assessment are made publicly accessible to encourage and facilitate future research and comparisons. Initially presented as a supplementary material, this work has been moved to the main text for easier access.

Using pretrained models as a foundation for continual learning has been shown in transfer learning to be highly effective. Nevertheless, our research reveals that even top-tier continual learning methods surpassing neural collapse utilization can outperform NMC when leveraging pretrained models. Nevertheless, a simple Prevalence Filter outdid NMC by a significant margin but fell short of continual learning algorithms designed for memory efficiency. Nevertheless, incorporating just the order in which tasks were learned into the Prevalence Model enabled it to match the performance of energy-based continual learning methods.

A key observation leading to our main finding is that the triviality of the second homotopy group of a path-connected space ensures that maps which are null-homotopic relative to one point in that space are automatically null-homotopic relative to both. As a direct result, we prove that if the second homotopy group of a path-connected space X is trivial, then any maps from the complex projective plane to X which are null-homotopic relative to one base point are identical in their null-homotopy structures relative to two base points. Furthermore, if a space is UW-homotopically finite in dimension 2, the uniqueness of null-homotopy implies the uniqueness of the entire null-homotopy structure.

Our focus lies on identifying conditions for stability and bifurcation behavior, which are determined by the rate of growth of $f(s)/s$ as it approaches zero, along with initial conditions in $L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap H^{1/2}(\mathbb R)$. To address the challenge of distinguishing between collective and single-particle behavior in nuclear models, we combined ab inituo forces with a shell model to investigate the excitation energy evolution in the 64Ni nucleus. 
This involves comparing shell model results to the stiffness parameter derived from semi-empirical models and analyzing the impact of the neutron subshell gap on nuclear deformations and the well-defined 64Ni shape. 
Furthermore, we investigated how this shape is affected by the gap's evolution, which is in turn explained by a realistic interaction through a large-scale shell model. 
These approaches allow us to differentiate between the 64Ni single-particle spectrum and low-lying collective states.

In game theory on weighted graphs, we explore the concept of strategy-space product games where each player's movement is constrained by their own Lipschitz values. This includes cases where all players share the same value or where values vary among them. We analyze game outcomes for three scenarios: guaranteed wins for a specific player, indefinite gains, and those with no assured benefits. Generalizing previous work, we explore the strategy-space games on weighted graphs defined by specific value values $\lambda_i \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$. This includes two specific cases: when all $\lambda_i = 1$ or when $\lambda_i$ represent infinite values. On unweighted graphs, we prove that finding specific guaranteed wins involves $\Sigma^p_2$-complete and $\Pi^p_1$-complete problems, respectively. This involves determining if a player can achieve a guaranteed win or indefinite gains in game play. We also investigate the complexity of finding specific players with guaranteed wins or indefinite gains on unweighted graphs. This involves determining if a player can achieve a guaranteed win or indefinite gains in game play. This involves determining if a player can achieve a guaranteed win or indefinite gains in game play.

This investigation into machine learning algorithm performance estimation uses J-K fold cross validation, a modified approach to standard K fold cross validation. In alJ-K fold, the standard process is repeated J times with distinct data shuffflings. This method is employed to better capture performance variability and facilitate statistical inference, particularly hypothesis testing. Two primary investigation questions are asked: How does alJ-K fold enhance performance estimate stability compared to alK fold, and how does it affect computational cost? A case study using text classification and the AG News dataset with J = 20, as well as various J values, is presented to address these questions.

Assistant Student Networks trained on Knowledge Distillation Logitsoften outperform independent Student Networks trained on their own, but comparing this advantage across different Teacher and Student combinations is challenging due to numerous variables influencing logit distributions. We investigate the effectiveness of Teacher-Student architectures by analyzing small, mid-range, and large Teacher models with high and low entropy logit distributions, demonstrating that Architecture Design spaces exist where a single Student network surpasses four alternative Teacher designs. Notably, our findings indicate that a Logits-soft Student network can exceed the performance of its High-Entropy logit distribution Teacher counterpart. To better understand these results we develop a model comparing relative entropy and mutual information between Student and Teacher logits.

A new variation of the Bucket Elimination (BE) method for solving Markov Random Field (MRF) problems has been developed, specifically for vector MRFs used in constructing sparse approximate inference models and optimization within generic MRFs. This proposed vector BE follows the traditional BE framework while incorporating efficient operations from operations research, including minimum-cut computation in graph models and flow-vertex capacity increase in network graphs. As a result, this model offers significant performance improvements over the existing version of BE by leveraging tailored operations and cutting out redundant computations of PE. Notably, this new approach achieves a up to $1000\times$ decrease in runtime when applied to a wide range of synthetic and practical problems.

The classic Lorentzian lineshape describing atomic resonance transitions deviates notably in highly saturated scenarios, especially in low-pressure gases where recoil effects of absorbed photons come into play. This research combines the principles of quantum optics and statistical physics to derive a comprehensive saturation lineshape formula applicable to gas systems. It incorporates key factors such as photon recoil, beamscope interactions, and the characteristics of the incident light. The derived expression reduces to previously established forms under specific conditions, including low saturation caused by weak light intensity or strong spatial filtering. Notably, in situations where the absorbing medium's thickness greatly exceeds its recoil length, the line broadens proportionally to the square root of the saturation parameter.

The study of static transitions in granular matter is influenced by the absence of a true equilibrium state, particularly in the context of the frictionless isotropic and frictional shear transitions. We compare the preparation routes, critical exponents, and order parameter structures of these transitions. We find that the preparation routes for frictionless isotropic and frictional shear transitions are distinct, with the former exhibiting a broader distribution of contact angles resembling anisotropic clusters, while the latter exhibits a sharper distribution resembling a isotropic granular crystal. Consequently, the critical exponent describing order parameter behavior differs between the two, with its value falling between $-1$ and $-2$.

Lieman-Tchebychev polynomials serve as basis elements for the centralizer of the name n (N >= 1) of the algebra so(3) within the universal enveloping algebra U(\so(3)). 
This paper explores the centralizer N+1 by examining the Grad algebra of the name n+1 based on the centralizer N. 
We apply this approach to derive a recursive formula for the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer N based on the centralizer N-1, 
and use this to derive a closed-form expression for the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer N (N >= 1) of \so(3).

The presence of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions can be modified based on the light source used to illuminate a thin film of B1-type B20 materials, specifically PtSi. Researchers have observed that changing the light intensity to darkness results in significant changes to the interaction strength, which can also be reversed by returning to the same light source. These interactions were found to be highly sensitive to both time and temperature, with their effects diminishing rapidly in warmer conditions or without continuous light illumination. Researchers have observed an increase in temperature leading to a decrease in Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction strength, which completely disappears above 50 degrees Celsius. They have also found that sample surface characteristics, characterized by lattice strain, play a crucial role in determining the dJ/dT ratio. This, in turn, determines how the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction strength varies with temperature. Researchers have observed a significant change in the interaction strength, resulting in up to a 50% decrease in the DM vector above 50 degrees Celsius, which can be reversed by returning to room temperature, which can be attributed to photo-induced changes in surface characteristics, specifically a decrease in lattice strain, specifically when illuminated by visible light.

This note highlights the non-uniform distribution of one-dimensional zero-crossing velocities, typically assumed to be uniform, within the context of incident halo WIMP velocities. A simple mathematical model demonstrates how the effective (zero-crossing) velocity distribution differs significantly from the full velocity distribution, potentially within the Earth's frame of reference. A straightforward correction to this apparent paradox is discussed, with implications for detecting WIMPs through threshold effects in the one-dimensional threshold distribution.

Knowing the limitations and prejudices inherent in technology's knowledge base is crucial for those working in the public sector who depend on search engine recommendations in their daily tasks. To achieve this awareness, a new education tool has been developed and tested with library school students to evaluate its effectiveness. The tool aims to provide a structured assessment of students' comprehension and the value of their feedback has been measured. The study's findings indicate that the tool's questions cover a diverse range of bias types and that the feedback gathered can lead to improvements in the tool itself, as well as inspire new research opportunities. Additionally, the study's data is made available publicly to facilitate future exploration.

Consider a future TeV-scale muon collider that has already delivered data at 1, 10, and 100 TeV center-of-mass energies before the full completion of the project. We outline the potential for particle physics research in this scenario, focusing on QCD and Higgs/partially vector-like fermion/dark matter physics. Our analysis includes both leading order and higher-order quantum corrections, as well as possible deviations from the Standard Model. With the given dataset, the cross section for Higgsstrahlung would be measured to within 5-20%, and the total Higgs width could be determined to within 0.05-0.5 times its natural decay width. The accuracy for studying new heavy particles could reach a few percent, and we can probe the imaginary part of their couplings for the first time. Additionally, we have an opportunity to investigate potential exotic scenarios, such as multi-Higgs doublet models and complex dark sector interactions involving multiple photons and missing energy signatures.

To enhance image contrast and resolution in white-light interferometry using sampled Bragg gratings, a new sampling technique called white-light aperture sampling (rCASPR) has been developed. Optimized for maximum coherence between rays, rCASPR outperforms conventional linear sampling by increasing central peak intensity from 22.5 times to 45 times while reducing side-peak intensity by 50 times.

This paper introduces a novel concept known as Higher-Order Control Barrier Functions (ICCBFs) to ensure safety in both linear and non-linear systems as well. Unlike ICCBFs which are limited to certain systems due to their requirement for access to higher dimensional states, ICCCBFs can be applied to a broader range of dynamical systems by utilizing access to a single measured state at the boundary, thereby ensuring the safety of the system. A rigorous proof of this concept for linear systems and a practical application of ICCCBFs in securing an unmanned aerial vehicle from colliding with obstacles is also provided in this paper.

In the study of CF-approximation spaces, two new concepts, namely CF-closed sets and CF-convergence, are introduced to capture the essential features of continuous domains. Specifically, a set is defined as CF-closed if it meets certain criteria related to three-valued neutrosophic open sets, whereas CF-convergence is DF-convergence expressed through CF-closed sets. To establish a connection between topological spaces and continuous domains, closed sets and convergence in topological spaces are defined, and then topological spaces can be constructed from CF-approximation spaces using CF-closed sets and CF-convergence. Additionally, the paper investigates the properties of topological spaces derived from CF-approximation spaces, namely T_0, T_1, and T_2 spaces.

We investigated numerous paired-permutation test examples across various fields,
which led us to pinpoint shared components usable for both precise computation
and rapid assessment of paired-permutation test values or $p$-values.
These tests involve counting how many times countable objects in a specific class
fall within a specified set, where the objects result from applying a
paired permutation to a base class and set. Objects classified include
partially filled tables, sequences with counts, trees, graphs, and others;
we provide detailed descriptions for each area and supply links to existing
code libraries. We discovered that paired-permutation tests can be solved
efficiently by combining objects class classification with pairing matrix analysis
under specific conditions, which also allows us to obtain upper and lower
estimates for some tests. We supplied test reports for 34 cases, including one
where our method outperformed paired t tests, as well as code to generate these
reports for an additional 14 examples. We included remarks on calculating
objects class sizes and offered some theoretical insights. We made our code open
source at https://paired-permutation-test.org/, enabling easy access to 84 pieces
of code for a wide array of paired-permutation test applications.

A sudden shift in the regulation of an industry can significantly impact its performance in a way that performs like a natural "experiments" to economists studying the effects of deregulation. One such example is the breakdown of monopolies in the shipping sector between 1928 and 1940, which occurred when straitened circumstances forced the owners of a group of vessels to sell their shares independently. Using data from this event, along with contemporaneous records, we found that the dissolution of these shipping monopolies had a lasting effect on freight prices, reducing them by approximately 25 to 35 percent, which also led to a substantial increase in the amount of goods being shipped (both elasticities being around 0.8). Interestingly, this performance boost was not entirely consistent with a permanent 25 to 35 percent rise in the elasticities of both freight prices and quantities being around 0.8. However, it partially abated once more after a decade, indicating that while the effects of deregulation can be long-lasting, they can also vary over time.

Graph neural networks excel in graph-related tasks primarily due to valuable graph structure information, not node features. To leverage this structural information, simple degree encoding is commonly used. In contrast, graph neural network layers' aggregation units possess inherent capabilities to utilize graph structure, suggesting a more effective encoding approach. Building upon this concept, we develop DegreeEncoding, an innovative encoding method. Experimental evaluations across node classification, transductive/inductive graph neural network training show that DegreeEncoding significantly outperforms node-feature-dependent encodings and degree encoding, with code available on GitHub.

A surprising development in recent years shows that using adaptive connectivity and embedding techniques for dimensionality reduction can significantly improve the reliability of conventional estimation methods like median and spectral estimation in estimating the structure of manifolds. To understand this phenomenon better, we investigate the combination of these techniques with a popular estimator of average distance between points. However, we discover that this combination is extremely vulnerable to the introduction of fake data. As a result, we prove that widely adopted approaches utilizing this estimator and the MostrosMap software are incapable of achieving deceptiveness. In contrast, we find that traditional estimator combinations under a random connectivity model are exceptionally secure against introduction of fake data, including the combination of spectral estimation and the Laplacian embedding. Although the adaptive input option provides advantages in terms of preserving data structure, we conclude that the random input option should still be preferred for algorithms like Nonnegative Laplacian Embedding and Normal Laplacian Embedding to ensure their robustness.

Style of surgery arguments have substantial value in analyzing geometries linked to singular compact volume minimizers. Building on this foundation, we extend previous work by K. K. Kim, offering a refined comparison of these techniques. Our method follows the surgery framework established in "Volume Minimizers, Their Volumes, and Their Curvatures" but with key differences in implementation and scope. Unlike its predecessor, which focused on specific curvature bounds, our approach is more general and applicable to a broader range of settings, including diverse lower curvature limits, signed volume comparisons, and unsigned volume inequalities.

In certain types of superconductors, particularly those with vortices, the core of the vortex core exhibits higher entropy in comparison to the moving magnetic flux line. To better understand this phenomenon, we employ a time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau model featuring a specific symmetry, which includes both moving flux line and vortex states. Our analysis involves a rigorous expansion to second order in a small parameter representing the difference between thick and thin vortex cores. The results of our calculations confirm the coexistence of these two distinct states and facilitate an explicit calculation of their potential energy and entropy, as well as the surface tension of the vortex. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the ratio of the moving flux line to total entropy within the vortex can be adjusted by manipulating various parameters.

This paper explores a non-linear communication approach, where an aggregator makes adjustments to a system operator's control, based on observed fluctuations in a building's energy consumption, without directly receiving that data. We develop and analyze maximum entropy feedback (MEF) to study this system, utilizing an agent-based model that simulates a smart grid with multiple connected buildings. Our results show that MEF enables effective load management, achieving energy savings comparable to direct-communication methods, while preventing cascading outages. Furthermore, the model's robustness to simultaneous, random, and intentional attacks on the no-communication model demonstrates the potential of MEF to enhance communication and stabilize grid performance, even in the face of such threats.

This paper addresses the challenges and limitations of stock market prediction research, which often overlook crucial features such as technical indicators and historical prices in their prediction models. We present a comprehensive dataset of 38 technical indicators for 10 prominent US stocks, which we used to develop and validate our predictive approach. Our method involves a sophisticated two-stage prediction model that leverages Technical Indicator-Level Stock Direction (TISD) prediction and Logistic Regression to accurately forecast stock movements. The model was successfully applied to our dataset, demonstrating its capability to predict the directional movements of these companies' stocks. Additionally, our study includes a pioneering deep learning model, specifically an Evolutionary Neural Network (ENN), which we employ in our experiments to pave the way for future research opportunities.

Our calculations of the merger rates of various celestial objects like white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes using the S4EMU hydrodynamical simulation reveal a significant connection between successful white dwarf - neutron star or white dwarf - white dwarf mergers and Type Ia/Ib/Ic supernovae events. This finding highlights the importance of incorporating stellar dynamics within galactic globular clusters and dwarf galaxies in astronomical observations. By providing a more accurate map of neutron star mergers when combined with traditional methods, our data could have an effect of up to ten times on the estimation of white dwarf - neutron star or white dwarf - white dwarf merger rates, thus influencing the scientific understanding of dark energy, gravitational waves' effect on celestial dynamics, and the origin of heavy elements through supernovae events and supernovae events events events.

To reduce theoretical uncertainties in the comparison between theory and experiment, a mixed approach to Effective Field Theories (EFTs) is proposed for studying double Higgs boson production. This method involves using the Established Higgs Effective Field Theory (EHEFT) framework, which combines the well-tested EHHiggs Effective Field Theory (H_EFT) and Full EFT (Full) theories. In the EHEFT, the leading coefficients of operators in the Extended Effective Field Theory (EEFT) are assumed to be small in comparison to the coefficients of the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) operators. As a result, when calculating the relevant matrix elements for double Higgs boson production, the EEFT contributions can be treated as corrections to the 1-loop level SMEFT calculations. This mixed EHEFT approach is then applied to the main kinematic regions dominating the hadronic level cross-section for process $pp \to HH$ and calculates the relevant cross-section in terms of the log-likelihood surface using various production channels at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) for various data sets provided by ATLAS and CMS collaborations. The analysis indicates that using various datasets from the CMS and ATLAS collaborations at 7, 8, 13 and 13.6 TeV, the updated limits on the lambda_3 and lambda_HHTT coefficients at 95% confidence level are obtained as 4.04, 2.27,

In this letter, we introduce a novel parametrization termed "pre-non-relativistic" that facilitates the analytical expansion process in general relativity. By incorporating the pre-non-relativistic scale factor into coordinate one-forms, the lengthy expressions for spatial metric perturbations can be resolved into a first-order differential equation. This equation reduces to the well-known Barrumiu equation under conditions of a flat Friedmann-Robertson-Walker background. Furthermore, the precision of the obtained first-order corrections aligns with prior results derived from both longitudinal gauge perturbation and fully general perturbations.

We revisit the computation of Eqs. state functions for massive vector fields in an asymptotically Anti-de Sitter space, specifically a p-GSK black hole in a scenario where the one-point function is non-zero. By applying the deconstruction method to the Einstein equations, we identify and solve two separate sets of resulting differential equations to evaluate the asymptotic behavior of the current. This approach allows us to express the result in terms of integration over the black hole's mass parameter $\mu$. Comparing our findings with previous methods, we confirm the consistency of our approach with zero-current boundary conditions and find that one method leads to an irrelevant constant integration, supporting our proposal to discard it. The computation reveals the emergence of a branch-cut structure in the result, in agreement with earlier computations, and we confirm the applicability of our approach even for cases where the one-point current is highly significant. The validity of our results is further confirmed by explicit examples, including the case where the one-point current is not dominated. To facilitate the computation of expectation values, we apply the deconstruction method to both sides of the holographic two-point function, allowing us to recover the correct branch-cut structure. The computation demonstrates the reliability of the deconstruction method in capturing the correct branch-cut structure, and we apply it to evaluate the difference between two access points in space, showing the method's potential for computational advantages over traditional methods.

We investigated the motion of a horizontally moving cylinder within granular material at various driving speeds, depths, and radii. A dual-load-cell apparatus was used to measure the drag force exerted on the cylinder as it moved through the granular bed. High-speed camera recordings allowed us to analyze the cylinder's motion and the surrounding granular material's flow patterns in real-time. Our study revealed two distinct regimes of motion characterized by different drag forces experienced by the cylinder. A transition between these regimes occurred at a critical driving speed, which was determined by the radius of the cylinder and the speed of its driving, but was unaffected by the driving speed, driving surface, and driving rate, and was further confirmed to be influenced by the ratio of the cylinder's radius to the depth of the granular material.

This study leverages our new insights into ionised gas dynamics from observations of six starbursting disk galaxies to re-evaluate the debris luminosity function (DLF) of dLMTs. Our goal for dLMT absorption line studies lies in deriving reliable distances and masses for dLMTs by studying their ionised gas outflows. Initially, we derive reliable distances to dLMTs by studying their H$\alpha$ and [NII]$\lambda$6584 absorption velocities in four cases. Assuming the outflows are non-relativistic and transverse to the line of sight, we derive minimum line-of-sight velocities in four cases. Moreover, we identify H$\alpha$ and [NII] doublet absorptions in three pairs of dLMTs and investigate their properties in terms of absorption velocities, equivalent widths, and column densities. We explore potential explanations for these pairs in context of gas outflows, interactions with brighter foreground galaxies, and the DLMTs' membership in local groups or clusters. Moreover, we identify two dLMTs with substantial equivalent widths in their H$\alpha$ and [NII]$\lambda$6584 spectra: HD 104396 and HD 104406. We explore the feasibility of observing their [OII]$\lambda$3727 emission to assess the possibility of these DLMTs being interacting or merging systems. We also discuss ion

Finding optimal configurations for complex systems with numerous adjustable parameters is crucial in scientific studies and commercial applications. While auto-tuning methods can increase efficiency in systems受参数影响, traditional techniques struggle with systems involving numerous or interconnected parameters due to their limited search spaces and lack of generality. To address these challenges, a new two-stage auto-tuning framework named BoAnon has been proposed, leveraging probabilistic models for global optimization. In the first stage, BoAnon refines a set of parameters for a customized baseline auto-tuned binary system within the same family of applications. As more members are generated for systematic optimization, BoAnon moves to a second stage, training and predicting probabilistic models for a broader range of architectures on specific processor platforms. Case studies in two distinct domains have demonstrated the effectiveness of BoAnon in significantly improving performance. For the same overall performance, BoAnon achieves substantial reductions in energy consumption when comparing stages, the first bringing about a notable improvement, while stage two brings an even more significant gain when compared to existing auto-tuning tools like Alibaba's auto-bench.

Our analysis of 3D periodic heavy-ion and proton-lead collisions using hydrodynamics reveals that the interdependence of triangular and elliptic flow ($v_3$ vs $v_2$) in a 200$${\rm TeV}$$ Pb-Pb collision is most similar to an elliptic collision with a comparable protons-to-neutrons difference. This observation holds true for various particle types across different centralities, negating the need to account for differences in mass or quantum statistics.

The growing size of Large RDF Datasets (LRDs) poses significant quality concerns. Traditionally, Quality Assessment (QA) has been facilitated by QA reports, which offer step-by-step explanations of calculated quality metrics. However, generating detailed QA reports for LRDs is a laborious and impractical endeavor. We address this issue by introducing DistQualityAssessment, a framework leveraging distributed document summaries to enhance the efficiency of quality assessments for LRDs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by implementing distinct strategies for both matching and semantic search over RDF data, showing substantial improvements in performance and user satisfaction.

This paper delves into the statistical process fitting associated with maximum likelihood estimation, specifically exploring its application to independent increment processes and their broader category, Brownian motion with drift. It also examines the mean square convergence of a minimum density power divergence estimator for these processes, along with a related lower confidence bound. An interesting comparison is made with the maximum likelihood estimator, and the paper draws a parallel to the normal distribution case. Additionally, the convergence convergence of the maximum likelihood estimator is studied within the context of discrete time chains and an ancillary result on score process convergence is provided.

When massive active galaxies undergo a shock-ionization process, highly energetic events occur, causing a significant impact on surrounding gas through coinflation. This process reveals new information about observable characteristics of gas in these active galaxies through a substantial increase in temperature and a major increase in specific entropy. We developed a model describing this shock-ionization process, taking into account the influence of a shock wave's magnetic field on ionized gas. The model shows that this process can raise gas temperatures to extremely high levels (greater than $10^9$ K), creating a challenge in identifying potential fuel for accretion onto a supermassive blackhole. We also identified three distinct phases in this ionization process: finding that the rate of entropy increase during the first phase is limited, but during the second and third phases, the rate of entropy increase can be highly variable, allowing for fuel ejection or retention. We found that the rate of entropy increase during the third phase can be regulated by factors such as the rate of mass accretion, enabling us to shift gas from being retained near the blackhole to being ejected away from it. This regulation plays a vital role in the behavior and activity of galaxies, making it essential to understand the ionization process better. Observations of high-velocity gas in active galaxies, such as high ionization lines and X-rays, provide valuable evidence of this process and its effects on the surrounding gas.

The evolving complexity of IoT applications is increasing their vulnerability to various security threats, making comprehensive and efficient testing essential for their safety. To accelerate and standardize the testing process, we propose the Frisbee framework, a security test suite built using Python. Frisbee focuses on automating the discovery of communication protocols used in IoT applications and facilitating in-depth analysis. The suite includes a set of communication exploration techniques and employs an associated metric to assess the achieved communication protocol depth. As evidence of its effectiveness, we applied Frisbee to two IoT applications, producing the source code for these tests in the accompanying directory. The testing process is video-documented to provide a clear, step-by-step guide to users.

This paper explores rare decays in beauty mesons, specifically the anomaly in the ratio of $f_{B_s}/f_{B_d}$ ratios from $B_s \to \ell^+ \ell^-$ and $B_d \to \ell^+\ell^-$ decays, the reported excess in the ratio of $p p \to B_s \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ over $p p \to B_d \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ observed by experiments at the Large Hadron Collider if interpreted at face value, the constraints imposed on rare decay processes and electric chirality asymmetry in $B_s \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $B_d \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ from experiments at the Large Hadron Collider, the implications of these observations for the two-Higgs-doublet (Type-II) and third-generation extended Higgs sectors, and the impact of the anomaly on the direction of future measurements and calculations, including the values of the Higgs-particle coupling to beauty quarks and the parameters of a pseudoscalar Higgs boson coupling to beauty quarks, derived from the shape of the $B_s \to \ell^+ \ell^-$ decay q\ell invariant mass distribution recorded by the LHC experiments.

A neural network-based method called Traffic Scene Generation (SceneGen) creates realistic driving scenarios with a desired target distribution. This framework, based on conditional variational autoencoders, encodes the target distribution and generates traffic scenes by reversing an image formation process. To apply variational autoencoders to real-world images, an additional process is needed to map 2D images to a structured vehicle-state graph representing the self-car and surrounding vehicles' states. This process involves detecting vehicles, segmenting them, estimating their motion, and linking them to targets. To train self-driving software, this forward process must be reversed to generate the target distribution. SceneGen accomplishes this by learning to invert the vehicle-state graph transformation through可differentiable approximations (reverseNet) and utilizing an alternative generation model (GenNet) to enhance performance and efficiency. As a result, SceneFrame, the complete system including self-driving data collectors and processors, can efficiently produce diverse training scenes automatically.

A Cayley tree can be effectively visualized as a Cayley graph representing the symmetric group $S_{n}$, with each of its $n!$ points connected by bonds. This effective visualization enables a precise understanding of how the tree's size influences the Ising model when modeled as a Cayley tree. Consequently, exact solutions can be achieved for $S_{n}$ at any given temperature, revealing that a Cayley tree is not static but dynamic, capable of exhibiting both paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases depending on the value of $n$.

To tackle highly underresolved systems, especially those resulting from filtered large Eddy simulations, the standard FGMRES iteration may require excessive memory and time.  We have developed a localized variant of the conjugate gradient method, designed to efficiently achieve a numerical solution while minimizing these resources.  This new approach incorporates two innovative components: an implicit preconditioning technique and an explicit smoothing algorithm.  We have examined the performance of this variant in simulated 3D turbulent boundary layer and channel flow scenarios, demonstrating its ability to converge with reasonable overhead in certain cases.  However, further research is needed to guarantee its applicability across a broader spectrum of simulations.

This research examines specific directed multigraphs where edges are assigned from a fixed non-degenerate probability distribution over any possible subset of edges. We will demonstrate that certain edge sets leave no invariant sets under the associated random transformations, with measure theory considerations, and derive implications such as first passage percolation on these graphs exhibits a positive speed, and both sliding window processes are transitive. We consider two scenarios: choosing edges independently based on the probability distribution (independent case), and selecting edges based on previous choices in a dependent scenario. Our results also combine new findings with existing results in the transitive dependent scenario.

We investigated the evolution of superbubbles (Sups) created by massive star clusters in surrounding gas environments, especially in cloud-mediated supers, where we also considered dust formation and destruction. Using multi-scale hydrodynamical simulations, we tracked dust production from pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae, as well as advection in wind phases, and dust destruction during interactions with accretion shocks and stellar winds. Our results indicate that a Sups forming within a nearby molecular cloud can contribute significantly to its own dust budget, with the dust growth during accretion phases potentially contributing up to 0.1-0.3 $M_{\odot}$, and dust supply from core-collapse SNe being sufficient to account for observed galactic dust levels. However, pair-instability SNe require more research. In contrast, pair-instability and core-collapse phases generally contribute less than 0.01-$M_{\odot}$ to the dust supply of cloud-mediated Sups. The Sups generally retain most of this dust, and we also considered the effect of dust supply on gas metallicity feedback.

This research addresses the challenge of detecting three-dimensional objects in the far-field using a complete dataset annotated with lidar and RGB data. We propose an advanced object detection method using both RGB and lidar inputs that leverages a pre-trained YOLO network for RGB input and a single-shot 3D object detection model for lidar input. By combining these two approaches with a decision fusion technique, we achieve superior performance on the newly created FFOJ dataset, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.
Using simulation, we test the effectiveness of using a parameterized quantum circuit as a generative quantum machine learning model to prepare quantum states on a potential energy surface.

During heart surgery, registering a preoperative heart model to real-time intraoperative data is impeded by noise generated from the datapoint cloud. To address this issue, leveraging a prior organ model to reduce intraoperative data noise is an option. Studies have demonstrated that applying heart model-based filtering to intraoperative datapoints can enhance the registration process. Nevertheless, failing to account for non-uniform scaling in heart model filtering leads to distorted results. This project aims to improve the organ model-based approach by scaling each datapoint towards the nearest point on the organ model. We conducted experiments on synthetic data with known ground truths as well as real MRI data to test the proposed method. Our results show that targeting organ model registration yields more accurate results, especially when significant scale deformations are involved. We observed an 18.54 mm reduction in registration point cloud error compared to traditional heart model filtering.

For non-degenerate energy-momentum tensors in a n-dimensional conformal matter spacetime, the conditions under which conformal matter collineations exist have been thoroughly analyzed. However, when the energy-momentum tensor becomes degenerate, the conditions for these collineations to occur, the resulting down-killed energy-momentum tensors, and the associated conformal factors have been specifically examined in detail for energy conditions in a n-dimensional context.

Self-supervised optical flow estimation is a complex process due to various surface changes in the process of object motion, including variations in appearance, orientation, and even the possibility of objects disappearing from view due to occlusions. Current approaches that rely on self-supervision, however, are incapable of accurately handling occlusions, ultimately compromising their performance. In an attempt to overcome this obstacle, we incorporate depth maps into the appearance term of our loss function to encourage depth values for pixels marked as occluded to converge toward identical values. As a consequence, pixels designated as occluded can still be utilized during the optimization process for parameter update, promoting more precise optical flow predictions. In addition, we introduce an term in the loss function to promote more precise matched pairs. In contrast to other methods, such as ranking, which has been frequently used in self-supervised learning, our approach is uniquely capable of handling occlusions. Nevertheless, our method is computationally more expensive, as it necessitates the calculation of an additional depth map, which has been found to be readily available in practical applications including video sequences, depth sensors, and monocular depth estimation networks. In the process of flow optimization, we incorporate a term in the loss function to encourage convergence of depth values for pixels designated as occluded to similar values. As a consequence, pixels designated as occluded can still be utilized during the optimization process for parameter update, promoting more precise optical flow predictions. In order to bypass this extra computation, we also present a neural

This paper introduces a novel type of neural network called Extreme sparsifying matrices (ESMs) that can serve as a highly efficient and versatile classifier. Despite the increasing demand for processing capabilities in mobile devices equipped with advanced features, there is a need for energy-efficient solutions, which our proposed solution aims to provide. By utilizing existing store-and-forward network architectures commonly found in modern SoCs, our implementation delivers a versatile and energy-efficient solution. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we trained and tested ESMs across multiple datasets for multiple classification tasks and found that they match or surpass the accuracy of conventional neural networks, including ResNet34, while offering significant power consumption reductions of up to 97%. Our comprehensive benchmarking experiments demonstrate the ESMs' capability to serve as a dependable and efficient alternative to traditional neural networks.

This study investigates the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field within the color flavor locking phase. We utilize the SU(3) perturbative QCD expansion to analyze this matter, specifically utilizing the next-to-leading order (NLO) equation of state. By constructing a two-fluid model that incorporates finite-density non-degenerate neutron matter, we examine binary systems in heavy ion collisions and neutron stars, particularly 2- star systems in a recent observational data set. Our comparison of model predictions with measured positions and total masses reveals that spin-polarized strange quark matter effectively accounts for the observed stability of these compact objects.

A cubic graph is considered even-2-factorable, or E2F for short, if all its 2-factors consist entirely of even length cycles. This paper proves that having a bipartite structure is not a prerequisite for E2F graphs, and provides a non-bipartite example. Furthermore, the article explores the property of being E2F in relation to edge coloring and shows that bipartite graphs exhibiting EA3 coloring are guaranteed to be E2F. Lastly, the paper establishes a connection between EA3 coloring and the precoloring extension of complete bipartite graphs.
Li's previous work on the Bateman-Horn Conjecture for quadratic polynomials of a single variable is refined and building on this the Bactan-Horn Conjecture for three power series is investigated.

Recent advances in optimized compilers for security enhancements have been counterbalanced by the rising vulnerability of applications written in interpreted languages like PHP and Python. Traditional virtual machines and just-in-time compilers struggle to execute aggressive security measures, such as Timeloops' filtering technique for system calls. To overcome this limitation, Timeloops' new method statically rewrites dynamic languages' binaries to limit unnecessary system calls, thereby improving performance and maintaining compatibility for applications like Mozilla Firefox, PHP, and Python 2.7 when subjected to heavy loads.

A particularly promising area of research suggests that certain axion-like dark matter could be an effective candidate due to its associated pseudo-Goldstone properties. Despite its promise, calculating the elastic scattering interactions between these potential dark matter particles and nucleons poses significant challenges, as it depends heavily on whether their interaction involves an odd or even number of dependent fields. This research aims to bridge the gap by presenting an general effective field theory that encompasses both scenarios and derives key consequences for elastic scattering interactions as well as relevant application-specific outcomes including the axion-like DM direct detection rate and the spin-dependent scattering cross-section. This framework can also serve as an useful tool in studying more complex scenarios such as the possible presence of explicit solitonic skyrmions in theories with Skew-field symmetries.

This paper addresses the challenge of continuously tracking targets that have been initially detected within a limited sensor field, despite not being detected at other time instances. A real-time target trajectory estimation algorithm based on probabilistic filtering is devised to track undetected targets based on previously detected data sequences, thereby providing accurate target trajectory estimates. Additionally, this study explores the impact of undetected targets on detection delays and presents optimal control strategies for a single sensor and a single actuated sensor to minimize undetected time. Notably, the algorithm and theoretical analysis presented here scale efficiently with sample size and do not increase computational complexity in tracking multiple targets, thereby suitable for real-time applications.

This research focuses on managing the complete disappearance of a population governed by a non-linear Schrödinger equation with a source term, which is less common than ensuring controllability to a steady state. We demonstrate that it's possible to achieve total extinction within a finite time through controllability to equilibrium points and observe that this strategy encompasses a wide range of domain equilibria. The success of this approach relies on having access to the entire boundary for control purposes, which limits its feasibility for bounded domains.

For the past decade, deep learning methodologies have significantly progressed and numerous studies utilize real-world data sets to evaluate their effectiveness and applicability beyond experimentation.  One breakthrough study demonstrated the utility of goal-oriented rewards in speeding up game-playing agents' development for Penalties and Possession scenarios in football.  However, adopting this goal-oriented reward structure for Open Play situations results in agents learning undesirable behaviors and relying on rare luck to score.  We investigate this issue by comparing different goal evaluation strategies and conclude that artificially inflating certain actions with high fixed values leads to improved goals by the training game-playing agent.  We further examine the benefits of this approach and suggest its potential to accelerate development and enhance performance when combined with goal-tracking algorithms.  We validate this hypothesis through a series of experiments in Open Play scenarios.

Formulating an inverse problem as a sequence of forward problems is a widely accepted strategy, and employing time-domain wavefields is an common approach for full waveform inversion (FWI). Although this method has significant advantages, utilizing time-domain wavefields poses various challenges, including memory requirements, ensuring a sufficient source spectrum, and difficulties with phase unwrapping. In contrast to time-domain FWI methods based on a wave equation adjoint state, our approach utilizes three-dimensional (3D) frequency-domain (FWI3D) techniques using complex-valued source spectra. The combination of 3D spatial dimensions and multiple frequency domains results in substantial memory demands when solving large-scale wave equation problems. The scarcity of accessible high-performance computing resources for seismic inversion exacerbates these limitations. The Lippman-Schwinger integral equation (LSIE) offers a more efficient alternative to the full-wave equation (FWE) by eliminating the need to calculate a homogeneous wave equation solution. The LSIE method has the additional advantage of automatically handling phase unwrapping. To address the inhomogeneity of the subsurface and ensure data accuracy, we consider both the contrast source formulation (CS-Lsie) and the preconditioner formulation (PC-Lsie). The performance of the LSIE method was evaluated on real data from the 2D salt dome experiment in Goose Flats, Texas. The results of this experiment were obtained with real frequency-domain wavefields generated using the SIGMA code, in comparison to time-domain data from

A new type of resonator interconnect has been developed to allow for non-reciprocal signal transmission. This interresonator structure enables the creation of optically active devices, including diodes and quasi-circulators. By implementing a negative magnetically aligned field near a resonator grating, perfect unidirectional transmission can be achieved. Furthermore, we have found that a quasi-circulator device can facilitate perfect non-reciprocal transmission between three resonators and that transmission from the third resonator to the others remains bidirectional. Also important is our discovery that a negative magnetically aligned field near a resonator grating allows for perfect non-reciprocal transmission in optical diodes.

We have conducted an in-depth investigation into the 2019 high-state outburst of IGR J19294+1816, which was observed from the 14 keV to 450 keV energy levels using the INTEGRAL ICGPC. We also factored in the 2017 observations from HETE-2 and XTE-UGM. The 2019 data can be described by a Comptonized spectrum with an energy of 59 keV and a cutoff at 300 keiv, while in 2017, the spectrum featured a cutoff at around 150 keiv. Notably, cyclotron line features were detected in both observations, with lines at 145 keiv in 2017 and 115 keiv in 2019.

To analyze this situation, we apply a space-time discrete asymmetric noisy voter model to an infinite line. In this model, at each time step, a random individual is selected as the source, and their opinion is adopted by their neighboring neighbors, with different probabilities to the left and right, subject to occasional noise. Given that one species initially occupies the left half of the line and the other species initially occupies the right half of the line, we examine how the interaction between these species, amplified by the asymmetry, can result in three possible outcomes: the coexistence of both species, the dominance of one species through its louder noise, and potentially sudden bursts of noise that lead to the dominance of one species in an otherwise quiet system.

Citizen science is an effective approach to collecting data over vast geographical regions, which can be enhanced through web technologies and mobile applications. One such initiative involved creating a digital database of Indonesian sundials using Google Maps, Facebook pages, and a custom web application called "Sundial Hunter." This user-friendly interface allowed users to explore the sundial information through various interactive features, ultimately leading to over 100 contributed submissions by users, which has resulted in a more durable and long-term project with valuable data for further research, including archaeological studies in Indonesia.

This research is centered on optimal data and energy dissemination from a supply node to multiple recipient nodes using two communication channels. We analyze this in the context of DED2D systems, where a serving mobile device efficiently shares content and charges data on demand from both the base station and other users. In our model, data requests are either fully met or skipped, with partial service not allowed. We investigate two primary objectives: maximizing successful disseminations while minimizing data requests failures, and balancing energy and data disseminations to maximize user satisfaction. We propose an online algorithm called Time-Partitioned Fractionation with energy and data dissemination (TFIET) that achieves near-optimal results. TFIET works by dividing time into slots, making data and energy dissemination decisions for each slot, and ensuring that each slot successfully disseminates at least the square root of both optimal energies from previous slots. As long as optimal energies do not grow too rapidly, we can guarantee that both data requests failures and energy disseminations are near-optimal under reasonable assumptions. To evaluate the effectiveness of TFIET, we conducted computer simulations and found that it produces highly satisfactory results in DED2D systems.

The telework mandates of recent years have accelerated the need to automate experimental arrangements through a distance. Consequently, we have developed a highly intricate experimental setup for studying room-temperature magnetotransport in two-dimensional electron systems on a wafer-scale InAs phosphide sample. This complex system was successfully automated via a distance using a specialized software interface, which we designed specifically for this purpose. The interface has Prolog-based scripting capabilities for protocol definition and includes features for secure remote access.

Developing a versatile algorithm to create custom phase plates using electrostatic patterns is a critical step in modeling and designing effective phase plates for optimized electron probes. An initial attempt to model voltage distributions based on arbitrary pixel patterns using 1D finite element analysis revealed a significant limitation: the model's predictions diverged from measurements made with real phase plates due to an unaccounted-for aspect. Electrons, when passing through the plate, experience deflection and a change in potential, leading to probe distortion and reduced current. A new model incorporating these dynamics is proposed, along with a refined algorithm to design phase plates with optimal probe performance. This algorithm iteratively adjusts pixel patterns to minimize probe distortion and reduce central probe current, aligning with experimental measurements. Two performance-defining parameters are established, and algorithm performance is evaluated using a comparison between modeled and real phase plates. Successful design examples, including oap probes and customized plates with specific pixel patterns, demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in creating efficient phase plates.

Although previous studies have applied pretrained masked language models to enhance RNNs and convolutional networks for understanding human conversations and visual scenes, no work has applied such models to Transformer-based structures and explored if they provide a comparable benefit. We examined the use of masked language models in enhancing two different Transformer architectures for the task of understanding conversations. We found that using BERT and attention mechanisms alone resulted in performance on par with or superior to models augmented with masked language models, achieving the best results to date on the FEVERSD and BLUESUMPO dialogue understanding benchmarks.

To navigate the complex and ever-changing terrain of mobile robots loop closure detection is a critical skill. Accurate detection of closures is vital for navigating environments using opportunistic slam techniques based on graph optimizations or predictive filters integrated into slam on board. Our research involved enhancing a deep learning network's ability to detect closures by incorporating an attention mechanism into a cross-stitch architecture, which allows the network to focus on salient features within the visual input. To test the robustness of this architecture, we did simulations using the Gazebo simulator with the robot navigating various indoor environments. Our results showed that adding an attention mechanism to the network could improve its performance on loop closures that weren't perfectly aligned and had significant disparities in image scale. Our findings suggest that this approach has the potential to enable robots to navigate complex and dynamic environments with greater ease.

Video-on-Demand (VoD) is becoming increasingly popular among users due to its flexibility and convenience, which aligns with the growing demand for high-quality digital video experiences. Providing VoD requires substantial bandwidth, storage, and processing resources, which necessitates reliable and performant network infrastructure. To meet these demands, Content Distribution Networks (CDNs) and cloud services collaborate to deliver smooth, uninterrupted video experiences. Building upon prior research in optimizing CDNs, this study extends the problem to incorporate cloud services, focusing on selecting and locating CDNs and cloud servers to minimize total costs, which includes server expenses, data transfer fees, and VoD operational costs. An iterative algorithm is proposed to address this complex problem, and its validity and superiority over random selection methods are demonstrated through numerical experiments.

We explore the thermal properties of a two-dimensional graphene sheet with a parabolic band structure and linear dispersion, subject to an external magnetic field and doping.
Using the semi-classical approach, we derive the density of states, then go on to examine the density, quasiparticle energy, and renormalized quasiparticle velocity.
This allows for an investigation of the impact of doping on the specific heat and magnetoplasma oscillations in the zero-temperature state.
Our findings reveal that in the overdoped regime, the volume of the Fermi surface becomes highly sensitive to the presence of Landau levels, leading to regular fluctuations in the zero-temperature specific heat.

Recent advances in voice synthesis using deep learning have achieved naturalness comparable to that of real human speech. While existing models excel at capturing speech content, they fall short in capturing expressiveness and emotional nuances. To bridge this gap, the MaskedSpeech system was proposed. Based on the framework of Masked Language Modeling, MaskedSpeech adapts by masking emotional expressions in target speech and masking semantic variations in neutral speech. ByMaskedSpeech training process involves two stages:MaskedSpeech loss and auxiliary masking loss. The training process was conducted both jointly and sequentially to optimize results. Experimental evaluations on the expression control task demonstrated superior performance of MaskedSpeech over existing controls by accurately capturing emotional expressiveness and naturalness. Furthermore, systematic evaluations confirmed the model's expression control capabilities and provided guidance for future research directions.

We examine a solitary wave system governed by a non-linear Schrödinger equation that incorporates both anharmonic oscillator and cubic non-linearity. Equilibrium states for this system are characterized using a minimum surface method that involves both potential and energy functionals. The anharmonic oscillator's non-cooperative nature disrupts the orbital stability of the equilibria, making them saddle points or unstable stationary points, ultimately leading to a decay of the wave's amplitude. In contrast, the non-cooperative behavior of the focusing equation does not have the same stabilizing effect, allowing the solitary waves to persist despite these influences.

This study explores the feasibility of Q-balls in theoretical frameworks featuring multiple stabilizing symmetries, regardless of whether they are identical or different. The researchers have determined the conditions under which Q-balls can form in scenarios where multiple symmetries are present. They also examined several specific cases and derived both general criteria for the existence of Q-balls as well as more limited conditions for scenarios where all symmetries are the same. The results indicate that both scalar and boson Q-ball densities are directly related to the product of the breaking vacuum expectation values of the equivalent scalars and both symmetry charges. The researchers found that Q-balls can form in scenarios where both same and different symmetries coexist, as long as certain conditions are met involving the potential energy, mass and self-coupling terms. Additionally, the researchers discovered that the formation of Q-balls in theories with multiple stabilizing symmetries is possible even when the same-symmetry case is not met, provided that the ratio between the potential energy and the product of the breaking vacuum expectation values of both scalaries falls within a certain range.

A universe model that evolves in cycles, ruled by a form of energy known as holographic dark energy, has been examined through the principles of cyclic cosmology and its corresponding boundary conditions. An analysis was conducted to determine the present and past entropies of the cosmos, based on the Hubble parameter's details within a cyclic $\\Lambda$-CDM model. The effect of the Granda-Oliveros cutoff on the model's behavior was also assessed. The study revealed that the cyclic model, influenced by a cyclic parameter called $\\tau$, can vary from mimicking an expanding de Sitter universe, characterized by constant dark energy density, to cyclical contraction and expansion, influenced by the universe's size at the transition point. Consequently, the cosmos' entropy within this model may exhibit either a cyclic pattern or an irreversible increase, depending on the cutoff's choice.

A function L(s) associated with a graph G and coefficients a_n can be expressed in terms of its covering graphs, specifically those with n edges, as a_n equals F_n times a_n for various n. Alternatively, an expression can be derived for the covering graphs Γ of G, having edge index f, which leads to the L-function LG(s) being represented as the sum from n equals 1 to infinity of a_n divided by n to the power s. Consequently, LG(s) can be written as the sum over LG(f(s-f), s) times a_n. Therefore, the L-function of the covering graph Γ is related to the L-function of G through this equation.

This paper delves into specific instances of a broader issue concerning adding Galois modules over finitely generated modules in highly ramified rational field extensions. Considerable interest exists in rational number field extensions in significant Galois modules when viewing applications to Iwasawa theory and global class field theory. Unfortunately, generally there is a substantial increase in the size of the resulting field tower when adding a single element to an existing Galois module, which often results in a highly complicated field with undesirable properties. Nevertheless, in this paper we make some exceptions to this rule concerning small-degree non-abelian field extensions in relation to the p-adic integers ring, its quotient, and its finite rank free module projections. Both theoretical aspects and practical algorithms are covered, along with several examples of size-four p-adic integers module generators identified for the maximal unramified p-adic Solvable-3 extension of the rational numbers.

The search for invisible decays of new particles with no electric charge is a primary focus for experiments at the Large Hadron Collider and the future electron-positron collider at ILC. Due to the varying nature of these particles, no unified approach to detecting them exists. This article outlines suitable search strategies based on the characteristics of neutral long-lived particles.

The number of factors that affect a word's meaning in a given situation varies across different contexts, which can significantly change the way we interpret changes in meaning over time. Rather than assuming that changes in contextual variance alone explain semantic shifts, our research highlights the importance of considering how context itself changes, using a dataset consisting of over thirteen million pairs of word-context pairs and demonstrating measurable effects on contextual representations.

Although highly constrained by experiments, the existence of ultra-light particles with masses in the micro-electron voltage range is still plausible. If such particles truly exist, they could significantly alter the characteristics of dark matter. This study aims to answer key questions about the particles, including their impact on dark matter's thermal equilibrium, interaction with photons, and detection possibilities. The findings reveal a rather sterile environment for the particles, with limited opportunities to interact with photons, making their detection challenging. However, more sensitive experiments may have the ability to detect the rare inelastic scattering events, providing valuable insights into the particles and potentially new ways to investigate the axion field.

To understand nuclear migration dynamics within the developing retina, a mathematical model employing a Stokes flow framework was created. This model accounts for collective movement induced by epithelial contraction, featuring a region representing the retinal neuroblastic layer with a varying rate of nuclear production. The model's results show that nuclei distribution within the retina is governed primarily by a source term, which aligns with anatomical observations and matches experimental data from live-imaged X. laevis retinae. Furthermore, this model defines three distinct zones where nuclei exhibit different migratory behaviors: an expansion area featuring spreading nuclei, a shrinking zone exhibiting condensed nuclei, and a transitional zone exhibiting random motion. The characteristics of these zones are directly influenced by rates of nuclear production and a unique shrinking threshold. The model predicts that nuclei accumulate within the retinal expanding region before migrating into contracting areas, where they condense into distinct retinal layers. These findings provide an mechanistic explanation for how x. laevis retinae organize themselves during development.

In compressed sensing, minimizing mutual coherence in the sensing matrix is vital for efficiently reconstructing images. To achieve this, a novel nonconvex mutual coherence minimization (MCM) model has been proposed. Theoretical guarantees of convergence for a specific iterative optimization algorithm have been established, and its effectiveness has been demonstrated through numerical experiments, including 2D color image compression tests. The results of these tests show that the proposed MCM model outperforms the conventional coherence matrix (PCM) in terms of performance.

We've developed a theoretical framework to explain the force-mediated interactions found in activity-limited systems, based on momentum-conserving hydrodynamics. This framework extends beyond the limitations of linearized hydrodynamics by incorporating nonlinear feedback between hydrodynamics and activity. Our model reveals that in dimensions between 2 and 5, the hydrodynamics are influenced by the intrinsic stochasticity of the particles' motion and that long-range hydrodynamic interactions can facilitate the self-organization of actively moving particles into flows, rotationals, and shapes, despite the possible effect of hydrodynamic turbulence in dimension 4.

This research delves into the underlying causes of vulnerability to social engineering in academic settings, focusing on one specific area, with broader implications applicable to other domains. Initially, we collected data from three sources: published VulnReports, actual data from the CRIPTO project, and surveys distributed to the Italian section of the LFX Consortium. Consequently, we identified and categorized the root causes of security issues within open-source project communities, as well as the efficacy of mitigation strategies. Additionally, we examined the influence of community events on security concerns, as well as the influence of social media on these security vulnerabilities. Finally, we propose a set of guidelines tailored to enhance the security of online academic communication communities, including mailing lists, forums, and collaboration platforms, by addressing the identified underlying causes.

A copper-based cuprate material, La$_3$Ru$_2$O$_7$, undergoes a structural transition at $T_c$ from cubic to rhombohedral symmetry. Using La$_3$Ru$_2$O$_7$ single crystals, a structural, electronic, and magnetic investigation was performed to understand the $T_c$-by-passing 'exceptional' transition. A 'soft' mode mode, linked to the $T_c$ transition, was not found, and DFT simulations showed that the cubic and non-cubic phases are separated by a 'critical' mode. At $T_c$, electronic and Hall resistivity exhibit kinks, and magnetoresistance shows a 'critical' peak. At $T_c$, specific heat $C_p/T$ shows a lambda-like peak, and NMR confirms that there is no spontaneous magnetic moment. These findings suggest that La$_3$Ru$_2$O$_7$ undergoes a 'critical' transition at $T_c$ to a non-collinear, non-itterate chiral magnet order. Notably, this transition is characterized 'by' an 'exceptional' van Hove singularity 'by' a Lifshitz transition. A model combining a 'critical' mode, a 'critical' interaction, and a 'critical' magnetization shows that the observed phenomena can be explained if the 'critical' mode couples linearly to the 'critical' interaction but quadratically to

Our study examined the performance of a digital liquid scintillator (S2190) enhanced with added Gadolinium for detecting neutrons, in response to a low-energy threshold of 250 keV_{ee}.  Using simulated events from the GENIE neutron interaction model and compared Monte Carlo simulations with real data, we found that adding Gadolinium increases the detection efficiency of neutrons by approximately 25% and raises their average reconstruction energy by ~150 keV, without significantly affecting the electronic recoil background (~5 keV).  Our results demonstrate that using S2190 with Gadolinium can effectively distinguish low-energy neutrons from electronic recoil events.

This paper formulates a version of the minimax principle suited for problems where the underlying space is not compact. We provide sufficient conditions for solution persistence under (PS) $c$-compactness assumptions. Key applications include establishing solution sets' lower semi-continuity in perturbed functionals, saddle point persistence in noncompact settings, and (PS) $0$-compactness implications.

According to recent studies, a star's characteristics significantly influence the planetary configurations within its system, thereby influencing the systems' overall diversity. Establishing this connection and characterizing this diversity are crucial steps toward developing effective retrieval strategies for exoplanets. We utilize mock data generated with the CHIRON model to create 10,000 simulated star systems, each containing one to three planets spanning 0.05-10 star habitable zones. We observe that retreating binaries, multiple habitable zone giants, and other archetypes occur frequently in these simulated systems. We also find that binary and star properties have distinct effects on architecture diversity. Specifically, star activity influences the occurrence of close giant planets, while binary and star activity show negligible effects on architecture diversity. We hope that these insights will aid the EXoplanet Characterisation Observatory in achieving its characterization goals.

Identifying information from ID cards involves extracting text from an image and verifying its accuracy through text correction techniques.
Traditionally, text correction was accomplished by translating text into structural rules using formal grammars in mathematical grammar systems.
However, this approach has limitations due to the complexity of natural language, which hinders accurate text representation.
This paper proposes a novel integration of neural networks in a mathematical grammar system by introducing a neural-enhanced mathematical grammar model (NEMG).
In this model, the extraction of text from IDs is facilitated by first performing character-level features learning through neural networks,
followed by parsing the features into structural syntax trees using formal grammars.
Experimental results demonstrate that NEMG significantly outperforms traditional methods, achieving a substantial increase in accuracy when IDs are obscured with noise,
with a text extraction accuracy of 93.03 percent compared to a baseline accuracy of 76.96 percent.

A new approach has been developed to study driven quantum systems under sudden changes, known as driven quantum calculations based on coherent states. This framework incorporates external forces and internal interactions, allowing for an efficient representation of the time-evolving density matrix. By minimizing the appropriate functional, a highly accurate approximation of the real system can be achieved, regardless of any parameter related to the size of the system. For two classic examples, the model yields predictions that closely match both experimental observations and theoretical findings, particularly in describing metastable behaviors and complex energy landscapes of a driven double-well system.

We present four new data points for the accelerating rotation of detected asteroids, 
derived from the fact that their echo chirp rates remain consistent across the detection 
duration. The fact that this acceleration persists despite the tidal forces exerted by 
Earth provides lower bounds on the tensile strength of these detections. Additionally, 
the data suggests that their mass must be insignificant in comparison to Earth's mass. 
If the echoes represent a solid surface reflecting a singular beam of light, the size 
of this surface is sufficient to explain the echo observations, with potential 
implications for the total mass of this surface being comparable to or exceeding Earth's 
mass. Alternatively, darker or rougher regions could scatter light in directions that 
account for the observed signals. We estimate that at least two out of four detections 
are likely man-made, given their accelerating rotation and infinite lifespan, although 
further analysis is needed to fully understand their nature.

The evolution of online communities is influenced by individual motivations to engage, as well as the dynamic nature of the internet, making it challenging to track. This study focuses on a online forum dedicated to political discussion, aiming to observe the stability of participant membership over time. By analyzing discussion frequency, online activity, user reputation, ideological alignment, and utterance content, researchers built a reputation score for over 10,000 users using a topic modeling approach. An Markov model then assessed the stability of community participation. The findings indicate that while most users maintain consistent political views, both new and established users can shift their alignment, resulting in users changing their forum participation status. The research demonstrates the limitations of online communities and highlights the difficulty of defining clear boundaries, as users often operate across multiple platforms.

If the subgroup G acts non-trivially on the interior of a compact surface that's embedded in a larger surface, then the action of G on this surface is both highly uniform and involves limited movement, according to research by Le Boudec.

We present an improved understanding of M-dwarf masses and sizes, based on a new analysis that incorporates a comprehensive dataset correcting for previously unaccounted selection effects in M-dwarf radius data. Our results reveal a new M-dwarf mass-radius relation, which when combined with refined radius values, yields an upgrade to M-dwarf density data. Through a stepwise regression method, we determined the best empirical formula for this mass-radius relation, which is then used to calculate corresponding M-dwarf density.
