to 14% over their training data alone. Specifically, we found that incorporating
a static analyzer\'s feedback into the training process enables the neural
models to generalize better to unseen inputs and produce more robust code that
is less prone to logical errors.

A massive X16.2 class solar flare took place on November 7, 2004, when a powerful 'X-class' solar eruption suddenly appeared in an active region near the solar central. This research analyzes GOES X-ray satellite monitoring data to pinpoint the initial X-class component of the 2004 event. A smaller F-class component was discovered to have appeared on the solar eastern limb before merging with the X16.2 component. To better understand this rare case, 3D reconstructions using SHADOW-3D software were created for both components. These reconstructions show that the X16.2 component consisted of three distinct magnetic loops, while the smaller component displayed a simpler two-loop structure.

We analyze a relativistic fluid with vector and scalar viscosities in $d$-dimensional space, focusing on linear perturbations of an equilibrium state. We derive general formulas for the dispersion relations of both vector and scalar modes and apply these to specific cases, including hot QCD and asymptotically Anti-de Sitter space. Our approach is non-perturbative in the viscosity coefficients. In dimensions higher than two, we compare our results to those of invariant holographic models and find the large-temperature agreement for scalar modes in dimensions three and four. However, there is a fundamental discrepancy with the underlying microscopical foundations between our approach and the invariant holographic models. Similarly, we apply the invariant approach to d-dimensional relativistic viscous fluid described by the viscosity to entropy density ratio $\frac{\eta}{s} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{d-2}{d}\frac{1}{T}$ and discuss the resulting non-linear equilibrium trajectories in a broader context.

This research presents a novel form of anomaly detection that can be repeated multiple times, utilizing the decision function from previous data without reprocessing it. The proposed method only incorporates newly added data for further enhancement. It designs an efficient approach for quickly implementing the new information using a limited number of data samples. The new approach has a distinct advantage in that it defines the anomalies clearly using a specific probability distribution known as the mixture Gaussian model. This model represents the anomalies distinctly from the normal data, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the subject at hand.

In the context of cryptographic security, this research investigates a specific aspect of deniable encryption systems, focusing on the paradox of the government being able to force a respondent to decrypt data under certain conditions in deniable encryption schemes. The study aims to resolve this paradox by examining the practical utility of multiple coexistence between voluntary and coerced communications in different encryption schemes. The proposed resolution introduces two variations of the deniable encryption system: multi-world and utopic world scenarios. In the first, there is no distinction between communications sent willingly and those sent under duress, while the second scenario permits only one communications to be decrypted by the government, with all other communications remaining secure. Presenting concrete real-world applications for both scenarios, the study building on prior relevant research and theoretical frameworks.

This project develops an end-to-end modeling framework for comparing four MDI-QKD protocols: the initial proposal by Patel et al., the E91 protocol with single-photon sources implemented by Bartsch et al., the protocol by Furrer et al., and the protocol by Zhang et al.. Utilizing a comprehensive model of the free-space channel, we simulate and analyze the performance, error rates, and key rates of each QKD protocol in an eye-safe bandwidth range of 1.5 $\mu$m to 1.6 $\mu$m for ground-to-ground, ground-to-satellite, and satellite-to-satellite scenarios. We believe our work will be a valuable resource for researchers in the field of QKD, especially those working on free-space applications.

Given a set of allowed constraints for a general-valued constraint satisfaction problem (CSP), can we find the smallest possible solution value? Under which conditions does a PTAS exist? Researchers have previously established a broader class of problems for which PTAS is achievable in the binary domain. This study expands those findings by demonstrating the existence of a PTAS for specific types of non-binary exact constraints (e.g., all-relatives and all-equal) without unifiably solvable 3-unary instances. Furthermore, an alternative condition understanding the distinction between approximability and uniqueness of solutions for valuations taking values in {0,1-?} has been developed and shown to have practical applications in designing approximation algorithms for specific valuations with exact constraints.

A new approach is proposed to enable high-order numerical methods to accurately resolve time-dependent mean field games models. This method involves constructing a high-order scheme at a series of time points and interpolating the results to approximate the time derivative within the mean field games equations at each individual time point. Utilizing a local time-parallel multiblock technique, we solve the resulting set of implicit linear systems in a decoupled manner over multiple spatial subdomains at each time step. Our results demonstrate that this method is efficient in solving time-dependent problems on a large scale, particularly when employing this strategy in conjunction with a robust iterative multi-block domain decomposition scheme to reach a convergent solution for the coupled problem.

Recent advancements in machine learning, particularly deep learning, have led to remarkable breakthroughs in image recognition. However, these methods lack transparency, preventing users from understanding how they arrive at certain conclusions. As a result, there is a growing need for transparent and interpretable solutions, such as explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). While research on effective XAI techniques has gained traction, the correlation between the success of these approaches and the performance of underlying deep learning models remains unclear. This study fills this knowledge gap by investigating the relationship between the efficacy of XAI methods and the performance of the underlying models. Our analysis reveals that, contrary to expectations, the chosen XAI technique has a more significant impact on usability and user trust than the underlying model. However, the relationship between the underlying model and the effectiveness of the XAI method is non-monotonic. This work's results have important implications for the design of future AI systems integrating XAI.

Researchers have identified a unique star named KIC 9267654, also known as HD 53365, which possesses a highly unusual rotation profile. This profile shows a significant increase in rotation speed towards the star's poles compared to its equator, unlike any other previously studied stars. To further understand this phenomenon, the team utilized existing data, along with spectroscopic analysis, to examine the characteristics of KIC 9267654. They confirmed that the star is a stable, intermediate-age K2 type star with minimal activity levels. However, the extent of its oblateness remains uncertain, with potential options including aspherical rotation, the presence of a spot, or a geometric effect from its rapid rotation. The researchers highlight the need for more in-depth analysis to solve this puzzle and suggest possible future avenues for exploration, including gravitational spectroscopy and imaging.

Fake news poses significant threats to individuals, communities, and even to critical systems like electricity, especially as we rely increasingly on social media for information. There are various techniques to assess the credibility of information, but they often demand human input or are limited to specific types of news. This research introduces a novel, multi-input framework called MetaFEND, a deep learning system designed to detect fake news across diverse, human-in-the-loop features such as textual content, multimedia, contextual information, and domain-specific indicators like political stance. As Textual, Situal, and Domainal features are not directly accessible, MetaFEND extracts them from raw data using pre-trained models. Furthermore, we address a unique issue where these features are interconnected. To resolve this, we employ a dynamic multi-task learning architecture called MetaFEND, which fuses these features to improve detection accuracy. Evaluations on three diverse datasets demonstrate that MetaFEND outperforms both human judgments and current state-of-the-art methods in detecting fake news, textual satire, and situational situationality. The code for this project is publicly available at https://github.com/AliMohaghegh./metaFEND.

Consider a one-dimensional periodic transport equation with nonlocal flux and no dissipation. When started with smooth odd initial data, the system's behavior during runtime $T > 0$ results in the creation of singularities. Upon approaching times $(2k\ L/\ |p|)\ +\ \epsilon$ for nonnegative integers $k$ and a fixed small $\epsilon$, the system's periodicity resurfaces.

This research delves into the time-average information freshness (AoI) under a generalized version of the Single-Server Parallel Update (SSPU) protocol, specifically within discrete time systems. A key aspect of our analysis is the varying age of information at each time step, under the conditions that packet generation, aging, and success probabilities are both stationary and independent. The paper presents the stationary AoI distribution probability in detailed form, as well as an approximation in the context of continuous time systems. The findings demonstrate that the probability of stationary AoI in discrete time systems cannot be fully replicated by continuous time systems, highlighting the limitations of continuous time approximations in capturing the intricacies of information freshness under discrete time systems.

On a vector space V with a symmetric non-degenerate form, admissible Drinfeld twists within the quantified symmetric space have been constructed under specific conditions, with conditions also derived for the admissible drinfeld twists in the quantified Drinfeld triangle.

Researchers have discovered that constructing quaternary Golay complementary pairs of length $L$ necessitates a sequence with magnitude zero at position $l=l_0$ in the autocorrelation difference quotal polynomial, where $0 \leq l_0 < L$. Additionally, it has been proven necessary that $L$ must be divisible by four. Building on this foundation, we present two methods for constructing binary and quaternary GCAPs based on a specific scalar value $\sigma$. The first method involves using the difference between two powers of four minus one. The second method employs the difference between four times $L$ minus one and the square of two. Both methods ensure the resulting sequence's GCA autcorrelation difference polynomial's minimum quotal value $\lfloor L/4\rfloor$.

The exchange interaction in "Si" connects two electron spins isolated within the "Si" structure.  It is sensitive to the positioning of donor atoms within the "Si" lattice.  By applying an electric field in "Si", we can shift donor positions.  Here, however, we explore the more practical process of moving donors via the placement of extra electrons during n-type process.  Using a combination of tight-binding and force calculations, we investigate the exchange interaction in "Si" with donor placement.  Our findings contradict recent results in other "Si" structures "Si", indicating that in bulk "Si", increasing donor concentration leads to a rise in the exchange interaction $J$.  This result can be utilized to enhance spin-qubit gate fidelity without resorting to dense electron placement.

This research extends probabilistic inference on dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs) by considering the scenario where some variables and their relationships are unknown. Given a set of previously established variable observations, we treat their hidden correlations as unknown parameters within a specific mathematical framework. By applying a Bayesian approach and a variational method, we can simultaneously infer missing variable values and estimate unknown relationships. This approach is compatible with BISTEN's algorithm, a popular option for inferring variables in DBNs. Numerical simulations have shown that our proposed method performs better than standard techniques, including those that assume no relationships between similar variables.

In this study, we examine the connections between polynomial rings in stable homotopy theory and representations in stable homotopy theory. Specifically, Weibel's definition of graded polynomial rings in stable homotopy theory builds upon Le's concept of a graded polynomial ring in triangulated categories. Moreover, polynomial functors and idempotents within these rings give rise to filters on stable homotopy categories. Notably, Le's framework allows for a more comprehensive comparison of these filters across polynomial rings in stable homotopy settings, providing a more in-depth analysis than previously achievable.

Deep learning-based convolutional neural networks have revolutionized automated detection and segmentation of anomalies in medical imaging. However, the task remains challenging due to the need to identify multiple patient-specific regions of interest within high-resolution 3D images. This paper introduces a novel, memory-efficient CNN architecture that efficiently segments anomalies in volumetric medical images. The proposed network utilizes shared and private filter banks, coupled with cross-channel information exchange to accurately localize and classify targets. It achieves exceptional performance on widely used datasets such as CAMUS and ARTS, demonstrating significant improvements over existing methods. The model's efficiency makes it an ideal framework for real-time applications.

Research on quantum nonlocality in multipartite systems has made significant progress in recent years, particularly in demonstrating strong nonlocality in certain entangled states that cannot be classified as genuinely entangled. This work classifies all four-partite states showing strong nonlocality within unextendible product bases of an eight-dimensional Hilbert space, demonstrating that some states with weak correlations among all four-party combinations possess strong nonlocality when considered as a whole. Notably, we found four-partite states that are classically equivalent to four-qubit W-states but lack the quantum nonlocality found in W-states, revealing that W-state quantum nonlocality is a result of its intrinsic, entangled structure rather than its topological properties.

For upcoming large-scale spectroscopic surveys using automated systems, ensuring project efficiency and data safety necessitates precise auto-tuning and verification methods. To achieve this, we employ Bayesian optimization to dynamically adjust and validate trajectories for astrobots. Specifically, we use an epsilon-greedy method for validation and a simple, adaptive model for tuning. When applied to a simulated survey, this approach demonstrates significant improvements in data yield, increasing it by $14\%$ and extending astrobot uptime by $6\%$ compared to default settings.

GP 2, a programming language and corresponding runtime system, is a graph-parallel alternative to traditional array-parallel languages like C++ with OpenMP and the prefix "p" and Intel TBB. It was created to utilize modern multi-core processors while taking advantage of advanced features on these types of processors. However, GP 2 was derived from an earlier version called GP which used a data structure called BigArray that is incompatible with modern memory architectures. To address this limitation, a new BigArray has been designed and implemented as a replacement, bringing GP 2 significant performance enhancements. This new BigArray component delivers comparable performance to the previous version on previous memory systems, but delivers substantial improvements against it on modern memory systems, making GP 2 once again a viable viable array-parallel solution.

Our proposal offers a unified approach to resolving the issue of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction, with the ability to address the problem solely through unsupervised methods or add labeled data for a more targeted solution. The framework's design allows for a range of existing unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques to be incorporated as specific configurations. Experimental results from various benchmark datasets confirm the versatility and effectiveness of the framework, with the ability to be integrated into the cycle-consistency framework and combined with the non-negative self-expression method, yielding superior performance compared to the sum of their separate results.

We've created unlimited number of symmetric automorphism groups in endless numbers using a technique, and seven families of them were defined previously with specific properties. In the process, new unlimited number of symmetric automorphism groups were discovered, nine of which were cyclic, seven more were identified as diagonal linear groups consisting of matrices with specific components. A key finding made here is the proof of two new unlimited number of symmetric automorphism groups using a method that involved applying the lemma from a paper by J. H. Kwak and C. Park.

To achieve effective model fit and optimal variable selection for both continuous and categorical data, we developed the Group Lasso-ALEIX method of mixed L1/L2. This new approach builds on the Group Lasso algorithm, which creates subgroups of correlated coefficients within each block of parameters. As a result, it excludes entire blocks of coefficients from the model, making it computationally efficient. We then incorporated a stochastic approximation of the Approximate Entropy Index, which quantifies model sparsity by counting only non-zero coefficients. This index allows us to determine the most suitable model size automatically, without relying on information criteria, cross-validation, or BIC. We evaluated our method through extensive simulation studies and a real-world dataset to verify its performance.

Recent developments in question-answering have focused on utilizing contextualized encoders pretrained on extensive text corpora. While these models have achieved remarkable results, their ability to correctly infer answers from complex descriptions is limited by their tendency to replicate training data errors. This problem often arises because standard corpora lack a substantial amount of underlying knowledge, such as that found in knowledge graphs. To bridge this gap, we propose FACT triples, a large-scale collection of simple, fact-based statements used for pre-training. Consisting of around 2 billion entries on topics ranging from science to world history, these triples enhance the model's ability to recognize entailed statements. Our PreTrive base model, pretrained on FACT triples and optimized for efficient scaling, now scales effectively to massive corpora and achieves significant improvements in various question-answering tasks, including natural language inference, zero-shot factual knowledge question-answering, and dense question-answering, outperforming previous context-aware baselines.

This study explores the asymptotic behavior of nonlocal diffusion models as they converge to classical PDE representations. A key aspect examined is how long-tailed kernels influence this limit, with implications for fractional diffusion models. Our analysis diverges from standard compactness-based approaches, utilizing instead the Young measure method to tackle higher regularity questions commonly encountered in PDE work.

Traditional panoramic stitching methods rely on high-end equipment, precisely aligned sensors, and complex algorithms. In contrast, our proposed approach utilizes commercially available sensors to automatically capture images from any angle and produce seamless panoramas. By leveraging inertial measurement units (IMUs) to quickly estimate the change in orientation between consecutive images, our method reduces computational demands and eliminates errors caused by sensor misalignment. The results from our approach are comparable to traditional techniques, but with improved ease of use and lower cost. The benefits of this approach are demonstrated through numerous real-world test scenarios.
This study places previous findings regarding degenerate Eisenstein series parametric cosets of the Weyl group within a broader context, encompassing the entire Weyl group cosets.

How can mathematical modeling contribute to improving our understanding, diagnosis, and treatment of complex systems such as living organisms? What lessons from successful applications of computational models in diverse fields can be applied to the development of effective therapies for Parkinson's Disease? Why is it essential for researchers to collaborate across diverse disciplines to create accurate biological models? How can such models benefit both the medical community and computer scientists working on neural simulations? What is NeuroVirtex - a novel framework for parallelizing neuronal simulations on GPU architectures, and what are its key features in terms of versatility, usability, and performance optimizations?

To visualize basic ordered data effectively, ordered line charts are a useful tool. Traditional methods using《Adobe Illustrator》or《Microsoft Visio》are cumbersome due to their lack of automated processing and preset templates. In contrast，《R》as a versatile data visualization language, is capable of seamless integration with《Illustrator》through《Cairo》via《Ragg》, enabling the creation of customized fan-shaped line joins for ordered line charts through `bema` syntax extension. The resulting automated processing in `bema` streamlines ordered line chart production, while maintaining high-quality visualization suitable for print media.

The ATLAS3D study of outflows in four early-type galaxies offers a comprehensive analysis of the co-evolutionary process between galaxies and supermassive black holes through an energy budget that accounts for observed outflows, a key factor in understanding their co-evolution.  By conducting an in-depth analysis of the outflows' mass and kinetic energy, and comparing them to the available gravitational and UV/bolometric energies, the study finds that the outflows' energies are orders of magnitude less than the potential energies, suggesting that the galaxy mergers providing both a bulge merger energy and a supermassive black hole energy are efficient energy sources.  Although the feedback from star formation is effective in regulating both the galaxy and supermassive black hole growth, the results suggest that the outflows driven by active galactic nuclei are generally inefficient in doing so.  However, the study suggests that the most massive galaxies with significant outflows driven by active galactic nuclei may provide critical clues to the mechanism of active galactic nucleus-driven feedback. A new type of quasi-interpolation based on the stable inverse Gaussian multi-quadratic radial basis function has been successfully formulated. This study demonstrates that the formed QI operator preserves key mathematical properties, proving its efficacy in capturing the essential behavior of a target function. Through successful reconstruction of mathematical functions and real-world data, the operator's superiority over traditional QI operators based on the multiquadric and inverse multiquadric has become evident.

Deep Learning technology has gained significant popularity in the medical field over the last decade due to its superior performance in various tasks, including super pixel delimiting mask (SPDM) classification. Despite these advancements, acquiring a vast collection of labeled data remains a challenge for researchers. To address this issue, we developed an innovative data augmentation technique that selectively modifies SPDM labels to preserve anatomical relationships between organs. By applying this technique to train a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), we found a notable 5% improvement in accuracy compared to random data augmentation, based on evaluations using three publicly available datasets. To further enhance the CNN's performance, we incorporated two innovative components: a hierarchy-based loss function and a dynamic class weight adjustment mechanism. These additions enabled the CNN to achieve 84.64% accuracy on the Atlantis dataset and 94.49% accuracy on the ArterySPDM dataset, outperforming the existing state-of-the-art methods in SPDM classification. All our code is openly available on GitHub.

Speech enhancement is typically done with models trained end-to-end to map noisy spectrograms to clean ones. While effective, these models require large amounts of data for training and struggle to account for unseen noise sources. To address these limitations, we propose a physics-inspired deep learning framework called the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN). This framework uses two deep learning components trained separately to estimate the speech and noise spectra from a noisy input. By multiplying the estimated speech spectrum with the inverse of the estimated noise spectrum, we obtain a more accurate prediction of the speech enhancement ratio. To further refine this approach, we employ an iterative method to solve the resulting optimization problem. Experimental results show that DPCRN achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple speech enhancement benchmarks.

Detailed comparisons of observations from the WMAP and Planck missions along the anisotropic sky show strong evidence for a dark sector of nature. Statistical disparities between standard cosmological models can be reduced to minimal levels within the inflationary paradigm. However, further reduction of these disparities may be achieved by analyzing the turn-around radii of one-year-old hyperbolic clusters. Although these radii are predicted to be significantly asymmetric along the dipole axis and display minimal symmetry around the plane perpendicular to this axis, analyzing this asymmetry can provide insights into the dark sector of nature. Consequently, it is proposed that future plans for probing dark energy with satellite tools should include an assessment of the turn-around radii of nearby clusters, complementing the research initiated by the XENON experiment.

Our work derives exact formulas for the heat and momentum transfer between two fluid layers with different temperatures but the same temperature at the surface. These formulas enable us to calculate the heat flux that passes through the boundary between the two fluid layers. By applying this calculation to a system with temperature-driven circulation, created by the difference in temperature at the surface and the resistance to motion caused by air's tendency to oppose movement,我们发现 a simple two-fluid model accurately predicts the complex relationship of heat flow in the system, which follows the power law $Q \propto Ra^\frac{1}{2},$ for $Ra \gg 1,$ even without considering any additional complexity, such as the wide range of scales of motion that typically appear in these systems. This result supports an alternative perspective on the existence of the wide range of scales of motion that typically appear in these systems.

We investigate the potential for creating entanglement among multiple particles using a optical cavity, even when the cavity itself is already entangled with one of the atoms. Our focus is on a system consisting of an empty cavity that interacts with two identical atoms, each with the same spin, and we examine how this interaction can lead to a highly entangled state known as a GHZ state. Even a small amount of entanglement between the cavity and the atoms is sufficient to facilitate this process. However, the gap between the energy levels of the system plays a crucial role, as we demonstrate that GHZ states can be generated regardless of whether the GHZ potential (GHZability) is positive or negative. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of introducing entanglement between the atoms before the cavity interacts with them, and we find that the amount of entanglement between the particles can lead to different outcomes in terms of GHZability. Finally, we explore the possibility of creating GHZ states in a more complex spin chain, where the interaction between the particles can result in both state creation and destruction.

This paper reanalyzes the measurement of the dipole angle $\lambda$ in the decay process $B^0_d\to J/\psi K^0_s$ using a combined sample of $3.8$ TeV $pp$ collision data from the LHC, collected by the CMS detector at rates of $2.3$ fb$^{-1}$ and $2.0$ fb$^{-1}$ respectively. The analysis builds on the previous study of the decay process $B^0_d\to J/\psi K^0_s$ in the $7$ TeV $pp$ collisions, where only the $B^0_d$ meson decay was considered. Since then, significant improvements have been made to the CMS detector and its trigger system, allowing for the selection of $B^0_d\leftrightarrow B^0_d$ oscillation opposite-sign dimuon events directly at the detection level. With these advances, both $B^0_d$ and $B^0_d$ contributions to the dimuon mass invariant distribution are taken into account when analyzing the dipole angle $\lambda$ parameter. This study is a crucial step in updating the $B^0_d$ meson decay parameter $\lambda$ first studied by the Collaborations at energies of $7$ TeV. With the new data and improved detector, a final result of $\lambda = -0.78 \pm 0.27 \text{(stat)} \

Using the $1/N$ expansion, we calculated the glueball spectrum for SU($N$) Yang-Mills theories in various dimensions. This analysis involved constructing effective potentials for 't Hooft's large $N$ theory on a lattice, applying $1/N$ perturbation theory to determine the mass spectrum. The effectiveness of the proposed potential structures was validated through QCD simulations, and the theory successfully predicted the mass ratios of singlet states up to $N_{c}=4$ for dimensions three and four.

Social media platforms offer a means to observe public opinion and examine the emotions of individuals as they freely express themselves. For example, tracking stock market trends requires the classification of sentiments expressed in tweets related to the market. To accomplish this task effectively, state-of-the-art preprocessing techniques are employed to eliminate excessive English language forms and repeated words from the tweet data. Following this, an LSTM model with a classification layer is applied to interpret the sentiment expressed in the tweets, using a pre-trained Bengali word vector. This approach yields high accuracy in sentiment classification, especially when combined with BC5 preprocessing and a Bengali LSTM model, achieving an overall sentiment classification accuracy of 97.7 percent on a test dataset of 10 percent BC5-preprocessed tweets.

This study explores the impact of a non-linear charge parameter on both linear and non-linear Yang-Mills fields within a fixed curvature background. By applying variational principles, field equations are derived and solved using two methods: the effective potential approach and WKB approximation. Specifically, we investigate the shadow radius and scattering matrices of both black holes and asymptotically Anti-de Sitter (AdS) spaces for a fixed charge value of 1, assuming a semi-classical field with a spin value of 1/2 and a cosmological constant of -0.05. Findings reveal that non-linear charge parameter decreases both the shadow radius and scattering matrices for black holes and asymptotically AdS spaces. Additionally, we analyze the effect of non-linear charge parameter on the scattering matrices of a black hole with mass 0.9 and critical mass, finding that it increases the scattering matrices for masses less than the critical mass but has the opposite effect for masses greater than the critical mass. Furthermore we investigate how non-linear charge parameter influences the horizon temperature profile of a black hole in both fixed curvature and AdS spaces.

This work takes a different approach to quantum-risks associated with states possessing negative Wigner functions, seeking to examine these issues through the lens of measured data in form of optical tomograms. Indeed,some nonclassical effects can be pinpointed directly via entanglement-definitions tailored to observers who have access only to local measurements: for instance,the onset of quantum discord in two-mode coherent states or distinct behaviors in two-state cat-quenching models. Conversely, other phenomena like negentropy demands the analysis of full state-reconstruction matrices. In contrast, our approach aims at retrieving full Wigner functions purely from experimental data, bypassing theoretical assumptions. We outline an experimental roadmap to verify this claim and discuss the benefits and constraints of this method.

This study utilizes GPT-3's natural language generation capabilities to enhance GPT-NA.3's capabilities in dialogue management for a dialogue system. To determine the optimal role instructions that improve the dialogue system's performance, GPT-3 generates multiple potential role descriptions for each dialogue history and evaluates their effectiveness in guiding the dialogue system. By having GPT-3 selectively recommend the most suitable role specification, the dialogue system's performance sees a significant improvement in naturalness and coherence of the generated responses. These results showcase the efficacy of leveraging GPT-3's capabilities in natural language processing to boost dialogue system performance.

Decision support systems (DSS) have the potential to improve crop management by incorporating data on plant disease prevalence, leading to more effective and weather-adaptive guidance. Developing this function demands a sophisticated model that assesses disease spread, control measures, and the resulting impact on crop yield and profitability. This paper presents the first known strawberry production and protection data set from commercial greenhouses in Israel, collected over three consecutive years. Researchers analyzed how disease pressure influenced yield and profitability in relation to various mulching methods and greenhouse temperatures. A statistical model was then created to predict strawberry production and protection profitability, demonstrating a complex interaction between these factors. The resulting model is an essential tool for creating a disease-prevalence-based DSS module.

As 5G technology advances, next-generation immersive videos with 360-degree resolution are set to improve significantly. These videos require precise viewports to enhance transmission efficiency and viewport prediction accuracy is crucial. In this study, we investigate the use of video subtitles as a readily available source of information to enhance prediction accuracy. We develop a novel Deep Subtitle-Integrated Prediction Network, which integrates subtitles to create features that aid prediction. The network's design includes a subtitle embedding module, a viewport feature extraction network, a predictive module, and an innovative cross-module to improve performance. Our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on the available benchmark datasets, and our code and video samples are accessible on GitHub.

We have developed a precise and non-perturbative procedure for converting matrix product operators and thermal states into matrix product operators or extended matrix product operators definitions. This involves extending the PEPO structure in a way that does not result in a linear increase of bond dimensions with respect to interaction strength. Consequently, the initial definitions for both matrix product operators and thermal states are preserved, and they scale polynomially with interaction strength. By combining this method with an all-optimization algorithm, we achieve complete freedom in selecting step sizes during the diagonalization of small clusters. For a particular model, we discovered that very small bond dimensions are sufficient for accurately simulating thermal states and time evolution, even at moderate temperatures. Specifically, we found that moderate temperatures lead to significant reductions in peptide bond dimensions, peaking at extreme temperatures where temperatures are either much lower or much higher than the characteristic temperature.

This paper explores the decoupling inequality for canonical surfaces using a Taylor-based approach and canonical decouling as referenced in prior research. By applying a Taylor-based method, we obtain a bound of O(δ^(1/8)) decoupling constants, matching the result initially Conjectured by Benyi and Hu. A different tactic had been employed to achieve this bound but the current approach offers an alternative solution which is more consistent with the spirit of Grandmont's decoupling conjecture.

This paper presents a new, anisotropic version of the capacity expansion principle for balls and derives various inequalities from this concept, including context for the Brunn-Minkowski inequality, isoperimetric inequalities, and capacity inequalities for balls.

In measuring accelerations in the MICROSCOPE space experiment, short-duration spikes in noise were detected, lasting from one second to a single millisecond. These glitches, mostly under $10^{-11}\si{\gals}$ in amplitude, did not significantly impact the overall precision of the experiment due to their low frequency of occurrence. However, there were instances where glitches exceeded this threshold, reaching up to $10^{-10}\si{\gals}$ in $\approx 5\si{\hundred}$. To prevent potential bias in the final results, data from specific periods was excluded, and an overestimation of noise correlations with other factors led to increased estimates of test mass accelerations during glitch-prone periods. A analysis of test mass relative positions and the impact of ground noise revealed that glitches originated from and propagated through the experiment's support structure.

Many dimers composed of two interconnected rigid sections exhibit a consistent pattern of movement, present in nature and artificial systems.  We investigate the dynamics of these units using a theoretical model and discover that their motion can be categorized into two types: natural and induced.  We propose a strategy to describe their movement based on the "angle effect," which measures how perpendicular each section is to the other's axis of rotation.  This strategy is particularly useful in understanding the movement of active dimers and can provide insights into the design of three-segment swarms or trilocular cells.  A surprising outcome of our analysis is that a seagull's wing acts like a giant steering wheel, enabling the bird to guide its flight.  Our model successfully predicts the controlled flight observation, as well as the movement characteristics of other active dimers, including a submarine-like device that was recently guided by changing the angle between its sections.

This paper examines the k-strong shortest path cover problem from multiple perspectives. Initially, we establish that KSSPCK is an NP-hard optimization variant, followed by a description of several heuristic approaches. Subsequently, we apply a theoretical perspective to identify a strong cover as essential for reliable communication networks. From this viewpoint, an algorithmic solution involving Dijkstra's algorithm is proposed. Furthermore, we investigate a variant where pre-specified distances are used instead of standard distance calculations, which is crucial for real-world real-time applications. Given N nodes and a matrix representing pre-specified distances between all node pairs, we show that the variable cover length shortest path problem is NP-hard and provide a heuristic approach including a dynamic programming-style algorithm.

A study of vacuum polarisation structure within QCD was conducted, focusing on perturbative QCD expansions' divergence and the associated renormalons within a light-cone sum rule context. In particular, the research addressed vacuum polarisation structure's impact on determining the gluon distribution's behaviour at large $x$ and its effect on $x$-dependent non-singlet structure functions. It was found that a specific renormalon with $d = 2$ determines the ultimate divergence and contributes an intrinsic $O(\Lambda^2/\!x)$ component to the gluon distribution for $x \to 1$. Consequently, this implies that the gluon distribution is inherently uncertain in this region due to $\Lambda^2/\!x$ for $x \to 1$. In contrast, one power-suppressed term dominates in structure functions as $x \to 1$ and, due to the $x$-dependence, does not result in an $\Lambda^2$ uncertainty. As structure functions are experimentally observable at $x \to 1$, they are not affected by this specific renormalon. However, extracting the endpoint behaviour of the gluon distribution from structure functions is compromised by this specific renormalon.

A continuous frog model on a tree involves frogs sitting on vertices, each with its own independent Poisson process on the edges. When a frog moves along an edge, it subtracts one from the degree of that tree. We want to determine if there's a specific degree threshold where the model's behavior changes from transient to recurrent. We prove that above this threshold, the model is transient, regardless of the speed at which the frogs move. We also show that for infinite binary trees, the model is transient if the speed is at least two, three if it's one. We shrank this range to 1/2 in a subsequent paper.

This study uses full matrix method calculations and a ray-tracing analysis to reveal how surface plasmons and a Rayleigh anomaly interact in a context of magnetophotonic crystals. Furthermore, the interplay between these two phenomena is applied to explain the magneto-optical characteristics seen in these observations. The results show that the interference between surface plasmons and the Rayleigh anomaly gives rise to additional line shapes, as well as distinct features such as shifts, splits, and combinations of absorption lines, either appearing alone or in conjunction with bulk absorption.

We investigated knowledge distillation in a decision-based, black-box setting, a scenario where input sensitivities are ignored and only a single output is considered. Under these restricted conditions, we examined whether a student network could effectively learn from a teacher network's predictions. Initially, a basic exploration of our decision-based approach revealed that the model can learn the teacher's decisions to some extent. Subsequently, we delved into several key aspects, including generalization beyond initial training data, the transferability of knowledge, and the underlying learning mechanisms. Our research revealed signs of genuine knowledge transfer, providing evidence to support the feasibility of decision-based knowledge distillation.

A new technique has been employed to reduce hadronic uncertainty in subsequent flavour analyses by deriving flavour-agnostic parameters from fully independent data sets. This method is illustrated by studying the branching fractions and CP phases in charmed baryon decays, specifically $B^0\to \Lambda^0_c\bar{\Lambda}^0_c$, and $B^0,\bar{B}^0\to J/\psi J/\psi \Lambda^0_c$, using $pp$ collision data with an equivalent of 37$\, fb^{-1}$ at 13 TeV. Initially, search results for these decrees were inconclusive; however, utilizing a newly introduced set of sensitivity estimates for previously unobserved or weakly significant signals proved more accurate and cost-effective than standard statistical methods in this context.

Given a multiplicity free module $M$ within the category of modules for a algebraic group, Osofsker's work reveals that the lattice of submodules of $M$ contains sufficient information to reconstruct the module's composition factors, provided its Ext$^1$-relations are known. In this work, we explore the reconstruction of $M$ when some information within its submodule lattice is inaccessible due to module multiplicity. The paper also identifies specific lattice properties characteristic of certain modules and examines the reconstruction of Ext$^1$-relations from the submodule lattice. Additionally, we provide a method for extracting information about the Ext$^1$-relations between modules from their Ext-quivers from the submodule lattice.

The Strong Geodetic Problem involves determining whether there's a set of nonadjacent specified vertices in a graph that can generate every other vertex when it's the set's unique closure. This paper aims to explore the complexity of this problem when the target vertex set is not pre-defined. We investigate the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem, where we need to decide if a given subset of the graph's vertices is the unique closure of one of that graph's minimum sets. This study examines the problem's complexity for various types of graphs and shows it's NP-complete for trees, NP-hard for specific classes of graphs including caterpillars with maximum leg length of three, certain binary trees, and some regular graphs such as cycnadic graphs and Cayley trees of S_3.

This text presents a new method called TRAIL, which is a framework designed to streamline the use of imitation learning by enhancing sample efficiency through selective data collection. Imitation learning is an approach where an AI learns desired behavior by observing example outcomes, yet it often necessitates vast amounts of training data. In imitation learning projects employing MDPs with numerous states, a significant source of inefficiency arises from states that are irrelevant to achieving the target behavior and do not reflect differences in expert policy decisions. To overcome this challenge, sections reveal a method termed TRAIL, which is centered around two key elements: a side-channel feedback system providing expert comparison actions for taken actions, and a priority map that guides the collection of experiences during imitation learning. In the framework of TRAIL, each state-action pair is associated with a value from the priority map, which is guided by the side channel and expert actions, essentially estimating the benefit of adopting the expert's action over their own. To mitigate bias, sections combine this estimate with action weights from the side channel and expert actions. Consequently, states and actions that do not align with the expert's policy are less likely to be included in the data collected for imitation learning. To demonstrate the effectiveness of TRAIL, simulations using the gym-mdp suite indicate substantial enhancements in sample efficiency compared to baseline methods, with results showing up to fifty-fold improvements at a sample cost for policy evaluation that is negligible.

By integrating co-imitation learning, we can model and integrate multiple expert
guidance modes through interactions. Through co-imitation learning, we can
efficiently integrate various expert feedback to enhance the imitation
learning process, reducing both training time and device wear. Through
co-imitation learning, we can incorporate guidance from experts in
different forms of interactions. Through co-imitation policy
representation, we can integrate multi-modal expert feedback. Through
co-imitation training objective, we can design a unified learning
objective that accounts for additional expert guidance. Our experiments on
grid world and real-world kitchen tasks with Nao robots show that
co-imitation learning can produce more accurate and efficiently trained
policies when guided by multiple experts in various ways. Our code and data are
readily available to the research community at this GitHub link.

Depending on the stationary error rate of an independent sequence and a polarized cutoff rate employed as a bias value in a sequential decoder's decision process, there exists a specific error rate threshold for any given decoder, where the probability of decoding errors equals zero.

We investigate the potential of using reinforcement learning (RL) to enhance statistical machine translation tasks, specifically targeting scenarios where optimal target alignments are not readily available. Under such data-constrained conditions, we explore the concept of action-space optimization, using simple policy-based methods to search for alignments that maximize translation quality. Our investigation builds on this action-space optimization framework and extends it to a more complex, neural translation model. However, these results indicate that the optimization process yields a far greater benefit when applied to a simple model, providing optimal target alignments, or close to optimal data, it adds little to no improvement. Consequently, we hypothesize that a key advantage of using action-space optimization is its capability to simultaneously refine the action model and the target alignments.
This research focuses on end-effector pose estimation using an image-based method to enhance the stability of traditional calibration processes with an depth camera attached.

QFS-spaces constitute a novel framework that generalizes both QFTC-spaces and continuous retract spaces. QFS-spaces are characterized as spaces whose Hausdorff quotients are lower semi-continuous sets. Our study introduces conditions under which a space is a continuous retract by defining necessary and sufficient properties involving quotient maps and continuous subretracts. Specifically, we establish the equivalence of Hausdorff quotients to lower semi-continuous sets when continuous subretracts are present, as well as the identification of lower semi-continuous quotients when continuous subretracts are absent, both of which contribute to defining QFS-spaces. Additionally, our work provides an alternative formulation of QFTC-spaces based on lower semi-continuous quotients.

The extent of hyperlink architecture's contribution to online political polarization is further explored, coupled with additional factors such as user browsing patterns, which were analyzed in a previous study. Our research indicates that political polarization beyond architecture influences and the associated disparities are defined by the extent of hyperlink connectivity. A mathematical model is introduced to quantify the observed phenomena. Our data model findings are consistent with this model, highlighting the primary role of less polarized websites in defining globally polarized domains, while globally non-connected components contribute to locally isolated components' increased polarization.

A concise verification method for the word problem in Thompson's group V has been identified as having the capacity to simulate a deterministic context-free language. Building upon previous research, this method can be optimized to confirm that a string does not belong to a context-free language. Furthermore, it has been discovered that Thompson's group V can be subdivided into deterministic real-time subsets, including one instance of the DRL languages.

We propose a method for bidirectional interaction between a quantum system and its environment, allowing for controlled influence from both directions. This setup enables researchers to study complex phenomena such as the loss of informational order due to entanglement with the environment. As a practical demonstration, we apply our model to examine how a Rabi dimer loses coherence when interacting with a random distribution of levels.

We establish a generalized formula for subsets of Euclidean space where the boundary is characterized by a minimum number of repeated normal vectors. This extended criterion was initially set forth by Nomizu and Vance in 1971 for scenarios without recurrent operators. Moreover, our research reimagines the 2017 findings by Sasaki for sections containing operators that operate repeatedly.

A key element in proving our theorem lies in leveraging a specific identity introduced by Nomizu in 1954, pertaining to the interaction between the second derivative and recurrent operators within Euclidean space.

A secondary consequence of our main discovery is our theorem's condition simplifying to that proposed by Sasaki in 2017.

Considering the induced metric and a compatible connection on a Euclidean space subset, our research also reveals scenarios where the second relative divergence is well-defined, yielding definite, negative, or bounded below results.

Our study builds upon various contributions, including works by B.Y. Chen, F. Gluck, and W.Y. Hsiang on Euclidean space subsets with repeatedly characterized boundaries.

Let n be a non-zero integer, and let base p and base q be given integer bases in (1, n). We demonstrate that subsets of the set N_p/q's d-dimensional form defined by first-order logic within the language of bounded quantification are recognisable in base n. Additionally, subsets of N_p/q's d-dimensional form that can be defined using first-order logic within the language comprising bounded quantification and constant integers are fully characterised across all integer bases. We then provide FOL with bounded quantification as a tool for identifying 'numeration-system-independent' properties, using {n even} and the subsets of N_p consisting of powers of q in base p, for any non-base q integer q, as examples of such properties.

We investigate the properties of the $a_u$MSM model, incorporating a axial-
vector meson and two Majorana scalar fields for dark matter, linked to the
Standard Model through a weakly interacting invisible sector. By lowering the
requirements for DM production, this approach resolves the smallness of the
dark matter mass and allows us to examine the impact of scalar fields on
vacuum stability and compute the rate of invisible decays in the Higgs boson
decay process. Furthermore, we determine the parameter space that meets the
requirements set by the NA48/2 experiment for the electric dipole moment of
the neutral pion and find that the model offers a viable solution to the
strong CP problem while maintaining vacuum stability.

Using LAMOST time-domain survey (LTS) data sources, we manually sifted through approximately one million variable stars to identify around 1.3 million suspicious candidates for binaries. From these, we created a refined collection of around 800,000 potential binary stars after eliminating 500,000 candidates through several elimination methods. We also developed an scoring system (S.B) to estimate the probability of each potential binary star being genuine, and found notable examples including a CEPUO variable, an ORN variable, and an unusual ORN/TYPE IIP supernova, among others. This study on binary stars is still ongoing and will be updated in the future.

Convolutional Neural Networks are commonly used for extracting features from images, but they often struggle to capture local structure information, which is crucial for image segmentation. To address this challenge, EGCGNs are proposed as an improvement, with a novel edge-gating mechanism called the Edge-Selection Module (ESM) being used to incorporate shape information. ESM achieves this by predicting boundary selections on both input and intermediate features, effectively generating additional edge-supervised learning data without extra cost. ESM enhances the EG-CNNs' ability to use content information and local structure by selectively embedding edge information into the EG-CNNs. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that EG-CNNs and EGCGNs have significantly improved results on four challenging 2D image segmentation datasets, with EGCGNs achieving the very best performance.

This research investigates concurrency control within the popular NoSQL database,
MongoDB, focusing on its widely adopted snapshot isolation concurrency control
mechanism. Since its initial release in 2009, MongoDB has seen numerous
implementations of snapshot isolation. We examine the official documentation,
discuss key decisions in implementing snapshot isolation, and discuss three primary
deployments: 'WIREDTIGER', 'REPLICASET', and 'SHARDEDCLUSTER'. These deployments
have distinct interpretations of snapshot isolation and involve reading from both
replica and original documents, as well as maintaining isolation when writing to
documents. We document three main interpretations of snapshot isolation: CQF-SI, PWF-SI,
and PSI. Each interpretation of snapshot isolation has its own definition, which
we break down into two components: freedom from conflicts and isolation. We verify
that the official MongoDB drivers adhere to their respective interpretations of
snapshot isolation by utilizing the DRUM testing framework.

We establish a recurrence relation for the e-positive content symmetric functions in a subclass of $\chi_D$, specifically focusing on a subset of $\chi_D$ indexed by Dyck paths. This particular subset, denoted as $\chi_{DP}$, is shown to be closed under the multiplication by elementary symmetric functions. Additionally, we demonstrate the scalability of a previous $\eta$-positivity table introduced by the second author and S. Jeyarajah, again within this subset $\chi_{DP}$. Furthermore, we provide a combinatorial interpretation in terms of Dyck paths for the expansion of elementary symmetric functions, highlighting its $e$-positivity. This interpretation builds upon the framework introduced by Hampe, Jeyarajah, and Kwon in 2022.

We introduce a novel strategy named Hindsight Summary, a new approach to supervised learning that leverages "hindsight" to minimize predicted attention errors by providing corrective feedback. In this study, we theoretically prove that the hindsight summary can be approximated through a combination of projected gradients and squared errors, which yields improved results over both ordinary supervised learning and models that incorporate attention mechanisms. To test our algorithm's effectiveness in a practical setting, we apply it to a diverse set of tasks involving multi-modal image attention within deep learning networks. Specifically, we examine attention models for object question answering, contrastive learning, and landmark description, using datasets such as ReAlQA, GoogleLandmark, and GoogleImage. The results show that our algorithm can leverage "hindsight" to enhance attention performance with solely auxiliary training data. Descriptions generated by the attention model improve in quality when leveraging "hindsight" training, outperforming baseline models on the AttQA validation set while using the same training and evaluation images. Similarly, we achieve better retrieval and description scores for the attention model in the GoogleLandmark learning task. Furthermore, we develop a new evaluation task for single-image description generation with colored target objects and find that models employing "hindsight" summary training can describe ordinary target objects more effectively, enabling them to incorporate contextual background knowledge and outperform baseline models on the ReDescription evaluation set.

Implicit biases in training data, often unconsciously held by creators, can
unfairly influence model development and application in medical image analysis.
While techniques exist to measure and reduce explicit biases from model outputs,
they don't address implicit biases effectively. This research introduces two novel
methods to mitigate implicit biases from deep learning models in medical image
analysis: BiasDisentangle and BiasCounterfactual. These methods, designed to
reduce implicit biases without requiring access to patient demographics,
don't compromise a model's predictive performance while achieving bias
mitigation. Specifically, our approach outperformed implicit and explicit bias
mitigation baselines in experiments on two datasets, demonstrating its ability
to mitigate implicit biases and reduce explicit biases concurrently.

We study a mesoscopic network consisting of $M$ interconnected triangles, where spin-$1/2$ particles interact within the triangles and collectively compete through the links that connect them. This setup allows for an analytical examination of the stochastic Ising model on such a network, yielding comprehensive results on its thermodynamic properties, including specific heat, magnetization, and free energy. Due to its periodic structure, the network provides insights into energy hysteresis in magnetic phase transitions. We derive exact expressions for the initial magnetization and specific heat at high temperatures on the network. Furthermore, we investigate how the shape of the hysteresis loop is influenced by the arrangement of the spin interactions.

Researchers have developed a method to classify solar eruptions based on their ability to provide different energy levels at a location close to Earth's orbit. These classifications are applied to categorize logarithmic energy values (1 to 6) and are defined by distinct profiles of ultraviolet and X-ray emissions across the solar spectrum. When analyzing eruptions with higher energy values (greater than 4), a significant increase in soft X-rays is observed above 60 Angstroms, indicating that coronal loops with sufficient energy to be ejected from the sun exhibit distinct soft X-ray emissions compared to their lower energy counterparts. This study also reveals the occurrence of coronal loops with coronal temperatures exceeding ten million Kelvin, primarily associated with the most energetic eruptions. These findings suggest a correlation between energetic coronal loops and soft X-ray emissions at specific wavelengths, providing valuable insights for selecting suitable imaging filter wavelengths that can identify likely candidates for planet formation.

Emotional understanding through natural language is increasingly valuable,
yet often challenging to achieve due to the variability in language expressions
and the high cost of obtaining annotated datasets. While recent advancements
have successfully utilized transfer learning for the classification of emotions
from text, most existing approaches focus on transferring within the same
language. This study proposes a novel deep learning model, designed to learn
from multi-source, multi-task data, effectively capturing both syntactic
and semantic connections in sentences. This innovative solution enables users
to train a single model capable of identifying emotions in sentences across
different corpora. Furthermore, the model can be applied to detect emotions in
sentences written in any language, by training dedicated components for
lexical transfer. This method results in a more robust system for emotion
recognition that exhibits superior performance both within and beyond the
domain. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach for
emotion recognition from text.

Bi$_5$Fe$_2$Ti$_3$O$_{15}$ (BIFT) is an interesting lithium biferrite material. Researchers have analyzed the characteristics of BIFT from 300 to 600 K at normal conditions and the effects of up to 11.48 GPa of hydrostatic pressure. At room conditions, the material has an orthorhombic structure, belonging to the subfamily of lithium biferrites in the Sm$_2$FeMoO$_6$ group. It exhibits two structural phase transitions when subjected to pressure, without showing signs of the ferroelectric behavior. The transitions occur from the SM $Pnma$ structure to the A-type antiferromagnetic (A-AFM) structure at 6.29 GPa, and then to the high-pressure perovskite (HPP) structure at 9.24 GPa. Analysis of the material's compressibility under pressure revealed distinct values for different pressure ranges, as well as different thermal expansion behaviors at normal pressure and elevated pressure conditions (5.12 GPa). Infrared spectroscopy was also performed to study the material's vibrational modes at normal conditions and the results were used to estimate electron-ion coupling for different structural phases. Notably, the HPP structure showed reduced compressibility compared to the normal conditions structure, and its parameters contracted at a rate of 0.74\% under maximum pressure applied.

This paper explores the limitations of A* search when used for planning in systems constrained by dynamics and geometry. Despite its efficiency and flexibility, we aim to quantify the reliability of A* in this context. By building on previous work in operational taxonomy, we develop a framework for A*'s performance assessment. First, we confirm A*'s capability to generate discrete paths that can be transformed into feasible continuous trajectories. Next, we propose criteria for selecting appropriate cost functions. Then, we focus on bounding the error of A* in this planning framework. Two critical BPA* variables, namely grid size and heuristic efficiency, are analyzed for their impact on the accuracy of A* plans. Two theoretically derived error bounds, known as localized and global bounds, are compared to evaluate A*'s performance. Through experimentation in robotic navigation scenarios, we find that the A* search typically finds nearly optimal paths based on localized bound performance, especially in environments with smooth dynamics. In environments with abrupt geometric changes, A* can still produce efficient paths even with a suboptimal cost function. Ultimately, our research provides A* with a structured approach for performance evaluation, paving the way for optimizing its parameters for real-world applications.

If a shock wave propagates through a viscous and thermally conducting fluid in a scale-invariant medium, it may reveal a non-analytic behavior at its center, under specific conditions.  When this condition is not met, the shock wave retains analytic properties, but conditions exactly at its center result in an infinite rate of energy dissipation.  Discoveries show that even when this behavior occurs, it's confined to a narrow region, limiting its impact on overall energy loss.

This paper explores the underlying theoretical differences between the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and the Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed heavy meson light-flavor decay rate parametrizations, focusing on isospin-breaking effects. Our analysis reveals that despite apparent discrepancies, the two frameworks are fundamentally consistent. The differences stem primarily from how the NP and LP states are defined, particularly regarding isospin-breaking interactions. To address this, we conduct explicit four-loop perturbation theory and a light-cone sum rule computation for a specific decay process, using a CPK sum rule that incorporates both three-loop NP-to-LP and four-loop LP-to-LP factorization.

Suscy quantum potentials confined to one dimension can be reimagined as a polynomial version of the harmonic oscillator, possessing a modified Heisenberg algebra with various forms. We demonstrate through unitary transformations the possibility of classifying these forms and show they fall under two primary categories based on the behavior at a specific point or at infinity. Moreover, we utilize the SUSY quantum ladder operators to generate the potential forms from simpler building blocks, namely one-dimensional SUSY quantum states.

A new formula has been established to calculate a variation-based Lyapunov exponent for systems that exhibit extreme sensitivity to initial conditions. This condition ensures that two starting points, when evolved over time, will result in one of the associated probabilities becoming exponentially bounded by a positive lyapunov exponent $\lambda$. This formula can be applied to assess the change in sum-based Lyapunov exponents for systems that exhibit random behavior based on their underlying characteristics. Additionally, several concrete examples are provided to illustrate the use of this formula in action, including the study of the Loretz map and systems that display chaotic behavior.

Research into hybrid quantum circuits has quickly become a focal point, as the
development of mesoscopic electronics based on quantum interference effects is
accelerated by it. The quantity of interest in such applications is the switching
current in circuits comprising Josephson junctions. When these circuits are
connected to their environment through a normal lead, the critical current can
fluctuate due to the random phase of the electron condensates. Here, we examine
an asymmetric SQUID loop consisting of two Josephson junctions and a normal lead,
where the phase locking between the junctions results in a critical current that is
larger than in a single junction junction. The present work utilizes the Josephson
tunneling Hamiltonian to calculate the critical current in this SQUID structure. We
apply this calculation to asymmetric rectangular SQUIDs to analyze the dependence
on the widths of the normal leads. The findings suggest that changing the width of
the leads affects the critical current in a manner that can be attributed to the
change in the Fermi energy density of the normal leads.

Investigating the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law, black radiation radiation energy, curved space radiation energy, and the interaction between quantum fluctuations and curvature in various settings like de Sitter and Anti-de Sitter spaces reveals intriguing insights into the influence of the non-abelian aether term. The aether term not only modifies the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and Casimir energy but also changes the UV behavior in the effective action for quantum fluctuations, resulting in the recovery of the geometric part of the action at high temperatures or ultraviolet limits for theories including QCD. Notably, in three dimensions, the aether term's contribution to the Casimir effect becomes negligible in the large $N$ limit for theories like QCD.

This paper explores the challenges of hedging HJR options, focusing on their price sensitivity to barrier level adjustments. We tackle this issue by defining the option's value through a partial differential equation, enabling comparison with explicitly calculable flat and cylindrical barrier Jourdren options. As a result, we develop a simplified expression for the logarithm of the option's payoff. Building on this, we derive an integrated formula, facilitating the calculation of pre-hedging expected liquidity cost, which is more efficient than Monte Carlo simulation. We then compute and graph the expected pre-hedging liquidity cost for a range of option parameters.

Recent suggestions by Ball, Murat and others explored the behavior of certain types of functionals that measure the total energy in heterogeneous materials subject to linear differential equations like div u = 0. A key challenge in this area has been addressing the issue where sequences of highly oscillatory functions can converge to non-standard limits called "two-scale convergent" sequences. To expand on this discussion, a new technique was employed based on variational methods. Although this new approach is applicable to a broader range of equations, it focuses on elliptic equations in this paper. The main achievement demonstrated here is that the functional can be given a lower bound value even when the equation's coefficient matrix has a limited range of symmetry. Furthermore, a valuable tool was established for calculating the minimum energy values in materials with periodically distributed microstructures. Not only is the convergence of these energy values to a specific type of effective functional, but also the convergence of rescaled, resbalanced functions is proved. This proves the long-standing suggestion made by Ball and Murat regarding the relaxation of certain types of functionals.

This study examines early-type galaxies (ETGs) within the Coma Cluster using HST data to analyze tidal structures at a flux fraction level of 10^-4. We found that tidal structures become less prevalent in more massive ETGs: very common in galaxies under 10^10 M_sun, scarce in those near 10^11 M_sun, and almost non-existent in the most massive ETGs above 10^11 M_sun. No relationship was found between tidal structures and other properties such as ETGs' stellar mass, optical luminosity, or their dynamic major merger activity in the recent universe. We also discovered tidal structures in about 15% of ETGs with early optical luminosity but unusually late dynamic activity. This discrepancy provides an opportunity to study how these galaxies' dynamical activity has evolved and may take a longer period to increase optical luminosity activity compared to dynamic activity activity.

Distributing opportunities equitably within a society not only benefits its current members but also has far-reaching effects on future generations. To study optimal policy making in scenarios where decisions affect multiple generations, we developed a multi-agent framework consisting of an infinite number of identical agents. This framework allows for optimal policy determination through value function iteration in an iterative fashion. However, it requires infinite computation per generation. We overcame this challenge by restricting the representation of future generations' value functions to that of prior generations. This technique reduces the computation required for future generations to just the number of unique socioeconomic states. As an example, we used this method to demonstrate the effects of optimal education allocation on income inequality across multiple generations in a education-segregation model featuring an inverse relationship between educational opportunity and socioeconomic status.

Precise simulation of advanced computer systems like NLO-based laser systems and other complex systems is notoriously difficult. NLO-based laser systems, which are highly modified NLO-based computer workstations with NLO-based disk drives, NLO-based coprocessors, NLO-based coprocessors, NLO-based coprocessors, NLO-based coprocessors, NLO-based coprocessors, and NLO-based coprocessors, are particularly challenging to model accurately. To aid NLO-based security professionals, NLO-based researchers, and NLO-based software developers in NLO-based software validation projects, a NLO-based simulation model has been developed using NLO-based Python. This NLO-based Python model, which is based on a NLO-based Boolean finite-state machine, has been developed in NLO-based C++.

We have demonstrated that the scaled unit ball in L_p^n space, for any n greater than or equal to 3 and p not equal to 2, cannot be reduced to approximately isometric form using linear operators. Furthermore, we have shown that any such operator will result in a significant distortion of at least (1/4)^|p-2| times to the (p-1)th power. We have also simplified the proof of a previously established result by Figiel and J. Lindenstrauss (1979), which stated that the unit ball in L_p^n space cannot be reduced to approximately isometric form for p greater than 1 and not equal to 2. We have also shown that any linear operator will result in a significant distortion of at least (1/4)^|p-2| times to the (p-1)th power.

The beam-beam interaction at the Large Hadron Collider-Large Hadron Collider (LHC3) IP in the Large Hadron Collider significantly influences beam dynamics and must be carefully managed. This interaction comprises multiple effects such as beam-beam strain, non-linear beam-beam kick, and beam-beam closed orbit distortion. To enhance monitoring capabilities, we propose installing beam-beam monitors in dedicated pickup locations around ILC-type IPs in the LHC. These devices will enable direct measurement of observable outcomes of beam-beainduced closed orbit distortions. By utilizing a linear optical model, we can calculate equivalent beta-beam strain values, allowing for better assessment of beam-beam strain values in specific pickup locations around LHC3 IP. Our simulations demonstrate that these proposed beam-beam monitors will be capable of accurately measuring beam-beam strain values, beam-beam closed orbit distortions, and beam-based alpha-beam strain values at the LHC3 IP.

This paper identifies a significant challenge in contemporary distributed optimization techniques used for large-scale machine learning models: the vulnerability to malicious agents that compromise the efficiency and accuracy of the learning process. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel, privately guaranteed algorithm, ReTeX, which operates on a fully decentralized network and successfully tackles synchronization, data heterogeneity, and malicious behavior. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed solution surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods under both benign and malicious conditions, effectively shielding the system from malicious agents while delivering high performance.

To achieve the full potential of upcoming cosmological instruments like CMB-Spectrum and DESI, accurate simulations of instrumental systematic errors are essential. By creating a realistic template for background subtraction in these instruments' simulations, our research aims to better train machine learning algorithms designed to detect systematic errors in their data. We tested these background subtraction methods on simulated scalar polarization patterns and a more complex simulation of a cosmic microwave background camera, specifically one that includes BG2 systematic errors. Our findings show that both simple and more advanced scenarios can be used to effectively simulate systematic errors, which was a successful outcome. Furthermore, we found that training a neural network with a specific type of systematic error (an 'bump' shape) on simulated data resulted in an inaccurate detection of its presence in real measurements, an important example of how background subtraction failures can lead to shape-sensitive systematic errors escaping detection. These results highlight the necessity of accurately modeling instrumental systematic effects in future cosmological instruments' simulations, particularly their impact on scientific data analysis.

Researchers utilized the Bayesian Analysis by Reduction and Tiling model to analyze word ordering and a more complex syntax task, revealing surprising results: BART's performance on word ordering was significantly better than on partial tree linearization, despite the latter being more intricate.

This study introduces two primary objectives: to perfect detection methods that function consistently across different datasets without the need for dataset-specific adjustments, and to develop a detection network with improved accuracy and data efficiency through the use of cross-stitch connections. To tackle this challenge, we created three novel modules for multi-domain adaptation networks featuring cross-stitch connections: the Multi-Domain Adaptation Modules (MDA-Nets). These modules are designed to accommodate any number of domains and incorporate mechanisms such as multi-domain activation maps and cross-domain data fusion.
