Initially presented at the PxTP workshop in 2011, the veriT proof format has undergone significant development ever since. Thanks to ongoing internal advancements in veriT, the generator now produces state-of-the-art SMT proofs in this format. Since then, multiple tools have demonstrated capability to verify solutions generated by veriT, including the proof formatter in veriT itself, K in its SMT-proof mode, and the pxsmt solver which can utilize solutions created by veriT. Additionally, the format's stability has been further ensured by integrating it into the PxTP research framework, allowing for regular testing and development of related components such as the generator, K, and pxsmt.

This paper introduces an enhanced FedBuff algorithm for training machine learning models in a federated setting, where participants train models on local data and share predictions instead of raw data. While this approach maintains high scalability and reduces transmission sizes to protected levels, our proposed method optimizes the selection of data contributors, improving the final model's performance. Our experiments on multiple datasets highlight improvements of up to 22% over existing FedBuff applications.

This paper explores transfer learning in speech recognition across different language pairs. Our research suggests that transfer learning is less beneficial for recognition systems comparing dissimilar languages. To validate this hypothesis, we conducted experiments using three distinct pairs: similar languages (Danish and Swedish) and dissimilar languages (Danish and German), as well as a system combining both German and German text representations. Our findings indicated that transfer learning works well for similar languages and less effective for dissimilar ones. Moreover our results showed that a system with German against German resulted in almost same performance.

To assess novel node embedding algorithms, a standard approach is to measure
their efficiency through downstream tasks. We observe that certain state-of-the-art
node embedding algorithms are challenging to optimize, which hinders the ability
to evaluate their performance. We propose that the outcome of node embedding
should serve as input for a down-stream task. We suggest using the computed
features to train a supervised learning classifier aimed at predicting node
labels. We develop a new assessment metric, downstream task accuracy, to evaluate
the quality of node embeddings. This metric assesses how well the computed
representations can be used to train a supervised classifier for predicting node
labels.

A study of the $B^+$ decay into $K^+$ and a pair of $K_S$ neutral B mesons in invariant mass has been conducted by the Belle experiment at 722 fb$^{-1}$ of collected data. A significant broad structure has been observed around 1.02 GeV/c$^2$ in this spectrum. We utilized an amplitude analysis to investigate the decay's dynamics. Employing the Isospin relation, we explored the $S$-wave contribution to the spectrum. An assessment of the wave function overlap between the $B^+$ meson and the $K^+$ and $K_S$ mesons suggests that a virtual $B^+$ meson decaying into an excited $K^*$ and a low-energy $K_S$ meson may be responsible for this structure. A quantitative description of this phenomenon has been provided with the help of the N/D method. Furthermore, we found that including this structure in the $S$-wave amplitude model significantly enhances the model's fit probability.

New extensions to the Standard Model of particle physics can naturally generate a substantial abundance of primordial black holes within the mass range of $10^{17}$ to $10^{24}$ grams. We analyze various parameters in novel particle physics frameworks to determine if a completely dark-matter primordial black hole scenario is natively supported by these models. Four such models are examined: the addition of a derivative self-interacting term to a scalar field model within inflation, two variants of axion models where the periodicity field $f_a$ lies between $10^{9.25}$ and $10^{10.25}$ gigaelectronvolts, and a semi-realistic primordial black hole scenario based on the Standard Model plus one Higgs doublet. In each case, we show that specific parameters can result in primordial black holes constituting all of the dark matter, without any residual stable scalar field to contend with.

Series elastic actuatures (SEAs) utilize a compliant element to generate an force sensing mechanism in robotic grippers and legs. Although this design choice enhances safety and stability, significant challenges arise in accurately measuring force due to the inherent nonlinearity and inaccuracies present in force sensors. A new algorithm has been developed to address this challenge by estimating measured force signals in real-time, effectively downsampling force sensors while accurately capturing force readings. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in measuring force with relatively simple force sensors, showcasing the algorithm's ability to accurately estimate force in dynamic scenarios with varying loads.

When a material fractures due to expansion, the interaction between rifts determines whether they merge or stay separate. In living organisms, rifts often merge, facilitating the continuous exchange of chemicals, but they also generate heat through friction, potentially restricting further expansion. In contrast, polar animals living on shrinking ice sheets experience different forces as the surrounding area compresses, increasing the distance between adjacent cracks and allowing for the safe entrance of the animal's rear while its front exits the opposing crack. To analyze this phenomenon, researchers built and tested a simulated model, a snowhouse constructed from fragmented and compacted ice, inhabited by the polar bear 'Benjamin Franklin.' To create a challenging test for the model, scientists induced rapid expansion and contraction in the surrounding chamber, simulating the movement of sea ice. If the surrounding ice is in motion, it can provide additional support, allowing the raft to grow larger. However, the edge currents that typically flow towards the poles are not fast enough to fully offset the Earth's rotational effects, leading to the accumulation of open spaces at the center of the ocean. To test the hypothesis that polar animals utilize ice floes as intended, but marine life may be forcing them to create open spaces in the center of the ocean where it is easier for them to move, the size of the simulated bear in the cooking experiment was not significantly enlarged, although some suggest that in the future, polar bears may have to share the planet with another large animal, the simulated bear in the cooking experiment was

Our study observes distinct transitions in a multicomponent complex scalar field on a lattice, including from the symmetric phase to a broken-symmetry phase, between two broken-symmetry phases, and in a real scalar field lattice between two broken-symmetry phases. These observations can be precisely matched with the theoretical prediction of renormalization-group flow in continuum field theories.

A notable aspect is that the starting phase on the lattice determines the flow direction in the case of the two broken-symmetry phases transition. This provides an opportunity to study the infrared behavior of a theory that has entered its IR fixed point through a specific entry angle.

The lattice model also exhibits a trajectory resembling a trajectory entry into its IR fixed point. This was observed by tracking the change in a latent heat to surface tension ratio along this trajectory.

In contrast to previous studies, our observations reveal that the location and nature of phase transitions in multi-component complex scalar field lattices are not fully understood, and show new transitions between two broken-symmetry phases. A method to analyze the latent heat to surface tension ratio in the broken phase is introduced, and its application reveals distinct values in the different phases.

A method to quantify the IR conformal window is also presented, and applied to determine the size of this window in a multi-component complex scalar field theory. Our findings also show a narrowed conformal window as the starting broken-symmetry phase gets larger.

Underwater navigation using AUVs using mobile robots as references has significant advantages, particularly in avoiding precise position information requirements and achieving higher relative navigation accuracy. However, this approach presents a complex learning challenge due to the high dimensionality of underwater environments. To address this, we developed an off-line reinforcement learning method called SPGP-SARSA, which integrates SPGP policy learning with Q-learning. By leveraging local linear approximations of value functions, SPGP models capture policy structures within similar state regions, while the GP regression manages the efficiency of policy evaluation. We implemented an active Q-learning process to dynamically optimize data collection for valuing those state regions. Using real-world data from three ATL-sized AUVs and one MARINER2 AUV, we demonstrated SPGP-SARSA's superior learning efficiency and robustness to noise when compared to on-line learning and other reference methods.

For comparison of networks, Benzer and Khrapchenko introduced the concept of minimal arity within a given network structure, along with related parameters. This paper extends this line of research by providing new insights into the behavior of minimal arity in comparison networks as the number of comparators per layer changes. Specifically, we discover that the minimal arity for sorting networks with depths up to 4 is not monotonic, specifically demonstrating non-monotonicity for 4-layered networks. Additionally, we establish the minimal arity for sorting networks with 3 layers is consistently monotonic. This paper also provides the first explicit, non-trivial monotonicity theorems for comparison networks. More precisely, it establishes the minimal arity of sorting networks with 2 layers, as well as pipelines of comparisons, is monotonic. It also demonstrates the minimal arity of sorting networks with 2 layers is approximately $\sqrt{2n}$ and within a factor of 2 of the expected value for general networks.

Building upon a previous study by the author and others, new exact solutions for relativistic stellar models consisting of two distinct fluids are presented. These solution models include the Thomas-Ehrenfest-Aharonov effect, where the second fluid is an effective description of quantized effects within the first fluid's framework. It has been confirmed that solutions for two-fluid systems can be obtained from known one-fluid solutions under specific conditions, notably when the two fluids are governed by linear equations of state and share the same mean free path. Furthermore, the paper explores the possibility of constructing viable one-fluid solutions from the two-fluid systems.

In this study, we investigate the connection between bar development in galactic disks and the characteristics of their density distributions. Using a generalized, non-exponential density scale length to describe the disks, we examine how the density distribution's properties, particularly the minimum and maximum values, affect bar formation. Our findings reveal that bars are more likely to form in disks with shorter minimum density lengths, while those with larger maximum density lengths are less prone to bar development. Furthermore, we find a direct correlation between the likelihood of bar formation and the generalized density distribution's parameters, which is prime for observation testing.

In order to understand how magnetic fields affect the formation of merger remnants in gas-rich major mergers, this study runs and analyzes gas-dynamic simulations that include magnetic fields. The results show that the effects of magnetic fields on the formation of merger remnants are substantial, with the fields promoting the creation of elongated, laminar structures by limiting gas fragmentation. The results also vary depending on the strength of the magnetic fields present in the system. We found that in gas-rich major mergers, the effects of magnetic fields on the formation of stellar bulges are quite substantial, particularly in systems where the fields are weaker. Furthermore, these findings indicate that the effects of magnetic fields are likely relevant to the formation of active galactic nuclei in merger systems.

This research develops a novel 3D contrastive learning framework, called 3D-CMC, 
for classifying music album difficulty levels based on auditory features and spatial 
configuration. Initially, we apply contrastive learning within a 3D neural network 
to extract music album representations. Following this, we employ a sequential 
learning framework to map these features to corresponding difficulty levels. To 
address challenges with skewed data distribution, we refine both the network 
and its hyperparameters using advanced techniques such as grouped batch normalisation 
and adaptive sequential learning. Experimental results show that our music album 
difficulty classification framework achieves superior performance, particularly 
demonstrating significant improvements of around 10% accuracy on the Music Difficulty 
Learning Benchmark (MuDiLa) dataset compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

Despite traditional single-task transfer learning methods showing superior performance over multi-task transfer learning approaches, there has been limited research exploring this concept in Spell Checking. We examined the transfer learning framework by examining neural neural network encoder-decoder architectures and Gaussian process models. We explored various model settings and explored the impact of shared tasks on model performance. Our results showed that our proposed Generalized Encoder Correction (GEC) method can be trained using just a single target task, resulting in significant improvements over both traditional and contemporary single-task GEC models. Furthermore, our proposed model achieved remarkable results, surpassing the baseline GEC adaptation model by +2.25 F1 for the English Development set.

A surprising finding revealed in research involves the inference of increased suicide rates in US counties following 9/11. This unintended consequence was brought about due to the unstable estimates resulting from rounding in census data. To avoid a similar mistake, it is crucial to consider the effects of rounding and discrete measurements on statistical conclusions, particularly when working with rate data commonly found in epidemiological studies. This note makes the following contributions: (1) an investigation into rounding effects on variance estimation for suicide rates surrounding 2001 on 9/11 in US counties, (2) an broader discussion on the implications of rounding and discrete data for rate stability, (3) the development of adjustment techniques for standard errors considering rounding effects, suitable for applications in public health, and (4) an empirical analysis of the effects of discrete measurements and rounding on variance estimation in census and county-level data, and (5) an analysis of the effects of rounding and discrete data on confidence intervals for cancer rates in New York State.

We have experimentally investigated the magnetic and structural characteristics of GdInO$_3$ single crystals across a broad temperature range. A gas-source molecular beam epitaxy process was used to grow these single crystals on strontium titanate substrates. A precise X-ray diffraction analysis revealed that the Gd$^{3+}$ ions form a body-centered trigonal lattice with slight distortion, and all indium and oxygen atoms fit perfectly within the spinel-like Gd$^{3+}$ lattice. A change in lattice symmetry from body-centered trigonal to rhombohedral was observed when the temperature exceeded 723 K. A long-range magnetization transition from paramagnetic to ferromagnetic state happened at 81.5 K. A more in-depth magnetic analysis using the experimental data and theoretical calculations with the effective Hamiltonian exposed that both In $^{3+}$ ions and Gd $^{3+}$ sites experience a reduction in symmetry from rhombohedral to distorted rhombohedral within the magnetic ground state. Additionally, an interesting magnetic transition from canting antiferromagnetism to ferromagnetism was discovered. A significant spin-canting angle of 20° was found to coexist with a 6.5 kHz precession frequency in the antiferromagnetic state. A precession frequency of approximately 250 Hz was precessing in a ferromagnetic state.

The round-robin protocol for allocating items among players has long been used in practice and studied through various implementations. A key proposal suggests that the round-robin allocation generated by certain players effectively corresponds to the allocation derived from the cut-and-choose algorithm executed by a specific set of players. This equivalence not only ensures the best possible fairness performance for the round-robin allocation but also reduces the required participation to achieve the same level of fairness as the cut-and-choose method for $n$ players. Another variation involves assigning each player a value for the item they select that others have already chosen, thereby utilizing the cut-and-choose allocation instead of the one from the standard procedure. This alternative approach also guarantees optimal fairness performance and has been experimentally shown to be more efficient than the traditional round-robin protocol. Furthermore, we provide an algorithm that can be significantly faster than both the $O(n^2)$ algorithm proposed by Buchta and a recently developed implementation, thereby enabling large-scale empirical testing.

Pseudo-labeling serves as a prominent paradigm for supervised learning in large-scale datasets. However, the reliance on manual annotation for a single reference image introduces introduced a significant bottleneck in the process. Another challenge arises from the inclusion of noisy pseudo-labels, which can also hinder model performance. To tackle these issues, we propose an innovative strategy in this work that involves translating a single target image into multiple versions in multiple domains. Then, we employ source images to generate robust pseudo-labels and more accurate predictions through pseudo-over-sampling. Our novel approach yields impressive segmentation results across two cross-domain image sets. The use of this technique in real-world applications, particularly in remote sensing and medical diagnosis, holds great promise for demonstrating its effectiveness.

Our study targets the spiral galaxy UGC 8839, which has an intermediate spiral pattern and a relatively open structure. Using radio telescope observations from DR8, we obtained HI data for this galaxy and analyzed its properties at both a spatial scale of 36.7 parsecs and a flux resolution of 6.4 km/s. An HI rotation curve was generated to map the galaxy's inner structure. In comparison to other spiral galaxies in the sample, UGC 8839 has a larger inner bulge-to-disk ratio and a centrally concentrated B/T ratio, suggesting the presence of a small bulge. A relationship was also found between the HI mass and SFR in the galaxy's disk. Additionally, an examination of the galaxy's HI distribution and its relationship with its optical data and CO data at 36.7pc scale was conducted. UGC 8839 has a regular HI distribution with a moderate HI flocculation pattern that follows its spiral arms. A significant concentration of young stellar populations is found along its spiral arms and at its center. The position-velocity diagrams and a dynamical model both support a flocculent pattern for this galaxy. A comparison with optical data and its star formation law was also performed using a sample of HII regions in UGC 8839. The regions follow the same galaxy-wide star formation law without any evidence of a distinct concentrated B/T ratio like the "Buddha Bump"

The concept of paleo-detectors offers a way to study the broader range of dark matter interaction possibilities that traditional experiments may miss, particularly in the realm of weak interactions. Since paleo-detectors have extremely large detection volumes, they are sensitive to non-point-like dark matter interactions governed by form factors. We analyze the effect of these factors on the predictive capabilities of paleo-detectors using a theoretical model that describes nucleon-based effective field theories. These impacts vary depending on the detector used but generally result in reduced sensitivity to sub-Weinberg-scale dark matter. For instance, in case of the NANO-LD detector, paleo-detectors lose effectiveness below a certain two-times unit of the Weinstein scale. However, in other detectors like the TROJAN and TROJAN-II, they continue to explore a further, more narrow range of even weaker interactions.

Today, sophisticated databases automatically generate detailed records of every data modification, creating comprehensive histories that can accurately reconstruct the update sequences of a target time period. The automated nature of this data collection process, coupled with its widespread data sharing, poses significant privacy risks for individuals whose information is included in these detailed temporal traces. To address this concern, researchers have started investigating the application of differential privacy to these comprehensive reconstruction histories. The primary objective of our work is to clarify the challenges associated with achieving differential privacy in these complex reconstruction histories and to pinpoint the crucial factors that play a pivotal role in these challenges. We establish a theoretical framework using a formalized model and utilize it to examine the challenges faced in typical and complex scenarios, both with and without access to underlying data. The case studies we present illustrate the utility of our findings in our theoretical analysis and also reveal the differential privacy challenges inherent in some real-world reconstruction histories. The insights we have gained from these analyses have informed the development of a strategy for engineers to engineer comprehensive reconstruction histories that adhere to the principles of differential privacy.

Including irrelevant or duplicative features can hinder a learner's performance even when some critical features are present in the input. To understand and visualize feature importance in SAT-based learning, we integrated the Loreto tool with MiniSat to develop a method that utilizes Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores (MUCs) from training iterations. This study focuses on the MUCs' focus and minimality in relation to feature importance, with results from the EXPLAIN experiment on three large-scale datasets supporting a correlation between the size of MUCs and feature importance. Furthermore, we leveraged the Minimal property to suggest that features appearing in multiple MUCs should be assigned equal importance.

This research paper examines the use of dual decoder attention networks (DDANet) for the automated identification of surgical tools. A significant amount of training data consisting of over 100 frames from various surgical videos has been utilized. The dataset features multiple cameras, lighting conditions, and different parts of the same surgical instrument. In our experiments, DDANet proved to be the most effective method among five deep learning models tested, achieving a mean intersection over union (IoU) score of 0.76 for automated surgical instrument detection. Furthermore, DDANet was observed to be particularly successful in scenarios where the same instrument was imaged from different perspectives across different camera views.

This research explores the potential of using contrastive learning in unsupervised Person Re-identification (ReID) by proposing two methods: unsupervised ReID by contrastive pre-training and fine-tuning without supervision, and unsupervised ReID with contrastively pre-trained domain adaptation. Our results show that contrastive learning frameworks can achieve significant improvements in unsupervised ReID tasks, whether for single-domain training or multi-domain training. Specifically, our pre-trained models outperform state-of-the-art models on the Market-1501 test set by 7.77 mAP, and our multi-domain learning USR-3 model exceeds the market ReID benchmark with 57.47 mAP. To support the community, our code and training models are made available online.

An innovative ground-testing framework is presented to evaluate and compare the performance of diverse ATPR (accurate time-series prediction) methods. This framework specifically targets GARCH-based baseline models, by assessing one-step-ahead value-at-risk forecasting for risky financial instruments such as the S&P500. A key framework component involves generating synthetic datasets, reflecting various theoretical distributions and GARCH model alternatives. This setup enables the creation of a synthetic data-based testing framework, which aims to systematically analyze the complexity of data and the discrepancies between GARCH models and true data-generation processes. This framework facilitates an organized investigation of the data's characteristics and the GARCH model's behavior, resulting in a comprehensive grid of scenarios for ATPR method evaluation. This comprehensive analysis focuses on the impact of data distribution and model choices on the frequency and average prediction error. The suggested framework is illustrated with real-world data-based GARCH models, leading to valuable, data-independent insights that are particularly relevant for ATPR applications.

The study analyzes the effectiveness of various sampling methods (MCMC, Nested Sampling, and deterministic) for exploring pulsar timing array parameter space using simulated data that mimics the collaboration's sensitivity, as well as real data from PTAs such as PTA9 and SKA1.5. Using simulated data, nested sampling and NUTS exhibited comparable performance, making them suitable for further analysis. For datasets with limited computational resources, such as real data, simpler MCMLP algorithm proved to be a more practical option. Nested sampling and NUTS were found to be equally efficient for analyzing data from existing systems, while the examination of future systems like PTAs and SKA demonstrated the necessity of more advanced sampling methods due to the significantly larger size of the search space.

Using the "reversal" method, we have examined the mass dependence of hadrons using a combination of direct and indirect derivatives. This study is based on original data from lattice QCD simulations. The derivative reversal technique was employed to study the mass dependence of light quarks. This method has been found to produce highly precise results for a wide range of physics scenarios. The mass dependence of the pion mass and momentum found through the reversal method was then compared to the results obtained from Chiral Perturbation Theory. The findings indicate that the lattice results derived from the reversal method match very closely the expectations from Partial Wave Analysis up to ultraperipheral masses, which is a significant finding as it has not been observed previously.

Researchers agree that the accretion process in classical T Tauri stars fluctuates wildly, yet this behavior complicates our ability to draw reliable conclusions about disk development. A thorough investigation of the system SS Aur has utilized the observed variability in continuum and line spectra to shed light on the accretion process and the development of the disk. A notable decrease in the accretion rate around 2010, as well as its subsequent rise to 2014 and 2015, has been tracked. Analyzing the ratio of line to continuum flux in the H$\alpha$ spectrum has shown that the pre-wedge solution model is still applicable, with only slight variations. A comparison of the absolute line fluxes reveals a link between the continuum sources and the line sources. Our findings suggest that the accretion flow's kinematics have remained consistent, albeit with varying accretion rates. A cross-sectional analysis of the mass inflow into the central star has been conducted, indicating a highly irregular development of the disk in SS Aur, with more accurate observations necessary to establish a clear pattern of evolution.

The nature of luck's impact on economic outcomes significantly influences people's willingness to redistribute its benefits. Although both scenarios allow for redistribution in a certain sense, it is crucial to distinguish between cases where luck solely affects opportunities (where those who lose opportunities do not necessarily experience a financial loss) and cases where luck directly determines income. Empirical evidence from online surveys with 1,200 participants indicates that those who believe in equal opportunities are more willing to redistribute income among people with the same opportunities compared to cases directly affecting income, and this effect is even more pronounced among liberals. These findings also hold when considering relevant demographic variables such as age, gender, political ideology, and education level.

This study seeks to clarify the behavior of maps from complex projective space to a complete intersection variety under stabilization, demonstrating that its associated moduli space has a finite number of connected components. This implies the Euler characteristic of these stabilized maps remains consistent with a direct product structure. To begin, we establish a formula linking the Euler characteristic of stabilized maps to their unsimplified counterparts through a formula involving quantum K-invariants, previously introduced by Tseng and the author. This relationship allows us to derive an alternative proof of the formula's consistency with quantum orbifold Gromov-Witten invariants as seen from the perspective of K-theory. Additionally, we explore applications to flag varieties and obtain refined versions of results from Li and the author, as well as Ponsaing and the author.

Debugging data pipelines within machine learning workflows can be time-consuming and lead to significant losses in productivity and revenue.
These complex pipelines often involve numerous interconnected steps, making it difficult to pinpoint errors when they occur.
When faulty data is identified, tracing its transformation across the pipeline becomes a vital but challenging task.
To address this issue, we introduce DataScope, a data debug visualization tool that enables the simultaneous visualization of intermediate pipeline results and user-defined slices.
By comparing the users' input with actual pipeline outputs, DataScope helps pinpoint potential problems and understand the transformation of specific data elements across pipeline stages.
User studies indicate that DataScope significantly boosts data pipeline efficiency, particularly for complex pipelines with many interconnected stages.

Researchers have posited that some distinct radio sources within the core regions of globular clusters could be aggregates of multiple millisecond pulsars or neutron star X-ray binaries rather than singular objects. To validate this hypothesis, we identify four promising candidates for further study: M28, NGC 6441, NGC 6656, and Terzan 5. By examining the characteristics of their sub-components, specifically spectral indices and position angles, we aim to detect signatures of multiple neutron stars at these locations. Our results show evidence of neutron star binaries in three of these locations; however, the data for one candidate in M28 appears consistent with a cluster of millisecond pulsars. These cases are ideal for study using next-generation radio telescopes, notably with advanced interferometers like those under development for the Square Kilometre Array, which will be capable of further investigating their complex structures.

Effectively reconstructing hypergraphs from basic node and edge counts has significant implications for recovering hidden relationships in complex, partially observed networks. Despite numerous recent attempts, the initial problem's solvability in its general form remained unclear. This research presents an innovative algorithm capable of reconstructing a hypergraph from its projected counts with minimal reconstruction errors. The method leverages a series of projections to create a series of auxiliary hypergraphs, ultimately combining them into a final product graph that accounts for the varying weights of interactions. The results of simulations and a real-world application using a co-authorship network demonstrate the superiority of this approach over existing methods in achieving accurate reconstructions.

We have developed a novel approach for calculating ultrafast laser pulses emitted in a single direction. By applying our method to LHC laser pulses, we obtained an efficient solution for their complex, directional emission. Our method, which is fast and capable of precise results, is highly beneficial for particle accelerator applications where precision timing is critical. For the LHC, our approach reduced computational time to a mere 0.01 seconds on a standard CPU. Additionally, we have established an analytical solution for ideal lasers emitting in divergence angles greater than 45 degrees.

We've developed an exact method to calculate the correlation function for coherent light interacting with systems of atoms. This approach is suitable for any scenario where Rayleigh scattering dominates, allowing us to utilize the full effects of an intense laser, including its capacity to excite significant numbers of photons in the scattered light. Consequently, our technique can be applied to various situations including the scattering of light by individual atoms or ensembles. As a result of this study, we observed the characteristic linear dispersion of the first spectral line and the non-linear relationship with frequency observed for the second. The outcomes are consistent with previous theoretical and experimental findings on Rayleigh and Brilloian scattering.

Offline training for multiple agents interacting in complex environments presents significant challenges. Online training can be accelerated through Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT), a framework where each agent learns its own policy independently, yet they all learn from the same shared experience. Unfortunately, traditional SIT methods do not account for correlations between the actions of the agents, a problem exacerbated in tasks with many agents. To solve this, we introduce a new framework that enables each agent to build its own view of the environment by fusing observations through attention-based mechanisms. This allows them to effectively model the traditional SIT assumption while reducing complexity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by integrating it with the Attention Is All You Need (AIAYN) model, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods on multiple tasks.

This study introduces a Convolutional Neural Network structure for 3D image registration, leveraging label fields from two images to minimize transformation alignment differences, thus avoiding low-level intensity reliance. Leveraging the convolutional network's capability to learn generic alignment features across various datasets, the proposed method showcases remarkable results with limited training data. Furthermore, the convolutional network's ability to generate lookup tables for rapid alignment minization enables rapid inference in real-time.

A long-standing dispute concerns whether local interactions can generate nonlocal entanglement between two noninteracting particles. This debate is resolved in favor of real-world experiments observing the unexpected behavior of those same particles. We investigate various aspects of this conundrum, including the distinction between intrinsic and observable properties, and the relationship between a singular entanglement density, quantum steering, and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. As an example, we examine a scenario involving three particles, where two interacting particles subsequently entangle a third distant particle without direct interaction, and demonstrate that this phenomenon is a form of quantum swarming.

The complexity and critical nature of Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) data have led to the implementation of secure authentication protocols, including the use of Trusted Authority and blockchain technology, in various research studies. Scholars have explored multiple blockchain-based authentication protocols for IoVs, with some utilizing encryption to protect sensitive data within IoVs. However, these approaches either result in compromised security through leaked credentials or involve time-consuming decryption processes that hinder real-time access to secure IoVs. In response, this research studies the vulnerabilities of specific protocols, such as Liao's, and evaluates the use of Encrypted Identity (EI) within IoVs, in order to minimize credential leakage and enable efficient decryption through public keys in a single step, while maintaining IoVs' ability to authenticate with multiple servers simultaneously.

This study examines the observed evolution of the binary system V392 Persei following its November 8th nova outburst, utilizing the results from our spectral analysis. A comparison with a prior study by Drellakis et al., which presented both optical and ultraviolet spectra obtained on November 14th, revealed the system's transition through an super-soft state, lasting about a week. Following this period, the spectrum showed a return to the bare accretion disk state, which was typical before the outburst, but with notable differences in the soft X-ray spectrum. A model suggests that a massive, hot plasma sphere enveloping the white dwarf could account for this spectral profile.

To accurately assess quantum logic circuit performance as complex scaling trends are expected, precise benchmarking of quantum circuits is crucial. Leveraging the connection between the code distance and error rates of quantum circuits, we developed a method to evaluate the accuracy of quantum logic circuits using the toric code. Our study involves deriving fault-tolerance thresholds for both ideal and non-ideal quantum circuits by analyzing the code's distance. Focusing on transversal T gates, we tested different circuit depth options and applied linear regression to determine the code distance. We then derived the fault-tolerance threshold angles for each circuit, combining theoretical error rates with code distances. Notably, we found that some circuits exhibit lower error rates than anticipated due to redundant error patterns, providing a benchmark for the development of quantum computing technology.

This research examines a feedback encoding approach for spatial modulation systems with multiple transmitters and receivers in a uniform environment. In open-loop setups, it develops a closed-cluster encoding method that reduces overhead by exchanging bits of information between transmitters and receivers, effectively approximating closed-cluster results. With just two way-linkage channels, it demonstrates that the proposed encoding method outperforms a traditional pilot-based approach by several decibels. For near optimal signal quality, it also shows that the proposed system requires significantly lower pilot overhead compared to the two other approaches, reducing overhead by several decibels for two way-linkage channels while achieving closed cluster results. For single way-linkage systems, it develops an open-cluster encoding method and derives a closed-form expression to compare with a closed cluster approximation, showing that it outpers traditional pilot-based systems by several decibels while requiring lower pilot overhead by several decibels to achieve near optimal signal quality.

We developed an operator method to calculate surface currents generated by quda sources or boundary masses in lattice theories, which can be directly applied to simulate current-current correlators and currents under real chemical potentials. This technique was used to examine the robustness of surface currents and the influence of surface currents on phase diagrams near phase transitions in both bosonic and fermionic lattice theories. The study demonstrates that surface currents remain resilient to variations in da sources and demonstrate that current-current correlations can be accurately computed from two-point functions of volume currents. The operator da is flexible and can be adjusted to represent different values of surface flux. For real chemical potentials, the da operator is straightforward to implement. The robustness of surface currents was investigated for two models: an O(2) lattice model with a real chemical potential and a 3+1D fermionic lattice Hubbard model with a real chemical potential. The results show that surface currents are primarily determined by the da source, and their behavior is consistent under different quda sources. The study also indicates that surface currents can influence the local order parameter and may lead to the coexistence of phases with opposite currents. The effects of surface currents on the phase diagram are such that they cause a shift towards smaller values of the bulk coupling constant. The development of the da operator is straightforward and does not require any additional parameters. The study demonstrates that surface currents are robust to variations in da sources and that they can influence the phase diagram by causing a shift towards smaller values of the bulk coupling

In a study of Brans-Dicke theory, we investigate the behavior of asymptotically flat spacetimes and identify the conditions for photons to reach null infinity without being trapped by the outgoing radiation. To analyze this, we an- ticipate the behavior of trapped surfaces and examine both linear and fully non-linear trapped photons. Our findings reveal that trapped surface and photons disappear when the rate of change of the radiation drops below a critical threshold. Additionally, we discuss the implications of these results and compare them to trapped surface and photons in general relativity and the late-time behavior of trapped surface and radiation in time-asymptotically flat spacetimes.

Our investigation centers on the merger rates of Population III (Pop III) binary systems in ultraviolet optical (UVO) gravitational waves. These systems, consisting of black holes or neutron stars formed from Pop III binary stars, are analyzed here. We utilize a detailed radiative hydrodynamic simulation to understand how these binary systems evolve in an UVO background. The results show that UVO radiation influences when and where these mergers occur, peaking at a cosmological depth of z=3.6 and happening at a rate of $1.6 \cdot 10^{-3} year^{-1} Gpc^{-3}$. Therefore, UVO radiation needs to be taken into account in present and future gravitational wave detectors catalogs to accurately identify sources that formed from Pop III binary systems.

To accurately investigate the effects of timing precision on the inferred source distances of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), a novel apparatus has been created. This device, called the GRB simulator, mimics a real GRB by using precisely controlled electronics and a microprocessor to trigger scintillation detectors. However, it introduces intentional timing variations similar to those found in actual GRB data, where the time jitter is approximately 8.1$\pm$0.1 microseconds. The GRB simulator was used in conjunction with the Fermi/GBT and Fermi/LM instruments to investigate how well these instruments can pinpoint the source location of the simulated event, similar to locating the B553527 GRB. The results show that in cases of moderate and large time uncertainties, there is a significant discrepancy between estimated and true source localization accuracies, implying that current methods of estimating source localization based solely on data may be flawed due to inaccurate timing estimates.

A operator T_g on a subset of polynomials in the L^p space is considered if 1 < p < 2.  We demonstrate that when T_g is weakly compact on Pol(L^q space),  g must be 2-smooth if  g belongs to the BMOA_p subset,  and conversely,  when g is not 2-smooth,  T_g exhibits extreme irregularity. The given pattern extracts specific information from research papers, known as the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), which measures the progression of knowledge within a field, such as NLP. To identify relevant literature that builds upon previous findings, researchers can use the KQI by examining the citations in subsequent works. This technique can be applied repeatedly, enabling the mapping of the evolution of knowledge within a field, including the discovery of influential papers that lay the foundation for subsequent breakthroughs. Nevertheless, the efficacy of the KQI pattern relies heavily on the comprehensiveness and precision of indexing the papers included in the literature database, which, despite the efforts of numerous NLP groups to index relevant papers for their respective tasks, currently falls short of encompassing the vast body of existing literature. Given that modern NLP systems leverage deep learning, which enables the system to draw conclusions from a greater number of citation connections, the KQI is poised to yield more accurate and reliable results. As an example, T5 and BERT models are employed to demonstrate the KQI in action, resulting in several notable achievements, including the identification of seminal NLP papers omitted from the existing index, as well as the correction of erroneous or incomplete KQI indices resulting from neglected citations.

This paper extends our previous research in Opinion20cArXiv by analyzing a scenario where two nodes, Base Station and User, engage in simultaneous deception within a multi-user, unlicensed access wireless network. The initial findings from our previous research, which indicated that the deception probabilities of Base Station and User have an inverse relationship, remain consistent in this expanded scenario. Moreover, our research has identified optimal power allocation strategies for Base Station and User that maximize the likelihood of their successful, mutual deception. The results demonstrate that unrestricted power allocation leads to both nodes achieving their maximum, mutual deception probabilities, further validating our results in Opinion20cArXiv.

Integrating quantum light sources with topological edge modes offers a promising path for creating non-classical entangled lights. By placing quantum emitters near the interface of a topological photonic device, researchers can generate complex, synchronized photon states. In this study, we investigate a specific configuration where the emitters interact with a single edge mode, an interaction that can be strengthened through a resonant condition. We propose a straightforward detection scheme to identify the signature correlations of this scenario. Additionally, we examine how factors such as emitter placement and energy, as well as environmental noise, impact the emitter-mode system. Our research indicates that a wide range of emitter frequencies can maintain stable performance, and we have identified an optimal frequency range where the system is resilient to variations in frequency and placement.

This research focuses on how traffic lights impact the decision-making process of autonomous vehicles navigating city crossroads. The goal is to incorporate traffic signals into the learning process of connected automated vehicles using reinforcement learning techniques, specifically Q-Learning. The study models urban intersections and evaluates various scenarios to determine if traffic lights affect collision avoidance and travel time. The results indicate that traffic lights do have an effect on decision-making processes, with red phases influencing travel time more than yellow and green phases. The study also reveals that YR (Yellow-Red) and RG (Red-Green) phases affect travel time differently, with RG allowing for more optimal speeds compared to YR. The research suggests that reinforcement learning models can effectively take into account the impact of traffic signals on connected automated vehicles' movement.

Interactive learning techniques like model-based policy optimization have gained traction in solving complex text-based games. These projects demand significant computational resources to simulate vast numbers of text game instances, particularly when supporting visualizations are involved. To accelerate this process by a factor of 100 and provide additional testing tools, we introduce TextWorldExpress, an ultra-fast text game simulator with enhanced features such as batch control and customizable output options. Leveraging this high-performance platform, we refine our efficient action-selection method for exploring complex virtual worlds without prior knowledge, showcasing its effectiveness on Adventurer's Quest.

Recent studies into oriented hardware design for deep learning have demonstrated the effectiveness of factorized matrices in reducing storage requirements and enhancing computation speed. Building upon this concept, we introduce a novel HD architecture for RNN called FDHT-LSTM, which extends factorized Hadamard decomposition to both weight bias matrices and LSTM operations. FDHT-LSTM incorporates three optimized HD circuits for the LSTM operations, which significantly surpass traditional tensor-decomposed models by up to $3.2\times$ in HD usage, a $4.7\times$ increase in computation speed, while maintaining nearly $1.1\times$ energy efficiency and a $1.1\times$ increase in memory access speed. We validate the FDHT-LSTM design with 180nm CMOS technology, utilizing a pre-trained CMT 2-3M LSTM for image classification, which achieves $4.7\times$ higher clock throughput and $1.1\times$ energy efficiency compared to the traditional model.

Current cutting-edge NLP models rely to a large extent on massive, collection-based data. This research is hindered by significant challenges, encompassing high expenses, data privacy concerns, and an inability to keep pace with up-to-date information. To address these issues, I explore a more realistic and practical alternative, which focuses on continual NLP learning utilizing personalized, real-world data. I devise a number of sophisticated, sophisticated data augmentation techniques that draw upon sophisticated concepts from numeraire analysis, including formulaic transformations, queries to online repositories, multimedia resources, and simulated conversations. This study demonstrates these techniques through numerous scenarios, utilizing a variety of settings, which include mastering multiple languages sequentially, solving math problems, summarizing content, and providing accurate answers to complex questions. This study utilizes subjects as individual investors, which necessitate making accurate, timely decisions, which involve number-driven information.  To illustrate the validity of this approach, my research indicates that formulating investment decisions as a stage in NLP learning opens up new, exciting possibilities, which brings together the fields of NLP and number processing.  To prove the effectiveness of this stage, my research focuses on data efficiency and showcases how data augmentation techniques, which include numeraire transformations, online queries, multimedial augmentation, and dialogue-based interactions, which lead to substantial improvements in subject performance, which outperforms my baseline and the publicly available APIs. For theories with gravity that operate in anti-de Sitter space, we propose a specific form of the Weak Gravity Conjecture that can be expressed in terms of self-binding energy. This form is applicable to both simple compound states, as well as certain types of stable black holes. To validate our idea, we demonstrate that it holds for scalar field theories in anti-de Sitter space, confirming its validity. Furthermore, in曲 spacetimes, we obtain a self-binding energy rule that relates to the Weak Gravity Conjecture in Minkowski space. If the potential in these spacetimes meets certain anti-domination criteria, we find that this law is equivalent to the Weak Gravity Conjecture in anti-de Sitter space. As a result, we conclude that for scalar field theories in曲 spacetimes, the combination of these two laws can be represented by a single statement.

A model-space approach is introduced for estimating multiple target states within quantum Monte Carlo simulations. This model-space framework involves constructing a set of orthogonal trial wave functions representing the target states and performing importance sampling to estimate their collective Hamiltonian. By manipulating this model through the stochasticestimator approach, low-lying target states can be efficiently obtained without biasing the wave functions. The methodology demonstrates efficiency in calculating several orthogonal excited states and the ability to estimate states with different symmetries using a single trial wave function.

In the European energy market, grid operators require some market participants to adjust the power output of their generation units in order to maintain the stability of the electricity network. This mandatory measure, known as redisdispatch, often results in additional costs being passed on to consumers. The primary objective of this research is to examine the impact of an unordered, all-or-nothing order design on the efficiency of redisdispatch market design. The experiment conducted under the AllOrNothing treatment shows that grid operators can procure more cost-effectively, generating up to $2000 less in costs compared to the baseline scenario, OngoingNeedToProcure. Furthermore, this design reduces the likelihood of generation units being ordered to participate in redisdispatch, potentially leading to lower costs for market participants and, as a consequence, lower electricity costs for consumers. The design's apparent cost savings are further enhanced when combined with strategies targeting social welfare, such as redistributing the required order distribution among generation units, thus avoiding situations where some units are required to generate excessive amounts of additional power, while others are required to generate much smaller amounts, in line with the marginal cost principle. This study focuses on Galois groups within polynomial extension fields over $\mathbb{F}_p$. Specifically, it aims to determine when a given finite group can be associated with an irreducible polynomial whose roots generate that group. This involves analyzing whether a particular condition related to prime numbers can be rephrased in terms of solvability of a particular Diophantine equation. Building on this, it proposes that applying a conjecture made by Bateman and Horn about prime numbers can provide answers to our original question for a broader set of groups, as well as yield explicit examples of such groups for certain other settings.

To discover a new scalar at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), one can utilize the method of resonance reconstruction in diphoton decays. However, the presence of top quark pair production creates an irreducible background in this detection process, which is irremovable no matter what analysis is applied. As a result, the significance of any observed resonance is limited by the top quark pair production cross-section times the branching ratio (B) for Higgs decay into two photons ($\sigma\times$B). Given the LHC's capabilities at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV with 1 $fb^{-1}$ of data collected, we have shown that we can fully exploit this top quark cross-section constraint by employing a likelihood analysis that incorporates results from separate experiments (CMS and ATLAS) and removes the B term from the analysis as a free parameter in order to determine the mass ($M$) of the Higgs boson. We have found that with 95% confidence, we can establish a range for the Higgs boson mass of $M_t \pm 45$ $GeV$, which is 5 times larger than the intrinsic uncertainty of a top quark mass measurement with $pb^{-1}$ of data using separate techniques.

To assess new physics beyond the Standard Model, particularly within extended scalar sector theories, combining a precise Higgs diphoton decay rate measurement, an accurate Higgsstrahlung process cross section measurement, and the PP->γγ+ jets final state data could be crucial. Utilizing a combined likelihood function, we investigate the implications of such a test on two models, the Two-Higgs-Doublet and singlet-extended Two-Higgs-Doublet models. It's predicted that even with a highly accurate Higgs boson mass measurement (<1%), excluding the parameter space corresponding to medium or larger mixing angles in the sE2DM model, without exceeding the existing LHC limits, is possible at the 13 TeV energy level.

This study investigates the continuous far-ultraviolet data collected by the HST/STIS instrument at Saturn's south pole from July to September 2005. During this period, a North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV) characterized by a cold, dense region of the stratosphere similar to that observed at the Earth's north pole in winter and spring. In contrast to the Earth's polar regions, Saturn's pole experiences a warm, turbulent summer due to active heat sources rising from the underlying cooler months. The data revealed the NPSV's intense cold temperatures (~-240 K) sufficient to freeze hydrogen monoxide in the stratosphere. Additionally, the STIS observations showed the NPSV's impact on hydrogen Lyman-alpha emissions, which were 10 to 50 times more than observed at the equator and in the south polar stratosphere during the summer. These findings suggest that the NPSV's cold temperatures significantly influence hydrogen Lyman-alpha emissions in the stratosphere.

We investigate solutions to the Schrödinger equation within a bounded domain, focusing on a subcritical range of parameters. In this range, we demonstrate that solutions will reach infinite magnitude at a finite time under the condition that there is continuous energy concentration in the space and time near the boundary. If the parameter is lower than another critical value and the initial state has a non-negative property, we show that the solution will develop a singularity near the boundary of the space, thus providing a criterion for local well-posedness of the equation.

This paper introduces a fresh perspective from commutative algebra to study representations of algebraic groups in characteristic zero. It suggests investigating modules over Witt vectors in characteristic zero as modules defined through their reduction modulo $p$ in a particular way. A key limitation of this approach is that it lacks a derived category, which hinders its applicability in representing algebraic groups in characteristic zero.

A comprehensive investigation into a one-dimensional Hubbard model with varying site interaction strengths has been carried out, utilizing the exact diagonalization method to explore the metal-insulator transition. As site interaction increases, a function-based expression for spectral weight sum rules becomes invalid, indicating that this breakdown may determine the transition point. Detailed analysis of diagonal and off-diagonal weight distribution provides a framework for identifying the insulating state's character. Our findings suggest that the expected quadratic increase in off-diagonal weight is characteristic of metals, while insulators exhibit significantly reduced weights distributed across a wide range of values. Furthermore, calculated exact energy eigenstates in real space reveal a form consistent with that of an electron polaron.

Researchers have used a numerical method to investigate a quantum double dark-soliton in one-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensates with interaction parameters set to unity. Through minimization of the energy functional, a stable, periodic wave function has been obtained that accurately represents the density distribution of this quantum double dark-soliton. When unitless time is greater than -1.5, the quantum states of the two dark solitons exhibit density profiles resembling an 'M' and 'W' shape. Moreover, a precise equation has been derived to describe the depth of the quantum density well in the center. Researchers have also successfully matched their findings with those from a Gross-Pitaevskii equation model, demonstrating the ability of their approach to accurately capture the quantum density well's size and location in a dense region.

The paper describes an iterative process in the creation of symmetric multi-fold vector bundles, extending from double (symplectical) vector bundles to k-fold ones. It begins by defining symmetric k-fold vector bundles and then explores the concept of a premanifold within the framework of symmetric k-fold vector bundles.

A new method to derive Kirillov's measure from synthetic geometry is presented here. By examining the analytic measure defined on orbits of algebraic groups within a Lie algebra, we prove its relation to geometric measure through the use of analytic transverse measures in real algebraic groups. Furthermore, this paper establishes the connection between analytic and geometric measures for symplectic Lie algebras and explores the possibility of a similar relationship in solvable Lie algebras, using the Newton-Oderstedt normal form as an avenue of investigation.

A novel algorithm for x-ray spectrum recovery from single-shot measurements is introduced. The method utilizes an optimized cost function and gradient descent to achieve this objective. The algorithm's performance is evaluated with simulated and real experimental data, demonstrating superior results compared to conventional techniques. In x-ray experiments, where spectrum recovery is compromised due to energy-dependent detector saturation and limited sensor range, the algorithm's development was essential. However, with significant advancements in counting detectors, there is now an opportunity to eliminate filter overlays and optimize the spending on scientific detector areas, given the rising costs of bright source and x-ray spectrum recovery costs.

A new perspective on the quantum error correcting codes (QECCs) paradigm is introduced, drawing from disordered statistical mechanics models of classical systems. Considerable variations in the performance of arbitrary, non-fault-tolerant, stabilizer QECCs are examined when implemented on a randomly selected set of equivalent code ensembles. This analysis is conducted for codes constructed by encoding logical qubits into a subset of physical qubits within a larger quantum system, utilizing any stabilizer measurements set. Two distinct quantities are explored through this framework: the decodable region, representing the error rates correctable by the QECC, and the threshold, exploring its connection to a classical disorder critical point. Both concepts are shown to be encoded in the average free energy of the system's Hamiltonian, enabling their study through existing quantum field theory (QFT) tools for disordered systems, with potential for further investigation using replica field theory.

To explore the potential of tellurene-based spintronics and quantum-metrology, we investigate the impact of applied strain and surrounding dielectric on the electronic properties of LCAO calculated tellurene quantum wells.  By applying strain and adjusting dielectric constants, we find the non-trivial band-gap in these quantum wells can be maintained, similar to the behavior seen in monolayers.  However, unlike their monolayer counterparts, our results show the particle-hole asymmetry in tellurene quantum wells is sensitive to dielectric constants.  Despite this, the spin-orbit coupling remains consistent across variations in dielectric constants and lattice strains.  Notably, utilizing strain as a tool to manage electronic properties offers a feasible approach to achieving a significant band-gap in HBC quantum wells, making them suitable for practical applications.

The recent modification to the Dirac $\beta$-function adds a $\beta\eta(x)$ term to the standard equation, effectively capturing the phenomenon of fracture blockage. Despite its benefits, the primary challenge lies in the computational complexity caused by the numerous local minima resulting from the $\beta\eta(x)$ function, which can significantly slow down the simulation. To mitigate this issue, we have developed a method to identify and track the lowest local minimum, allowing for more efficient computation. Additionally, we have created a faster algorithm specifically tailored to locate and follow the desired minimum. Both of these solutions have been incorporated into the BFToys code to significantly enhance its performance. Our experiments have shown a substantial speedup of over two orders of magnitude, with minimal impact on accuracy, when using these new methods in comparison to the original code.

This study investigates spin-valves composed of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic layers, specifically looking at their vulnerability to the magnetization reversal process at low exchange fields. We observed that these devices exhibit two distinct states at moderately low fields, where one state can be easily switched with a minute magnetic field while the other requires a significant increase. A key insight from our research is that low-field domains behave like traditional single-stator spin valves, whereas high-field domains are subject to strong coupling with the adjacent magnetic layers. The KKM effect, which causes the domain wall to experience a moderate low-field state, can be attributed to this phenomenon. We also observed that the strong high-field domain state results in a significant impact on the magnetic hysteresis loop, specifically showing that the "upper" branch is dominated by these high-field domains while the "lower" branch is less affected. To eliminate these strong high-field domains, we developed a method involving the introduction of a gradient in the thickness of the adjacent magnetic layers, resulting in a more traditional single-stated hysteresis loop at low fields. The exchange of magnetic moments between the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic layers has a negligible influence on the two-state behavior, while introducing a moderate vacuum gap between these layers results in a slight exchange of magnetic moments that has a negligible impact on the two-state behavior.

In this paper, we explore the challenges of choosing a hypothesis and a course of action to avoid costly mistakes, particularly when multiple pieces of evidence require a decision under uncertainty. To tackle this problem, we focus on leveraging utility functions and decision-theory to choose the best hypothesis. We develop a probabilistic framework incorporating utility functions and hypothesis selection, followed by a practical approach using score functions and decision networks. Our method is demonstrated through simpler examples and a more complex case study in medical diagnosis, where we use hypothesis selection to balance the benefits of a correct diagnosis against the limitations of available testing resources. We evaluate our approach through simulations and compare it to other score functions, revealing that a novel network yields a more accurate and cost-effective decision than its alternatives.

The widespread use ofDiscsense is attributed to discourse markers, which facilitate smooth communication by signaling semantic relationships between sentences.  Unfortunately, existing datasets capturing complex semantic relations mediated byDiscsense are limited due to the scarcity of annotated data.  In contrast, the newly createdDiscsense dataset contains over 10,000 annotated instances of mediated semantic relations withDiscsense, consisting of short textual passages in which the first sentence poses an open-ended question and the second sentence provides the anticipated answer containing the targeted semantic relation.  Notably, theDiscsense dataset is distinctive in that it contains only positive samples, encompassing all ten GNILP-taxonomy relations, and is unique in that it is entirely multilingual with annotation in five languages, includingEnglish, Spanish, Portuguese, French, and Dutch.  Furthermore, theDiscsense dataset is accompanied by a comprehensive benchmark suite for modeling mediated semantic relations withDiscsense, while our initial exploration ofCRDiscsense subset with 10,000 EnglishMediated relations demonstrates the potential efficacy of existing capture models, while also serving as the foundational basis for more sophisticated relational capture models that leverage pre-trained language models such asDiscsenseBART.

A detailed investigation into nonradiative decay pathways of a fluorine donor electron in a silicon atom has been conducted using an electron spin based model. This study reveals distinct energy barriers to nonradiative decay, governed by configuration coordinate and isomerization rates, in line with the Mott-Seitz framework. Analysis shows the energy barrier arises from a transition point where certain decay pathways shift from being radiative to nonradiative. Notably, a reduction in isotope mass lowers this barrier significantly, making nonradiative decay pathways more viable in lighter silicon isotopes. These findings hold relevance for improving the security of communication systems based on quantum key distribution.

A new learning rule is proposed for training multilayer perceptrons, called a simple training algorithm. This algorithm determines error calculation automatically based on the network's operation during the training process, rather than relying on a formal derivation of the error function with respect to the weights, as required by backpropagation. In the algorithm, the error for each weight is represented as the product of two elements: the error resulting from an incorrect network output and the impact of that weight on the network's output. A significant advantage of this algorithm is its potential to yield a more accurate error computation compared to backpropagation, as it eliminates errors caused by the graphical formalism used to represent the multilayer perceptron's operation. Initial results indicate that its performance surpasses that of backpropagation.

A theoretical framework is proposed to analyze the stability of topological defects, such as magnetic skyrmions, in a way that accounts for their energy characteristics. The general model applies to any model defined within the context of homotopy theory, with specific examples defined within a coherent category framework. In a study of energy-minimizing configurations, it is found that a model's homotopy group determines the skyrmons' possible behaviors. Furthermore, an estimated lower-bound energy formula is developed to explain why certain configurations remain stable. This model is suitable for studying the dynamics and evolution of D-branes in topological field theories, leading to an exact expression for the energy in some scenarios initially described by Jackson in 2011.

Approximate methods to solve Schrödinger's equation for many-body systems, such as the HF method, have a long history. We've implemented the method and can now answer systems and molecules' questions with up to 50 electrons and hundreds of atomic orbitals in real time on a desktop computer. Our implementation ensures the Hermitian nature of the Fock operator at every self-consistent step, allowing us to handle large systems efficiently. As an extension to standard HF theory, we have a set of formulas to apply correlation corrections based on perturbation, ensuring the correctness of our results. Our method can be seen as a precursor to more complex correlation correction techniques, such as Coupled Cluster theory, and we have demonstrated its effectiveness in obtaining such corrections for systems and molecules with up to 50 electrons.

A sudden transition to synchronization in systems that aren't uniform has been discovered. As dynamic variability across a network of coupled oscillators heightens, there's an explosive synchronization transition to be observed. This phenomenon corresponds directly to structural disorder in the network itself. Our research reveals that both dynamic and structural heterogeneities drive the synchronization transition in an explosive manner. Furthermore, there's an optimal level of variability necessary to guarantee the occurrence of this transition.

This paper examines a non-convex and non-convex optimization problem, specifically one with a rank-deficient solution, and investigates its behavior under the projection of a manifold. We establish relationships between the local curvature and smoothness properties of the factorized objective and those of its original form. Under certain assumptions, we derive convergence rates for the gradient descent algorithm applied to a semipositive Stiefel manifold. However, these rates exhibit an exponential slowdown as the dimensions of the matrices increase, prompting us to propose a constant step-size rule to prevent this slowdown. We compare this new rule to the traditional one, and provide theoretical guarantees of linear convergence for low-rank matrix projections on a Euclidean cone and a Grassmann manifold. Additionally, we offer an algorithm that achieves this improved convergence rate.

The edge chromatic number $\chi_e(G)$ of a graph $G$ determines the minimum number of colors required for proper edge coloring. A long-standing conjecture from 1990 by Glebov, Kierstead, and Ku$\ell$ar posits that strong edge-coloring numbers of bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of 3 grow quadratically. This study presents a proof of this conjecture.

This article examines various identities related to Dirichlet L-functions at the point s=0. We derive new formulas connecting these identities to Gauss sums and classify relationships between them. In addition, we present explicit formulas for Gauss sums involving primitive and non-primitive Dirichlet characters. Furthermore, we investigate a character sum appearing in J. Zhao's research on zeta functions of curves over finite fields, and demonstrate that it can be expressed in terms of Gauss sums, particularly when the underlying modulus m is square-free.

The early universe was marked by the presence of substantial particle populations that left indelible imprints on the gravitational-wave background (GWB). Despite various strategies for GWB detection, a combination of approaches may be necessary for a complete understanding. One potentially useful method involves observing chemical composition as mediated by gravitational waves. Although initially thought to be unfeasible, it has been found that sub-feasibility studies can reveal new possibilities. It is now possible that combining such sub-observable constraints with traditional detection methods will lead to discoveries of significant scientific importance.

We present an analytical solution to the Biot-Savart equation for a helix in a fluid at a constant rate of rotation. Our model yields a precise description of the swaying motion of the helix as it moves through the fluid, which can be represented as a snowman-like structure. This analysis has significant implications for understanding swimmers designed in the shape of a helix, including biological organisms like bacteria and genetic material. As an example of this theory in action, we apply it to a helical bacterium, showing how it moves forward and rotates as it travels, and we also investigate the bacterium's flagellar interaction and the potential for it to effectively navigate its environment when including the rotating flagellum.

This study employs a genetic algorithm through a mechanism of evolutionary learning 
to investigate the issue of coordination games. In these scenarios, two agents 
attempting to reach a specific, yet unknown, target color must coordinate on the 
same hue to receive a reward. We collected and analyzed numerous independent 
run results to identify whether there exists a steady average difference in color 
choice from the optimal solution at Nash Equilibrium - specifically, whether 
this average difference tends to be less than half of the total available colors. 
This was tested for two approaches: one where both players update their strategy 
simultaneously (social learning) and another sequential learning scenario where 
only one player is influenced by the other's response. We also investigated 
whether this average difference is more prevalent in the social learning case 
than in its counterpart. In addition, we explored the average difference in the 
separate maximization of fitness and target location expectation. Finally, this 
study concluded without a clear answer to the following question: under what 
circumstances can the equilibrium achieved through co-evolutionary learning with 
a delay be considered successful?

To protect users on open platforms, it's vital to classify comments as either secure or risky. These assessments often rely on the extraction of key security concepts from text, but no prior studies have explored using Bidirectional LSTMs for this purpose. We've explored several strategies to enhance the BLM's ability to learn from textual data, focusing on using pre-trained embeddings and boosting techniques. Our goal was to evaluate their effectiveness in concept extraction, using a dataset of Facebook comments from users reporting product defects on a leading e-commerce site. We found that combining an bidirectional LSTM with a prediction layer and utilizing external word embeddings significantly improves performance, achieving the best results with no additional data preprocessing. This approach showcases the potential of BLMs for text-based concept extraction tasks.

We investigate the coexistence of two opposing behaviors in a dynamic voting process where agents hold either opinion $A$ or $B$. Influenced by an external magnetizing field, $A$ becomes more favorable; however, strong conflict or influence leads to unnecessary conformity. Combining precise computational simulations and theoretical analysis on random structures, we discover a striking balance: the average magnetization on these random structures mirrors that on complete networks where every $A$-supporter is adjacent to every $B$-supporter. Moreover, the average magnetization at equilibrium on these random structures is four times the square root of that of a pure Ising model influenced by the same external support for $A$. This dynamic reveals the potential for external influence to favor $A$ while resulting in a net preference for $B$ due to unquenched conflict.

This research offers a novel mathematical model for airborn COVID-19 virus dissemination, incorporating a crucial yet often overlooked aspect: respiratory droplets as a discrete entity subject to environmental conditions and defining properties such as size, which can result in droplet evaporation or settling on surfaces, thus affecting infection spread.
